In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. Specifically, for two or more spatial dimensions, the estimates' strict monotony ensures that the solution's maximum norm remains bound by the initial conditions' maximum norm. Furthermore, the estimates include a logarithmic factor in multi-dimensional space, aligning with recent findings. Conversely, in one spatial dimension, the estimates are strict and logarithm-free, reflecting prior results. Ultimately, the 2D case yields nearly optimal logarithmic estimates, with corrections applicable to a broad class of similar hydrodynamic systems, including the Quasi-Geostrophic equations and the Beltrami equations. The primary method employed involves the use of a Littlewood-Paley decomposition in combination with a four-step commutator method. Additionally, the 2D results heavily rely on the maximal regularity of the Navier-Stokes equations' linearized form, proved using a Fourier multiplier approach and a novel 'ping-pong' correlation argument. In one spatial dimension, the estimates' strict monotony is proven via a correlation argument tied to the solution's center of mass dynamics. In multi-dimensional space, the estimates' strict monotony is proven via a divergence-based correlation argument, coupled with a Fourier multiplier approach designed to analyze the solution's translation dynamics. This general correlation argument can be applied to a broad class of similar parabolic equations, including the heat equations with nonlinear damping and the Beltrami-Laplace equations. In addition, the results' breadth can be extended to a class of nonlinear equations describing incompressible fluid flow in complex media with friction. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of synthetic cells with actual cell growth, mitosis and lung cancer cells exhibiting complex protrusions. Our results demonstrate the generation of realistic synthetic cells with similar characteristics to real cells, including the production of plausible topological cell shape sequences in three-dimensional space over time. Moreover our approach enables the creation of realistic synthetic topologies and provides a flexible representation for high-resolution high-resolution imaging of cell shapes. Finally we also observe that our trained model can be used to create new and unseen cellular shapes by adjusting the latent code without needing real-world examples making it suitable for generalization. To achieve these results a new reward scheme is proposed that optimizes fluidd's fitness function to provide a direction for generation as well as a new loss function that measures the difference in fluorescence between real and synthetic cells to constrain the generation of new synthetic topologies. Furthermore the developed methods can be applied to other cellular processes such as locomotion by controlling and optimizing shape and topology to guide cell shape and topology generation. Recent advancements in spatial AI have led to significant breakthroughs using Cartesian coordinate systems. Despite their efficacy, this research investigates multiple alternative spatial representations that can facilitate more inherent spatial perception and navigation. Focusing on man-made environments, this study examines non-Cartesian approaches including topological models derived from occupancy grids and graph navigation with node positional distributions. Building on previous work, this paper introduces a unified framework for generating topological models and presents an effective training method for learning navigation policies on complex mazes using few demonstrations. Additionally, this study highlights the potential of positional distribution models in regulating the exploration-ex Exploitation trade-off in goal-directed navigation. We begin by demonstrating the strict reversibility of these ECMC algorithms in a detailed mathematical argument, which justifies their suitability for simulations requiring precise reliability. We then adapt an existing ECMC algorithm for a 2D Lennard-Jones system and assess its practical implications for molecular simulations, specifically in the case of a neon-like system. This analysis encompasses a comprehensive examination of the following key aspects: step acceptance rates, linear progression, temperature scaling, equilibrium conditions, persistent dynamics, energetic evaluations, and difference calculations. This in-depth assessment allows us to compare the conventional Metropolis algorithm with the ECMC method, highlighting their respective advantages and drawbacks. Notably, the ECMC method exhibits greater efficiency in terms of computational speed, but lacks the straightforward interpretability of the Metropolis algorithm. Notably, certain variables, like displacement steps and chain links, play a crucial role in understanding the performance of the ECMC algorithm. We also investigate multiple strategies for advancing the chain to uncover the optimal path, emphasizing the potential of directional moves to enhance computational speed and efficiency. Ultimately, the combination of our detailed mathematical argument and thorough computational analysis enables a precise evaluation of the ECMC method's performance, paving the way for its potential applications in coating simulations. We anticipate that the insights gleaned from this study will encourage the development of new, innovative Monte Carlo algorithms for complex simulations. Additionally, we make available our computational code and analytical math for the benefit of fellow researchers and researchers. The challenge of Sound Event Localization and Detection involves pinpointing the presence of multiple overlapping sounds, accurately categorizing their types, and estimating their source locations. Recently, neural networks have emerged as the leading solution for this problem, with Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks being a prominent architecture used in such applications. A novel system submitted to the 2020 Challenge for Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events uses a specific type of Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network with rectangular filters, optimized for recognizing distinct sound features. By employing data augmentation through channel rotation and reflection in the First Order Ambisonic domain, the training dataset was expanded, allowing for more robust performance and improved Accuracy in locating sound sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach surpasses baseline results, significantly reducing Error Rates and increasing F-scores for location-aware detection. Furthermore, the implementation of an augmentation technique called Bigger Sensor Field (BSF), which simulates a wider field of view by amassing more Ambisonic channels, boosted the MIREX F-scores by 8.2% for location-aware detection and 6.3% for scene-classification. A corresponding source code is available on the GitHub repository, along with the challenge's dataset and evaluation tools. Moreover, a tutorial and data-augmentation code for Transformable Convolutional Recurrent Networks can also be found there. To our knowledge, this method of data augmentation, as well as the use of Convolutional Recurrent Networks in combination with Ambisonic augmentation, represents an original contribution to Sound Event Localization and Detection. For this reason, the approach has been designated as the Challenge Baseline for the 2021 competition. In traditional communication systems, signal interference is generally seen as unwanted noise that distorts transmitted signals, but a new perspective has emerged where multiple transmissions occur simultaneously and potentially benefit from one another. Various wireless applications have taken advantage of this principle, as evidenced by non-orthogonal multiple access and other methods such as joint source-channel coding, computational codes, and federated learning, which were initially influenced by techniques like network coding and consensus algorithms. The fundamental thread running through these applications is the superposition property, allowing multiple signals to be transmitted concurrently, thereby yielding benefits in areas like security, mobility, localization, and energy harvesting. The applications outlined above, despite existing independently in literature, can bring significant improvements in IoT enabled remote monitoring systems, as demonstrated by a detailed analysis in this study, utilizing a hospital as a case study to showcase their merits in mobile IoT applications, particularly in remote monitoring systems, as exemplified by a stochastic mobility model for hospital patients and staff. The study further delves into how underlying technical challenges can be addressed to achieve substantial practical benefits in such systems, as exemplified by a high-density wireless sensing system. The study presents an innovative consensus-based deep learning framework for designing wide area wireless sensing systems, showcasing its substantial practical benefits in both low and high-density scenarios compared to conventional methods. The study's findings are grounded in both theoretical and practical arguments and benchmarks, as demonstrated by numerous Monte-Carlo simulations and practical experiments. The research was inspired by three key breakthroughs: 1) the development of an electronic money system, 2) the construction of an integral wireless sensor network in a large building, and 3) the creation of a wide area wireless sensing system that spans an entire city. The study contributes to the existing literature by introducing a new system design approach inspired by these applications and showcases its benefits in wireless sensing systems, as evidenced by both numerical simulations and practical experiments, thereby illustrating the vast potential for designing new wireless communication systems that cater to a wide range of IoT enabled remote monitoring systems. The study presents an introduction to simultaneous transmission and its various applications, as evidenced by system design and experimentation, marked by two key milestones - the development of Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access and the creation of a wide area wireless sensing system. The study achieves this goal by examining the different methodologies and outcomes associated with simultaneous transmission, as exemplified by network coding, federated learning, computational codes, and joint source-channel coding, and demonstrates their distinct approaches, benefits, and system design requirements. The study marks an important transition from literature to practical applications

Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a crucial component derived from the short time Fourier transform (STFT). The traditional approach focuses on the maxima of spectrogram peaks. Recent research has shifted towards exploring minima and zeros, revealing links to Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs). Despite these connections, theoretical analysis of GAF zero sets remains challenging due to their complex stochastic structure. Statistical methods applied to spatial data are used but primarily understood empirically. This work explores the geometric stochastic properties of spectrogram level sets, providing rigorous theorems that underpin an innovative spectrogram level sets approach for signal detection and estimation. This approach, rooted in a concrete statistical framework, is implemented as an alternative to the classical peak-tracking method. Comparative assessments are conducted, demonstrating that level sets perform similarly to peaks in most scenarios. However, peak-tracking is more robust in the presence of interference; thus, both methods complement each other. Spectrograms level sets prove beneficial for signal detection and estimation across various scenarios, yielding superior results in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, this approach outperforms peak-tracking in two distinct case studies. Additionally, both methods are advantageous compared to existing signal processing techniques for signal recovery and source localization. This contribution offers a versatile and efficient Spectrogram Level Sets technique that serves as a standalone tool or complements peak-tracking methods to enhance spectrogram-based signal analysis and estimation. Moreover, this work provides theoretical underpinnings that facilitate the development of new statistical tools for Gaussian analytic functions. These results pave the way for novel applications in signal processing, as evidenced by the significant performance gains achieved in relevant signal processing challenges. Finally, this study proposes a novel Spectrogram Level Sets technique that complements existing peak-tracking methods while providing a standalone tool for spectrogram-based signal analysis and estimation. Moreover, this work provides rigorous theoretical justification for Gaussian analytic functions, providing crucial insights into their geometric-stochastic properties. This theoretical understanding can be applied to various Gaussian analytic function representations, including the STFT, to provide concrete statistical insights into spectrogram-based signal analysis and estimation. In particular, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of Spectrogram Level Sets in signal detection, estimation, and localization, as well as providing valuable comparative insights into peak-tracking methods. Furthermore, this work offers a broader perspective on the potential of Gaussian analytic functions in signal processing, highlighting significant performance gains in relevant challenge studies. Ultimately, this research contributes to the ongoing quest to derive meaningful statistical properties from Gaussian analytic functions that can inform spectrogram-based signal analysis and estimation.

A novel module is presented, allowing researchers to model complex systems influenced by random forces impacting particle motion, a phenomenon anticipated to occur within environments like turbulent planetary disks and the remnants of planetesimal disks. This module streamlines the creation of synchronized noise with variable intensity and auto-correlation time for each particle, with low memory requirements, and is available at no cost through the REBOUNDx supplementary module suite. Despite being designed with smaller codes in mind, this noise model remains compatible with even the largest, high-precision simulations, and has been thoroughly tested with a range of target applications in mind. Furthermore, benchmark simulations have been conducted to gauge the impact of noise intensity on final particle distribution under various thermodynamic conditions. These studies highlight the significant advantage of using the presented method over alternative approaches, and demonstrate its high level of flexibility and versatility. Finally, guidance is provided on properly assigning physical parameters, such as sound speeds and eddy viscosities, to the noise model, ensuring accurate modeling of the turbulent environment. Although primarily designed with drag forces in mind, this module can be used in conjunction with a variety of force algorithms to model a broad range of astrophysical systems. Additional resources, including demo codes and further information about the module's functionality, can be accessed via the REBOUNDx website at https://reboundx.github.io/NbodyNoiseModule/. A Python version of the noise model is also available for use at https://reboundx.github.io/NbodyNoiseModule/docs.html. A Git version, rebranching from the original REBOUNDx module, can be found at https://github.com/jaslele/NbodyNoiseModule. A separate, standalone C version of the noise model is provided at https://github.com/jaslele/NbodyNoiseModule-C. Both versions allow researchers to model dynamic systems influenced by random forces. Ultimately, this approach holds great promise for simulating a wide range of astrophysical systems, and holds potential for future extension to include thermodynamic effects. Examples of such dynamic environments include the turbulent discs surrounding stars, discs containing massive objects and high-density particles, and the discs resulting from the destruction of planetary bodies within these environments. Examples of included noise types are the white noise, red noise, power spectral density noise, locally interpolated simulation, and Stratonovich noise. Additional resources, including demo codes and further information about the module's functionality, can be accessed via the REBOUNDx website at https://reboundx.github.io/NbodyNoiseModule/. A Python version of the noise model is also available

Key aspects of quantum science include precise measurement and feedback mechanisms from experimental to quantum information realms. Implementing feedback control is often complicated by the need to observe quantum systems without disturbing them, particularly when working with small-scale systems. This thesis tackles the challenge of feedback control by leveraging the capabilities of ultra-short pulse spectroscopy and modulation, enabling the precise manipulation of magnetic properties of light on a femtosecond timescale. This methodology yields an unparalleled level of sensitivity to optical reflections, enables rapid adjustment of optical characteristics, and paves the way for new forms of light-matter interaction and optical regulation. To demonstrate this method's potential, we develop a, precision optical sensor that detects the magnetic properties of light and serves as a high-precision detector of optical signals, as well as a foundation for advanced forms of optical regulation and the efficient transmission of data through optical fibers. This achievement opens doors to new applications in quantum technology, including the use of spin waves as information carriers and the ability to modulate light with adjustable timing. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework for femtosecond pulse modulation and demonstrate its implementation with the aid of magnetic nanoparticles, as well as spin-orbit coupled gases. Ultimately, this method enhances our ability to control quantum processes on an ultra-short timescale and paves the way for groundbreaking innovations in the field of quantum technology. To date, this method remains the fastest known means of adjusting optical signals on a femtosecond scale, boasting more than 100 gigahertz of frequency modulation capacity and near-total conversion of light into spin waves with minimal energy loss. Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on behavior IDs that are based on past user-ad interactions. However, using behavior IDs is impractical when predicting CTR for new ads without prior interactions. To overcome these limitations, our approach utilizes ad visuals to enhance the performance of CTR prediction models. We achieve this by converting each ad into a set of visual identifiers that reflect its content. These identifiers are then used to generate visual embeddings, which can improve CTR predictions. The process of generating these identifiers is cast as a supervised quantization problem. Due to the absence of labels for commercial images, we instead utilize text descriptions to optimize our image extractor and create effective visual identifiers. Since traditional hard quantization operations are non-differentiable, we employ a softened quantization approach to support end-to-end network training. The resulting visual identifiers can then be paired with historical user-ad interactions to learn corresponding embeddings. Notably, the embedding derived from the visual content of an ad can effectively generalize to new ads. When paired with traditional ad behavior IDs, the performance of CTR models can be further enhanced. Experimental findings confirm the efficacy of our approach in advancing CTR models. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed functional networks are consistently present across all sites, and inter-site effects were relatively minor. Through Monte-Carlo simulations, we evaluated the effects of multisite data on our ability to detect changes and predict group labels, revealing that our ability to detect changes was minimally impacted, but prediction accuracy did decline slightly compared to single-site studies of equal sample size. Our results imply that large sample sizes can make multisite research in rs-fMRI a viable option. In a related study, we demonstrated the value of incorporating multisite data in mapping resting-state functional connections in young, healthy individuals, and our data is now available online for further research. In addition to our primary research, we conducted an extensive examination of the effects of scanning parameters, such as resolution, on connectivity measures and the detection of group differences. Our analysis suggests that higher resolution can minimize the detection of false positives while reducing the detection power for genuine effects. Notably, our research justifies the use of moderately sized functional auto-correlation values as valid reference criteria for rs-fMRI research involving healthy individuals. Our findings will serve as a foundation for further research, addressing additional systemic biases that our data may reveal, as well as investigating the effects of various scanning protocols on connectivity measures and the detection of group differences. In addition, our results may be used to inform future multisite research in rs-fMRI, focusing on clinical populations. Decentralized learning technique, federated learning, has a major limitation that remains to achieve optimal performance due to statistical data discrepancies. Overcoming this issue, researchers have focused on personalizing machine learning models, which typically rely on having complete datasets, an unrealistic scenario given data labeling complexities. When models receive limited labeling, they experience reduced adaptability to local distributions and, subsequently, suffer performance degradation. Addressing this issue with partially labeled data challenges, our proposed FedUnlabelFromScratch approach eliminates the need for complete labeling by utilizing labeling efforts more efficiently. By separating learnable and non-learnable components of a neural network, it enables separating distribution parameters and reduces the impact of unlabelled data issues. Our approach enables sharing of these separable parameters without compromising on performance by using a novel ratio objective that minimizes discrepancy between the shared and local parameters' distributions. This method enables improved personalization without sharing private data, as validated by our experiments on benchmark datasets and complex real-world applications. Moreover, our analysis shows that the ratio objective reduces uncertainty associated with a classifier's posterior distribution, resulting in enhanced generalization capabilities. Our approach provides improved robustness to data noises, excessive regularization, and incorrect class assignments, exhibiting superior performance compared to existing personalized federated learning methods. Our code is accessible via https://github.com/ajaybansal91/FedUnlabelFromScratch. Jegatomtanon et al. (2020) provided an important foundation for decentralized learning from scratch with partial labeling; our study builds upon this work to enhance their model's representational capabilities. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and angular momentum transfer.  The subsequent mass ejection by viscous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence begins roughly 300-500 milliseconds post-merger, persists for several hundred milliseconds; meanwhile, a magnetosphere is formed around the black hole, producing a focused strong electromagnetic outflow lasting about 0.1-2 seconds.  The model without equatorial-plane symmetry shows inverted magnetic polarity in the magnetosphere, caused by a magnetorotational instability dynamo, whereas a model initially comprising toroidal fields demonstrates a late post-merger stage characterized by a tilted disk and magnetosphere, due to anisotropic mass ejection effects, potentially shortening the Poynting-luminosity phase to 0.5-2 seconds.  The initial eccentricity affects the timing and intensity of both mass ejection and Poynting-luminosity phases but does not alter the general picture; an eccentricity of 0.01-0.04 is found to yield a range of 0.5-2 seconds for the Poynting-luminosity phase.  The Poynting-luminosity radiation's total amount emitted is estimated to be 0.1-10% of neutron star binding energy, rendering it undetectable by GW170817's emitted gamma-ray emission.  Consequently, a potential detection of a post-merger electromagnetic emission, in combination with a late late-time emission decrease, might indicate a black hole-neutron star merger occurrence.  Furthermore, a Possibility of a black hole-neutron star merger contributing to a short gamma-ray burst's origin remains.  The Possibility of identical processes governing diverse gamma-ray bursts, including both GW170817's emission and certain short gamma-ray bursts, is also presented. Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to increase with collision peripherality. Calculations accounting for effects of background that arise from charge and anisotropic flow patterns, while able to partially explain observed results, did not capture the entirety of the CME signal measurements. A comparison of the CME and mixed-harmonics correlator signals further highlighted the significant influence of background contributions. The outcomes of these research efforts may be used to interpret future experiments conducted at higher energy levels with larger collision numbers. Additionally, the results underscore the necessity of properly controlling systematic errors in calculations for corrections for background effects. Finally, the study highlighted the importance of further investigating the sources of these background effects, specifically impact of flow anisotropies, within the context of relativistic quantum field theories. The research also included an assessment of the sensitivity of the CME effect to assumptions made about the behavior of quark-gluon plasma at finite chemical potential and temperature. The outcomes of this analysis confirm the CME to be distinct from other effects influencing charge-dependent correlations in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. The study further proposed modifications to be applied to CME effect calculations to minimize reliance on approximate transport coefficients when estimating key physical properties such as the collision rate and relative amounts of quark and anti-quark interactions. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning framework, allowing multiple organisations to co-create and train a robust ML-based intrusion detection system without compromising their data's privacy. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to collect and process network traffic data in a common format that can be used to develop an effective ML model. Moreover, to address the data's uneven distribution across organisations and a lack of control over the number of clients and data instances, a novel federated learning approach is employed, using specialised neural network architectures. Our solution is evaluated using three intrusion detection datasets and compares its effectiveness against several established baseline models. Results indicate that the proposed framework achieves outstanding accuracy and performance for heterogeneous data sources, significantly outperforming traditional baseline methods by 88.5% for imbalanced datasets and 72% for balanced datasets. Conversely, models designed for balanced datasets but applied to imbalanced datasets experienced a substantial decline in performance, highlighting the importance of data preprocessing and scaling techniques. To address the issue of missing feature values, different approaches are evaluated, and the one that yielded the best results used a combination of imputation and feature extraction techniques. Ultimately, the proposed framework presents a versatile and efficient ML-based intrusion detection system, capable of tackling multiple key challenges during the training process. These findings contribute to the existing literature on federated learning and ML-based intrusion detection, presenting novel and practicable strategies to address critical difficulties. Moreover, our solution presents a groundbreaking way for organisations to collaborate on developing effective ML models without compromising their data's privacy. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even overshadowing the overall task duration. Our analysis reveals that the optimal approach for a robot performing tasks in a confined space involves a distinct sequence, independent of the route, making the primary concern reducing the level of congestion or interference between tasks. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel algorithm to quickly and effectively determine a suitable task sequence, ensuring a substantial decrease in processing time while maintaining a low error rate, far exceeding the traditional TSP solutions. This innovative approach generates a task sequence in under 10 milliseconds, achieving an error rate of less than 1% and reducing the average completion time by a factor of 300 times. Furthermore, we validate the optimal nature of the sequence through theoretical justification and mathematical proof. In addition, we have developed a Q-learning based reinforcement learning method that searches for an optimal sequence with minimal interference between tasks, achieving an average error rate of less than 2% and reducing the level of interference by a factor of 100 times in the worst case. In contrast, the standard TSP solutions result in an error rate of 14% and 20%, respectively, with little to no improvement in reducing the level of congestion. In order to facilitate the comparison of different algorithms, we have introduced a custom metric to assess the quality of the sequence, which takes into account both the time taken to complete tasks and the level of congestion or interference between them. Thorough experiments have been conducted across a range of environments and scenarios, involving both static and dynamic task sets, as well as different robots and bases, where our new algorithm has proven to be superior to the existing solutions in reducing the time taken to execute tasks and the level of congestion or interference between them. The approach entails comparing the outputs of five prominent search engines, comprising four Western and one non-Western search engines, for both English and Russian language queries. The research reveals significant variation in source diversity according to language, with English search queries yielding more diverse results. Additionally, the analysis discovers that the video-sharing platform YouTube dominates the search outputs of the Western search engines evaluated. Interestingly, the sampled search engines exhibited minimal bias toward their respective parent companies. Our study's findings highlight potential explanations for these patterns, including differing ranking algorithms, intended audiences, and revenue models of the various search engines. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, and determining the optimal parameters that minimize these delays, this study proposes two distinct operating modes, correlation mitigation and delay optimization. While both protocols can effectively counteract the impact of interference correlation when there is a balanced distribution of active nodes, ALOHA exhibits a higher capacity in the scenario of uneven node activation rates. Furthermore, this study finds that an anti-correlated mode can be achieved when frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA adjust their parameters accordingly, and identifies the key factors that differentiate these protocols in terms of their capacity in both correlation mitigation and delay optimization scenarios. This study also establishes a relationship between the variance of local transmission delays and the variance of interference, and reveals an inequality that connects these two quantities, which holds for both protocols. Notably, this inequality can be expressed as $\mathrm{Var}[D] \leq 2 \mathrm{Var}[I]$ for both correlation mitigation and delay optimization scenarios. This study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, offering practical recommendations that can improve wireless network performance and illustrating the benefits of parameter adjustment in counteracting the adverse effects of interference correlation. In addition, this study computes the minimum average local transmission delay for both protocols, yielding important results that can inform wireless system design. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with class-balanced regularization in the model re-training process. Comprehensive experiments on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and robust self-supervised methods on graph-related tasks. The source code of InfoGNN can be found at https://github.com/IndigoPin/InfoGNN.

Specifically, we contrast the efficiency of two approaches: assigning a single set of features to each spatial location (pixel-wise) versus deriving distinct sets of attributes for defined regions (patch-wise). Our research in the latter domain yields a straightforward, extensively tested model that outperforms current standards in video classification. Moreover, this approach reduces the computation required per data sample, thereby substantially decreasing training and evaluation times. Ultimately, cluster-based patch-wise feature extraction provides a more adaptable and scalable solution for complex, low-level data processing applications like video processing. Our model's performance also extends to other attribute extraction tasks beyond video classification, including image analysis and editable string recognition. Last, the low-dependency nature of this model allows for seamless integration into existing cluster-based pipelines for further acceleration. As a result of this investigation, we introduce EvalLib, a comprehensive library for cluster-based machine learning model evaluation and SFrame, a versatile, cluster-compatible data representation framework. A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, utilizing a dual-objective resource allocation technique that balances the requirements of multiple USB devices and a wireless information and power transfer (W IPT) access point. To optimize this system, we develop a dual of the Birkhoff von Neumann algebraic quantity method for allocating resources, demonstrating the benefits of our approach through comparative simulations. Furthermore, our solution aligns with real-world technology by complying with IEEE 802.15.3e Waveform 1 specifications, thereby showcasing its applicability to real-world applications such as virtual reality head-mounted displays. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in diverse environments, we conduct simulations under different weather conditions, showcasing its capability to function optimally in both stable and dynamic environments for a VR application using IEEE 802.15.3e. Focusing on energy-harvesting devices, our results indicate that our allocation strategy can increase average network throughput by up to 105%, while enhancing end-to-end delay performance by up to 60%. This evidence highlights the efficacy of our proposed algorithm in overcoming weather-related challenges and improving overall system performance for low-data-rate applications such as VR head-mounted displays. This study investigates chiral aspects in 2-dimensional spacetimes with a capping time structure. We examine the characteristics of chiral observables and develop the framework for representing these observables in Hilbert spaces, while ensuring they have the property of being locally undetermined. We further establish the link between these constructs and those in the traditional algebraic QFT approach, while also introducing a category of bundles that describe the interconnection between chirality structures and spacetime configurations. Our work culminates in a strategy for building a capping time version of the Haag-Kastler net, constructed from any given theory that incorporates a time structure. To support this effort, we must verify that certain commutators associated with the field operators of the theory generate a family of local algebras at each time, which is a crucial aspect in this context. We also demonstrate that the resulting constructed theory is type-II compatible with respect to the original theory it is based on. Additionally, this study sets forth a strategy for building a capping time version of the Wightman field, while ensuring it adheres to standard field positivity requirements. We prove that this constructed field possesses a mass gap, along with other supporting requirements such as hyperconvexity and reflection positivity at each time. Notably, this study reveals that the constructed theory exhibits a mass gap if the original theory also has one, although the mass gap in the constructed theory may be larger than in the original theory. We examine specific Haag-duality consequences that arise from this construction, while also introducing and proving a generalized version of Haag-duality theorem for 2-dimensional spacetimes with a capping time structure. Furthermore, our work also allows us to investigate chiral Haag-duality in this context, while also responding to an open problem posed by D. Pratici. We show that the constructed theory exhibits chiral Haag-duality if the original theory already does so, provided that a certain condition involving the central charge is met. If the central charge is zero, we demonstrate the existence of chiral Haag-duality through the use of a different construction involving spatial structures and decoherence, while also introducing and proving a Haag-Kastler net dualism consequence. We examine specific Haag-duality consequences that arise from this construction, which includes the existence of the Haag-Kastler net dualism. Furthermore, our work allows us to investigate chiral Haag-duality in this context, while responding to an open problem posed by D. Pratici.

Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and achieved notable results, demonstrating a 4% improvement in accuracy and F1-score over standard RGB image performance, as well as enhanced performance compared to existing methods. Notably, our technique achieves this improvement while maintaining low false positive rates, which is critical in clinical settings due to the need to prioritize true positive detections of smoke over false positives to ensure effective removal. In a real-world context, we have successfully applied our method to facilitate smoke detection in laparoscopic surgery video datasets, which has potential for use in training neural networks for this application. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. The outcome provides an alternative to existing robust gate designs for trapped-ion quantum computers, particularly those employing large, linear arrays of ions. The GMMS gate has also been adapted for other optical trapping systems, offering potential applications in experimentations and future quantum computations utilizing these systems.  Additional work has been done to integrate this gate into the overall quantum computation process, the efficiency of which is examined using the standard benchmarking metric in the field, finding that for long chains, certain methods of computation may be susceptible to errors due to the limitations of current frequency stabilization technology. Conversely, protocols that rely on repeated applications of single-qubit operations and gate connections see significant improvements in efficiency as the length of these chains increases. Specifically, these chains of ions see reductions in efficiency losses from twenty-five percent for chains of three ions to nearly fifty percent for chains of thirty-three ions when using the conventional decomposition method. We have also integrated this gate into an efficient quantum simulation program, finding that the same efficiency limitations exist, but see significant reductions in computation time compared to traditional methods of quantum simulation due to the exponential relationship between chain length and the standard decomposition time. Specifically, this chain of thirty-three ions sees reductions in computation time of over three hundred fifty percent for local interactions, over two thousand percent for entangled chains, and over eight thousand percent for three dimensional structures. The successful integration of the GMMS gate also allows for the exploration of new quantum computation methods that take advantage of local interactions and reduce the complexity of future quantum computations based on trapped ions. In conclusion, this research delves into the principles and efficiency of a robust frequency-resistant quantum gate, while also examining potential applications in the near term, and future far term, scenarios of trapped-ion quantum computing. The main content of this research has been shared at CQME 2020, also known at the 2020 International Conference on Quantum Computing and Measurement. Researchers have developed new methods by combining the concepts of multivariate Gaussian processes with graphical models, allowing for relationships between individual components of the process to be visualized and analyzed. Two specific approaches, functional Gaussian graphical models and graphical GPs, provide different frameworks for understanding these relationships, the former using a mathematical expansion to describe the process, and the latter by combining smaller processes in a specific order. Our study connects these two models by proving that certain functional models with selected variables can be seen as graphical GPs. This finding is used to show the equivalence between truncating certain functional models and stitching lower-order GPs. These theoretical relationships allow for the creation of new statistical tools that can maintain both overall relationships and individual distributions within the multivariate process, when conforming to specific structural assumptions about inter-variable connections. One such tool, a procedure for model selection, uses a metric that balances the complexity of assumed relationships and the accuracy of fit to the data observations, making this method applicable to data with low sample sizes. Our method's effectiveness is confirmed through simulations and real-world studies that allow for the identification of relationships and individual distributions within three-dimensional data sets, and further confirms these inferences through confidence intervals and comparative analyses with other models. Two real-world studies using breast cancer cell sample data and precipitation pattern survey data provide significant insights into the structure of high-dimensional data sets, and reveal new possible hypotheses for further research. Our contribution establishes a relationship between the eigenvalue density at the edges of this distribution and the optimality gap, thus narrowing the statistical assumptions. We also establish that certain properties of these matrices, such as sub-Gaussian singular values, can accommodate non-normal data scenarios. Leveraging these results, we derive new bounds for stochastic gradient descent's performance in such scenarios. Furthermore, we present a complex system optimization problem whose optimality gap cannot be captured by worst-case or even average-case convergence guarantees, yet we demonstrate the efficacy of SGD in achieving nearly optimal performance in this scenario. Finally, we investigate the performance of optimization algorithms on random data and explore the dynamic behavior of SGD on such problems. Our work sheds light on the algorithms' ability to approach the optimal solution as it iteratively improves the optimality gap. Specifically, we examine the behavior of SGD on the quadratic optimization problem and develop a novel 'anticipation' strategy, which could serve as a valuable guide for developing more advanced algorithms in the future. We hope this provides a thorough understanding of optimization, allowing researchers to develop new, efficient optimization tools. Our work also opens up possibilities for creating more sophisticated prediction tools by connecting it with the realm of optimization. Moreover, our analysis illuminates the intricate relationship between the eigenvalues at the edges of the data's expected spectral distribution and the optimization's difficulty, thus shedding light on the eigenvalue density's impact on the complexity of the optimization problem. Lastly, our work highlights the significance of the eigenvalue density at the edges in predicting the performance of optimization algorithms on random data, thus connecting it with the limited success of worst-case convergence guarantees in efficiently solving optimization problems. Our most striking discovery, however, is the remarkable performance of SGD in nearly approaching the optimal solution, thus inspiring further research into its properties and potential applications of its predictions. One such potential application is seen in the acceleration of computational convex optimization through change of variables, which can potentially transform exponential optimization problems into polynomial ones. We hope this marks a significant starting point for creating an optimization framework that combines the efficiency of prediction with the breadth of optimization, thus paving the way for a more efficient optimization toolkit. The measurements of individual and combined WZ and ZZ events are consistent with theoretical predictions in the standard model, specifically with the predicted ratios of cross-sections for different processes. This is achieved by leveraging Watson's formula, which allows us to recast our investigation as a tractable problem related to L-functions, ultimately facilitating the application of Soundararajan and Harper's methods for deriving sharp bounds on the moments of the Riemann zeta function. We aim to enhance the accuracy of structured text recognition by incorporating predefined formats defined through regular expressions, thereby facilitating the identification of specific patterns. Our method, involving a Weighted Finite-State Transducer model, boosts recognition accuracy on targeted formats, with minimal losses in other instances. A key parameter governs the intensity of the formatting influence. The proposed technique finds applications in text analysis, particularly relevant to documents containing forms, tables, financial statements, and medical records, featuring formats that can be predefined. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using a dataset of technical documents, with pre-defined formats specified in a compact manner, revealing a notable enhancement in overall recognition accuracy and table structure detection. Our analysis underscores the benefit of incorporating prior knowledge on structured text recognition. Moreover, we highlight potential difficulties and areas for further improvement. The associated code and formatting specifications can be accessed via a public repository.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, cross-sectional measurements were recorded for singular top quark production and were found to be in alignment with theoretical predictions. The study further examined differential top quark production characteristics, including momentum distribution, rapidity, and transverse momentum, across various kinematic intervals. The investigation also yielded constraints on the parton distribution functions of the proton in the context of scale dependence, revealing a preference for distributive functions at a scale of 1.3 times the proton mass and accounting for 91% of relevant parton interactions, with a preference for a dampened behavior at a scale of 1.9 times the proton mass with a corresponding reduction to 85% of relevant parton interactions. The discovery represents the LHC's initial recognition of top quark production in proton-lead collisions and lays groundwork for future studies in quantum chromodynamics and nuclear physics. The research is also interpreted within a model describing nuclear attachments between quarks and gluons, revealing the significance of nuclear factor $K$ for a specified range of momenta and rapidities in the standard model. Furthermore, the study quantifies nuclear effects within the context of the standard model by examining ratios of nuclear-dependent cross-sectional measurements to those in neutral-hadron collisions, finding these effects to be predominantly driven by $Q$-dependence and revealing a nuclear attachment factor $f_2/N_{\rm disc}$ in the standard model, where $f_2$ is a specific nuclear form factor and $N_{\rm disc}$ is the discrete-nucleus parton distribution function. Lastly, the research explores constraints on the nuclear-dependent attachments between quarks and gluons and those between jets, discovering a nuclear attachment factor $R_{\rm g}$ for gluons that exceeds that of quarks and that both attachment factors exceed 1, indicating a more pronounced nuclear impact on gluon distribution functions

Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications requiring more detailed output. By integrating these components, a comprehensive zero-shot framework is established, yielding the top overall performance on the Spider-Bank dataset and excelling at schema linking on the Spider-Google dataset. Moreover, our work achieves the highest cross-domain evaluation score on the Spider-Bank dataset. As an extension to our main approach, an interactive version is developed, demonstrating promise in handling more intricate queries. Both our core and interactive models are available for evaluation at https://github.com/A0D0/SDC. For practical use, we suggest zero-shot parsing in applications where both column name and value data are required for query synthesis, whereas interactive parsing is more suitable for situations where more complex query synthesis is needed with the interaction benefit. For Text-to-SQL parsing in the same domain, our approach exhibits potential, especially with the incorporation of interaction, though this requires substantial additional computational cost. For cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, our approach exhibits a considerable time disadvantage due to the requirement of filling values. To overcome this drawback, we propose an alternative approach, SPICE, which achieves comparable accuracy to our core approach on the Spider-Bank dataset but is subject to a considerable time disadvantage. To overcome this limitation, we then developed an interactive version of SPICE, demonstrating a significant time improvement while still maintaining comparable accuracy to our core approach. Interestingly, our study finds that the cross-domain evaluation score on Spider-Bank can be notably elevated by incorporating both schema linking and value filling capabilities. To validate the practical utility of our work in real-world applications, our approach achieves an impressive 87.98% relative improvement over the existing zero-shot parser on Spider-Bank when evaluating practical value filling performance using manually set criteria, using an independently developed ground truth dataset prepared for this paper. Similarly, our study discovers a notable 133.81% relative improvement over the existing zero-shot parser on Spider-Bank when assessing practical schema linking performance using an independently established ground truth dataset. Consequently, our work presents an advanced zero-shot text-to-SQL parsing framework, offering invaluable lessons to zero-shot parsing, cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, and the wider NLP community. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to nondifferentiability. Building on the adaptive sieving strategy from the Exclusive Lasso problem, we introduce a novel algorithm to tackle the HDR Lasso problem. By adapting the Cholesky decomposition in each sieving step, our method successfully avoids the complexity of dealing with block-wise correlation matrices. Our extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed algorithm, which shows improved computational efficiency and robustness comparable to or even better than existing methods. Additionally, our efficient algorithm has opened the door for large-scale applications of the HDR Lasso, taking advantage of modern parallel computing capabilities. As a testament to its practical utility, we also highlight the HDR Lasso's success in successfully extracting key nonparametric features from real-world data sets. Specifically, the technique was used to extract distinct patterns in a dataset of daily drinking water pH levels in Cincinnati, Ohio, and a dataset of stock market data from the Center for Geospatial Analysis at the University of Buffalo. Our findings were surprising and reveal potential insights into these markets, demonstrating the potential for the HDR Lasso to extract meaningful, interpretable signals from real-world data, which requires further verification to validate its statistical assumptions. By leveraging a comprehensive suite of software implementation details and theoretical proofs, our work aims to facilitate the replication of our results, encompassing both theoretical and practical aspects of the HDR Lasso approach. Specifically, the publicly accessible code can be utilized for reproducing our numerical experiments, whereas the theoretical section provides the necessary mathematical justifications and analytical proofs for the HDR Lasso. To ensure maximum accessibility, our work is presented in a flexible manner, balancing both practical computing techniques and the more abstract mathematical reasoning. By adopting this hybrid approach, our contribution aims to facilitate the understanding and replication of our results, striking a balance between the computational techniques used to implement the HDR Lasso and the mathematical rigor underlying these algorithms. Furthermore, the accompanying software has been thoroughly revised to ensure clarity, including the replacement of previously utilized Fortran code with more modern, cross-platform Python implementations based on the Pandas library. However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (dubbed AI for Green) has been undertaken, focusing exclusively on greenhouse gas emissions. In this article, we seek to address this gap by analyzing potential negative outcomes associated with AI-driven environmental solutions. Initially, we will categorize various types of AI's environmental impacts. Subsequently, we will conduct a thorough review of existing research evaluating the environmental trade-offs of utilizing AI in the context of environmental applications. Additionally, we will highlight existing vulnerabilities within current approaches to AI-driven environmental solutions that may exacerbate their adverse environmental effects. Lastly, we will suggest promising avenues for future research in this domain. By doing so, we aim to contribute to the development of more sustainable AI solutions with minimized environmental repercussions. These efforts will foster responsible AI technologies that promote a greener future. Furthermore, we create a research map to visualize the environmental impacts of AI applications on the environment, showcasing notable research and its publication details. This map caters to researchers for navigation and inspiration. We categorize various types of AI's environmental impacts, including energy consumption, e-waste generation, water pollution through cooling, land transformation resulting from large data centers, and carbon emissions. Existing research evaluating the environmental trade-offs of utilizing AI in the context of environmental applications applies various methodologies, including life cycle assessment and cost-benefit analysis. These existing approaches demonstrate several vulnerabilities, including the limited scope of consideration for AI model performance, reliance on present computational capabilities, and failure to account for the AI's potential long-term benefits in addressing environmental concerns. Existing approaches also demonstrate a need for improved evaluation of the AI's performance, considering its potential long-term benefits, and the environmental impacts of AI-driven solutions extending beyond energy consumption. To this end, we propose novel evaluation methodologies grounded in multi-criteria decision-making and life cycle assessment to address these existing vulnerabilities. These proposed methodologies assess various AI general solution strategies in relation to their performance and environmental impacts, considering performance as a benefit and environmental impacts as drawbacks. This study introduces an error control strategy for a Boussinesq model with adaptive coefficients, where temperature-dependent properties of heat transfer and fluid viscosity are taken into account. The coupled system of the Navier-Stokes and heat equations is solved in a unified manner. The primary goal is to utilize the dual-weighted residual method for estimating the errors of various goal functions with the help of an adjoint problem. To localize the errors, we utilize a partition-of-unity method within a weak formulation framework that is well-suited for solving coupled problems. This approach enables the implementation of adaptive algorithms that are validated by a range of numerical experiments, including one benchmark problem and two further investigations inspired by laser material processing. The efficiency and robustness of the developed framework are confirmed by the observed reductions in errors and effectivity indices. The efficiency gains are then measured in terms of the computational cost, both in terms of time and memory requirements, which reveals substantial advantages of the adaptive method over a fixed mesh strategy. In specific cases, we document up to a hundred-fold improvement when using the adaptive algorithm to achieve the same level of accuracy as was achieved with a fixed mesh approach. In addition to discussing the potential applications of this error control method to other problems, we also reflect on its development as part of a larger effort to create an open-source software library dedicated to solving a range of fluid dynamics problems with advanced numerical techniques. We identify a required and confirming criterion for pairs of group codes $(C,D)$ in group algebra $R[G]$ to be a linear complementary pair, subsequently proving the equivalence in terms of permutations between codes $C$ and the dual code $D^{\perp}$. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. We also applied FABE to solve practical inference problems within graphical models, achieving success in two challenging scenarios: constraining image generation from text and optimal image filtering. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a controlled environment for studying 3D object localization in real-time is established, involving an embodied robotic agent, a camera, and a microphone that identify a dropped object in a room.  The robot achieves this by synthesizing audio and visual cues along with the principles of physical mechanics.  A dataset called Fallen Objects has been developed for studying this complex challenge.  The dataset is based on the ThreeDWorld platform and includes over 8000 simulations of various object types in 64 settings.  As an initial step toward resolving this problem, different agent architectures based on imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and modular planning are designed and evaluated to provide an in-depth analysis of this new task.  The research indicates that the integration of asynchronous multi-sensory cues presents novel and difficult localization issues.  The source code and the dataset are accessible at https://github.com/yoyotl/LocObj and https://github.com/yoyotl/Fallen_Objects respectively.  The ThreeDWorld platform can be found at https://www.threedworld.ai.  This research did not receive any specific funding.  It was conducted at Cornell University as part of a course and at individual research settings.  The key contributions of this study involve the creation of a new control environment for the study of asynchronous multi-sensory cues, the development of a comprehensive dataset for the localization of 3D objects, and an in-depth analysis of different approaches to this challenge.  The implementation of a robust camera system is another key contribution of this research.  The most effective approach to this challenge is also explored and evaluated along with an examination of the impact of sensing modalities and the structure of the environment on object localization.  The evaluation of different approaches is conducted using the developed dataset and a benchmark task.  The most effective approach to this challenge is an embodiment of active learning and reinforcement learning for object localization.  The integration of asynchronous multi-sensory cues presents novel and difficult localization issues.  The environment and the dataset developed for studying this challenge can be used for a wide array of research in multi-sensory cue integration and object localization. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. Our study's findings show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's results highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's findings are in line with other studies focusing on the potential adverse effects of Web search personalisation on citizens' judgments and decisions. Our data's analysis further sheds light on the implications of Web search personalisation on search results and the potential Advertisements and promotes bias against specific groups, requiring further research to confirm these findings' extent and implications. This study's outcomes are likely to be instrumental in shaping judgment and decision-making processes in the public sector and beyond. This research fits into the theory of extended mind and further examines the implications of Web search personalisation on search outcomes' trustworthiness. As such, we propose additional investigations into the adverse effects of Web search personalisation that is grounded in the theory of extended mind, encompassing cognition and its external manifestations. Ultimately, we hope to obtain a deeper understanding of the adverse effects of Web search personalisation that is grounded in a broader cognitive theory. In this study, we focus on Web search personalisation's influence on search outcome trustworthiness, an aspect that is likely to be prevalent in other adverse effects of Web search personalisation. This research excercises a high degree of caution in drawing inferences about behavior following an analysis of search patterns using search data that contain a substantial amount of noise. Testing on data from six patients revealed that the model can automatically complete this process in under two minutes, providing fast and efficient support for daily MR-Linac treatments. The model's accuracy in calculating exposure weights also means fewer radiation beams are required to deliver the prescribed dose, potentially shortening treatment periods. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The Matrix Corona (Mat-Cor) decomposition is an alternative to Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) that was adapted for positive semi-definite matrices. We applied Mat-Cor to analyze the directional life-quality index for 112 Spanish provinces in 1978, a compositional data set from the 'occip' package. The research demonstrated the efficacy of Mat-Cor in extracting spatial patterns from the data, as these features align with geographical distributions in the Iberian Peninsula, and the variables capture regional characteristics and trends, according to a spatial similarity analysis. These findings corresponded to those obtained with CPD, but the Mat-Cor decomposition possessed higher statistical stability and consistency. Furthermore, the method enables the identification of latent components that are difficult to interpret, such as the third component in our case, which poses a challenge for purely factor-based methods like CPD. We propose Mat-Cor decomposition as a viable technique for compositional data analysis and advocate for its more frequent application in this domain. The method has been implemented in the R software package "Kalekta", available on CRAN.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory.  In contrast, stochastic accretion models (e.g. Jackson et al., 2009) may provide a possible explanation for these outcomes. Existing empirical models of planetary formation (e.g. Mordasini et al., 2009; Nelson, 2009; Mamajek et al., 2003; Fortier et al., 2013; Egan & Guilbert, 2015; Egan et al., 2017; Loeb & Spergel, 1998; Hatzidimitriou & Kramer, 2018; Lee & Grinstein, 2019; Grinstein et al., 2020) are incapable of replicating the non-linear relationship between the mass of a planet and its distance from its host star as evidenced by these surveys, necessitating a revision of these models to align with observational evidence.  Ultimately, a thorough understanding of the planetary formation process remains elusive, and further outreach is necessary to foster collaboration between the observational and theoretical astrophysics communities in order to elucidate the complex and nuanced nature of a planetary system's evolution.  This research was conducted in accordance with the principles of science by collecting and analyzing data through peer review and feedback. Additionally, a detailed description of the data analysis methods used in this study is presented.  Key words: exoplanets, planetary formation, core accretion, runaway accretion, stochastic accretion, gravitational microlensing, CORALIE/HARPS, MOA. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and compositionality, but their extensive connection structure can hinder large-scale network training and data efficiency. To address this issue, we introduce locality-masked RNNs (LM-RNNs), a class of RNNs with reduced connections between distant units. This modification introduces a regularization effect, mitigating the risk of overfitting. Moreover, connecting local units promotes the formation of independent functional sub-networks. As a result, LM-RNNs exhibit improved training stability, accelerated convergence, and enhanced data efficiency, surpassing conventional RNNs. Additionally, they offer a powerful framework for discovering novel algorithms in computer science. To demonstrate this potential, we utilized the DeepMath method and used two examples of symbolic problems in linear algebra and polynomial system solving to verify that LM-RNNs can develop efficient algorithms. Our research showcases the efficacy of masked RNNs as a highly efficient and flexible algorithmic discovery tool. Furthermore, the developed algorithms validated the versatility of LM-RNNs in tackling complex, algorithmic challenges. Finally, our study highlights the risks of overfitting and data efficiency issues in RNNs, which can be significantly mitigated through the incorporation of locality constraints. These constraints can be adjusted to achieve a balance between accuracy and connectivity, providing a valuable direction for future research in the development of efficient and scalable deep RNNs. The code for our study has been publicly released at https://github.com/DeepMath/DeepRNN. The DeepRNN package supports training both standard and locality-masked RNNs to solve various symbolic challenges in linear algebra and polynomial system solving. To replicate our study's results, please refer to the accompanying jupyter notebook file, which contains the necessary code and settings. Additionally, the research paper, along with the code and the DeepRNN package, can be accessed via https://arthurfinkelstein.github.io/publications/DeepRNN.pdf. Observations indicate that there is a sudden change in the power and speed of these jets as they transition from large-scale to small-scale observations.
