This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes determination of the feature's sparsity, or lack of data, as well as the application of a circular shift to the image, both of which are impossible to achieve through classical linear operations.  To achieve symmetry invariance, we use the set-wise Normalized Cordelian Transform (NCT) applied to both local neighborhood intensity images and shape files.  The feature's sparsity is determined via a calculated sparsity measure, and a circular shift is performed based on this sparsity value.  Similar to traditional image features, a Salient Binary Pattern (Salient BPs) descriptor is computed for the shifted image, and the feature's sparsity measure is incorporated into a multi-dimensional codebook.  To achieve contrast invariance, a Salient Binary Pattern (Salient BPs) descriptor is computed from both the original neighborhood intensity image and the neighborhood intensity image inverted via NCT.  The combined feature is computed as the concatenation of both contrast-invariant Salient BPs descriptors.  Performance evaluation of the proposed approach via rigorous testing on challenging datasets reveals its superiority to state-of-the-art methods.  Specifically, our approach surpasses existing techniques in 3D image registration via both sparse and dense subset-based as well as dense feature-based point-set registration tasks.  Moreover, our salient features exhibit sparsity-based robustness to image degradation via both Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, as well as other types of distortion.  Ultimately, the proposed features prove compatible with state-of-the-art image registration algorithms and demonstrate great potential in 3D image processing applications.  The proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to various registration algorithms, making it suitable for 3D image registration tasks. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm is designed, which offers better numerical stability and improved ability to our empirical studies. The proposed UOTP layers are then tested across several applications including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification, and are found to be capable of either mimicking existing pooling layers or developing novel, combining properties. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed models, several experiments are conducted using the Euclidean and Bregman distances as examples. The performance of the models is compared with state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets for multi-instance learning and graph classification. Moreover, the capability of the models to produce interpretable features is also evaluated using both accurate and distorted distance measures. The proposed models are found to be highly effective across various evaluation metrics. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training on a smaller dataset covering
single-view driving scenes. The code for our study is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/depth-seg.git. The results mentioned above and

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Additionally, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. Furthermore, 9.5% of these professionals expressed a willingness to use TCube in real-world scenarios, with 4.8% stating that they would integrate it into their current workflows. Our study also highlights the importance of transparent explanations for AI models that rely on pre-trained components, such as language models, when working on autonomous data narration tasks. We discuss potential challenges and present a set of recommendations to address them, thereby fostering innovative applications of neural methods in time-series narration. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. In addition, data analyses of $B^0_s \to J/\psi K^{\ast 0}$ decays have been conducted to assess violations of CP and to establish fundamental limits on rare phenomena such as $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays. Ultimately, these analyses have led to enhanced understanding of the rare electroweak transitions of quarks and contributed to restrictions on additional sources of CP violation beyond the Standard Model that could explain the matter-dominated universe.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures exhibit intriguing, often sign-variable periodic patterns dependent on temperature and magnetic field strength. Notably, specific stress measures display periodic behavior despite not being directly related to group elements or their characters. Furthermore, high system size limits allow us to rescale our findings, revealing both periodic and divergent measures. In addition, for specific index-2 subgroups, we identify one-to-one correspondences between measures and elements of the subgroup, also determining how these measures evolve as system size increases in accordance with the scaling of the magnetic field. Lastly, by leveraging these results, we outline a systematic approach to constructing Ising model measures related to any normal subgroup of the group representing its index-2 image under the mapping of these subgroups. Conversely, starting from a general stress measure, we show how to identify the corresponding index-2 normal subgroup and its group representation. Additionally, our analysis confirms prior findings on stress measures in [J. Math. Phys. 57, 063301 (2016); J. Stat. Phys. 162, 1431 (2016)]. The introduced method proves versatile, allowing us to derive new periodic measures, including those linked to braid groups, particularly the braid group on three strands. Moreover, in contrast to prior works on solvable groups, our results demonstrate the versatility of our method in capturing the essence of stress measures for groups that cannot be solved. Last but not least, our analysis also yields novel high-system-size limits of stress measures in a manner parallel to the approach in [Phys. Rev. E 91, 042103 (2020)]. The introduced method also enables us to derive stress measures for solvable groups, offering a previously missing connection in the context of the Ising model. Lastly, our computational code is available at https://github.com/ark1k/Ising_model_stress_measures/tree/master/Ising_model_stress_measures. This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $\ln^k(\ln^l(\lvert t \rvert))$. By manipulating the equations to reveal a lower-order hyperbolic component, we can analyze the solutions' behavior and understand the effects of coefficients and lower-order terms. Our findings demonstrate that moderate blow-up in coefficients or lower-order terms may result in the loss of certain regularity compared to the initial solution, a phenomenon that cannot be avoided. The study also compares the loss of regularity with the growth properties of certain subspaces of ultrahyperspaces, such as those studied by Kulikov and Novik and by Daini, Kamiya, and Nagayama. To parallel these investigations, we focus on the effects of blow-up in coefficients or other terms rather than ultrahyperspaces' properties as the primary factor for the loss of regularity. Notably, the study's results are consistent with previous findings for ultrahyperspaces as well as with those for hyperbolic equations with polynomial coefficients, yielding an extensive generalization. To access the study's main conclusions, we employed the use of Sobolev spaces whose exponent exceeds the Lebesgue space's exponent, a property analogous to Lebesgue space's density within ultrahyperspaces. Finally, we present a counterexample demonstrating that the loss of regularity is not solely a product of the chosen Sobolev spaces but rather a characteristic feature of the equations in question. The example involves a specific equation with a polynomial coefficient to illustrate this point. The combination of these investigations and results offers an extensive analysis encompassing hyperbolic equations, ultrahyperspaces, and related generalizations and applications. The study's outcomes are applicable to equations with other types of non-smooth coefficients as well as to corresponding problems in ultrahyperspaces, a relationship facilitated through the parallel analysis of corresponding Sobolev spaces and ultrahyperspaces, a property shared by these mathematical entities. The shared properties comprise the existence of subspaces with certain growth characteristics and the inability to achieve certain smoothness levels for certain functions. The existence of certain functions with significant but moderate growth rates also plays a significant role in the study’s findings, a phenomenon observed within both Sobolev spaces and ultrahyperspaces.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of inner slopes. Observations suggest a higher frequency of steep slopes in the local universe than predicted by current cosmological models. To explain this discrepancy, we need new dark matter physics or baryonic feedback processes affecting normal matter. To explore the possibility of the former, we employed a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model and conducted an extensive clustering spelling test using semi-analytical techniques and detailed galaxy simulations. Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source.
Also, our proposed approach pre-trains the language model using relevant but unmarked text for enhanced data representation. 
Experimental results show that incorporating these strategies significantly enhances symptom extraction accuracy when comparing source and target datasets. 
We observe improved performance with an ensemble of adaptive strategies, achieving an F-score of 72.23 on the SymPhASE challenge dataset. 
A remarkable achievement, as our model is trained on diverse patient data and medical institutions, thereby showcasing scalability and applicability in real-world symptom extraction tasks.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite its potential, a major limitation of deep reinforcement learning is its reliance on substantial interaction with the environment, which poses significant challenges for hazardous tasks such as autonomous driving. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel strategy that leverages large datasets of annotated road maps to guide autonomous vehicles towards optimal pathways using targeted advice from a teacher. By dividing the road map into discrete sections and training a teacher model to generate advice for each scenario, we achieve interactive guidance without necessitating extensive interaction with the environment. According to our evaluations, a system we developed and tested on a miniature racing track could complete complex tasks with high success rates and speed, outperforming a comparison system that relied on deep reinforcement learning without guidance. Moreover, we observed that our approach allowed the model to accomplish tasks at a fraction of the computational cost of deep reinforcement learning. Upon scaling the size of the road maps and adding more sophisticated tasks to the test environment, we observed that our approach remained effective and efficient. Finally, we noted that our system possessed a high degree of interpretability due to its division of the road map into distinct sections, which facilitated the incorporation of easy-to-interpret weak supervision for the teacher model. In accordance with our findings, we believe that deep reinforcement learning with guided advice presents a promising and efficient method for achieving autonomous driving capabilities. In addition, we propose that this approach may serve as a bridge between current data-driven AI technologies and more recent goal-oriented AI methodologies such as plan-and-monitor architectures. Last but not least, we outline potential avenues for further research in this area. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe. Grounded in the principles of volunteer computing and the versatility of JavaScript, Pando's design refrains from incorporating redundant mechanisms to leverage the trustworthiness of volunteer nodes, instead relying on declarative programming to safeguard its operation. As a result, Pando has shown potential in enabling innovative applications, and demonstrated significant performance gains, reaching up to a 350-fold improvement in processing time compared to single-threaded execution on a volunteer node. Moreover, our analysis highlights substantial energy savings of almost 90% when utilizing Pando for parallel computation. To showcase the versatility of our approach, Pando has also been deployed on mobile devices, connecting personal devices and their browsers to form a powerful parallel computing system tailored for mobile devices. Leveraging its modularity and the flexibility of JavaScript, Pando's design allows for a flexible volunteer computing framework with a wide range of potential applications and use cases. These features have been implemented in open-source code and made available on GitHub for the benefit of volunteer computing researchers and developers. Finally, our study emphasizes the significance of considering the trustworthiness of volunteer nodes and their connections when designing a volunteer computing system, leading to the introduction of novel concepts, such as performance vs safety trade-offs and volunteer isolation. This thesis's findings serve as a benchmark for evaluating other volunteer computing systems in the future. With Pando's code available on GitHub, we hope to inspire future research in this domain by incorporating a volunteer computing benchmark into computational science curricula. By doing so, the field can benefit from ongoing research, and the potential of volunteer computing can continue to be explored and developed. As a result, we anticipate will see improved and more resilient systems for parallel computation in the future. A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. Several numerical demonstrations highlight the performance of this solution strategy. Initially, it is compared to an alternative approach for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems that involves a direct search for eigenvalues. Results show that the proposed solution method is more effective, not only in terms of computational efficiency but also in terms of accuracy. Additionally, this solution method was successfully applied to a practical problem in structural mechanics. Specifically, it was used to resolve a nonlinear eigenvalue problem in the vibration analysis of a geometrically imperfect shell. Researchers were able to use the solutions for the first two eigenvalues and eigenvectors to conduct a detailed nonlinear vibration analysis, applying the proposed solution method again for comparison. It was discovered that the solutions for the first three eigenvalues and eigenvectors were accurate to a level of less than 0.01 percent error. For this application, both the direct and indirect approaches were compared in terms of computational efficiency, demonstrating that the proposed solution method was more efficient, regardless of whether it was applied in isolation or as part of a larger solution strategy. Specifically, it was discovered that the computational cost associated with the proposed solution method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems was significantly lower than the direct approach, at less than 1/300, 1/100, and 1/60 of the cost for the first, second, and third eigenvalue solutions, respectively. Furthermore, when applied to the vibration analysis of the geometrically imperfect shell, the proposed solution method was discovered to be even more efficient, at less than 1/300, 1/100, and 1/60 of the cost for the three respective eigenvalues. These findings confirm that the proposed solution method is both efficient and accurate in the resolution of nonlinear eigenvalue problems. For instance, for the vibration analysis of the geometrically imperfect shell, the second eigenvalue and eigenvector were accurate to a level of less than 0.00001 percent error. Similarly, the third eigenvalue and eigenvector were accurate to a level of less than 0.00001 percent error, indicating that the proposed solution method was both efficient and accurate in the resolution of nonlinear eigenvalue problems

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain detailed information about the dynamics of these transformations, including information about their inverse maps and the morphology of associated fractals, specifically their interactions with the hole at zero. Specifically, we show that certain areas within the parameter space of beta-transformations are composed of compact, accretive sets that contain particular subspaces, and that they share certain topological characteristics with other transformation families, including those resulting from the combination of beta-transformations with shifts at their singular points. Furthermore, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a set that arises when performing a certain limit operation on regions that contain the hole at zero, and we show that this set bears a unique relationship to the Solomonov-Zubov curve. Additionally, we calculate the Hausdorff dimension of this set, which then allows us to calculate the Hausdorff dimension of various other sets that arise in the morphology of beta-transformations with a hole at zero. These results complement and extend the findings of Boshier and Vagvolgyi. We also model and study the behavior of a dynamical system in which a token moves through a chain of related spaces, which helps us better understand the Hausdorff dimension of the set that arises from the inverse maps of certain beta-transformations with a hole at zero. Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity in how their predictions are made, as demonstrated on real-world data and further validated in simulation studies where it was found to surpass alternative methods in recovering predictive models. Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights. From a practical perspective, a publicly available implementation of DAC can be accessed at https://github.com/jiashunxu/DAC, where various demonstration datasets are also available for download. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. Evaluation on standard datasets showcases Flatee's efficacy in producing accurate models, with results comparable to state-of-the-art baselines. Most notably, Flatee strikes a desirable balance between overhead and security, outperforming existing solutions in terms of overall performance. As such, it presents a viable solution for securing privacy-preserving machine learning in real-world scenarios. The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was validated through various test protocols. The framework is suitable for verifying drivers in applications such as robotics, industrial control systems, and IoT devices. The testing architecture can also be applied to evaluate software components that interact with external peripherals across different system types, including microcontrollers and Linux-based platforms. The presented test cases cover a wide range of topics, including input validation, buffer management, and handling of exceptional conditions. The outcome of this research provides essential guidelines for creating reliable and high-quality driver code through a thorough testing process. The test cases developed under this framework have been incorporated into the Linux kernel source code, ensuring better embedded software quality. Galactic centers, especially those with supermassive black holes, can form dense, starless cores when they reach a certain mass threshold. These cores may develop into massive, luminous stars, such as massive early-type stars, which can be detected by observing the near-infrared light from nearby stars using the VeILa survey at the Large/BRIGHT survey site. By identifying these stars, the VeILa survey was able to determine the mass function of late-type stars within one light day of the Large Magellan Cloud's center and found a notable decrease in the mass of these stars closer to the galactic center, indicating the presence of a'star desert'. This behavior can be attributed to the influence of a central black hole, specifically a 'puffing rain' effect caused by early-type stars being ejected at high velocities and creating a low-mass density region. Furthermore, the VeILa survey discovered a'mass gap' in the mass function of late-type stars, where the frequency of stars with masses between 8 and 20 times that of the sun is significantly lower than expected. This mass gap may indicate the presence of another early-type star ejection mechanism, such as a dynamical process, in addition to mass loss through stellar winds. We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures. We've also derived theoretical guarantees for our method's convergence and the convergence of the estimated posterior distribution. To facilitate practical use, we've implemented our method in a publicly available R package, ppinference, which includes detailed documentation and numerous examples of its application to various statistical models and scenarios. Thorough case studies are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of our approach in addressing critical issues of model specification and posterior convergence within complex models. We argue that our method offers a more reliable alternative to Laplace Approximation and other ad-hoc techniques for variable selection and the exploration of relevant structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. To further enhance the accuracy of our results, we recommend combining our approach with techniques for the correction of model misspecification, such as those involving the utilization of negative logistic functions in the context of logistic regression. We anticipate that our contribution will stimulate the development of novel projection predictive inference techniques for the selection of variables and structures in a diverse range of statistical models. Nexus to other disciplines such as machine learning, chemical engineering, genetics, and pharmacometrics may also provide valuable insights for the creation of new intellectual connections. As such, we have included a comprehensive list of relevant literature at the conclusion of this work. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies a new aspect of these storm sources associated with minor flares. It reveals the existence of two distinct modes of co-evolution: a "sausage-like" mode, in which storm intensity decreases while size increases, and a "torsional" mode, in which storm size changes correlate with sky-orientation changes. The researchers have also observed, for the first time in this context, the transition of these storm sources from the "torsional" mode to the "saussian-like" mode, facilitated by a flare. These findings support the theory of increased magnetic stress in complex active region structures that produce these storm sources and facilitate the acceleration of energetic particles. The researchers hypothesize that these storm sources could be either twisted flux tubes or thin magnetic filaments, based on the observed behavior. Observations of these storm sources in X-ray and optical spectra, though limited, support this hypothesis. The researchers stress the necessity of further research into the properties and behavior of these storm sources, as they may offer new insights into the underlying magnetic field dynamics in active regions. The knowledge gained from such a research could even provide new avenues for investigating the magnetic field dynamics in major flares. The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to compute steady-state solutions, from Newtonian infall of radial particles to a general relativistic model with particles possessing angular momentum. We compute the mass accretion rate and transport coefficients, such as radiative and viscous diffusion coefficients, in order to analyze the net inflow of matter. Our models demonstrate that angular momentum in the cloud significantly influences the mass accretion rate and transport processes. Consequently, our models are applicable to the early stages of massive star formation. Additionally, our work highlights the potential of kinetic modeling to analyze accretion processes in supermassive black holes. Furthermore, our study shows that kinetic effects play a crucial role in determining various transport coefficients, even at large distances from the hole, where effects of kinetic energy and pressure are negligible. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror. Furthermore, our study investigates the influence of initial correlations between the atom and the field on photon emission. Conversely, the Neumann boundary conditions yield second-time-derivative couplings, resulting in an emission suppression with increasing acceleration. These findings can be attributed to the increased correlation between the atom's quadrupole moments and the field's dynamical phenomena such as resonant phenomena and antiresonantphenomena. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, distinguished by their extinctions and K magnitudes.  Spectra from two extremely luminous early-type stars, showing widths in the range of 2-4 Angstroms, were obtained through the ALICEP 2.5m telescope at the CASLEO observatory.  This project is now augmented by new, retrievable spectra from the ING George Baker Ultraviolet Monitoring System, with a total of seven new and two previous classifications combined.  Two of these stars were classified as B-type (B3 and B8), with the remainder as O-type (one O6, one O8, and five O9).  Using their absolute magnitudes and a number of extinction parameters, the distances of these stars were determined in the range of 2-5 kpc and were identified as being outside of the Westerlund 2 cluster in half of the cases, with nine out of eleven having reduced molecular gas content.  This research implies a reduced association with massive star clusters and cometary shapes and, possibly, multiple star-forming entities in the region of Westerlund 2.  Further investigation into the region is needed to understand its role in massive star formation and evolution.  Future studies should concentrate on identifying signs of mass ejection in the region at the edge of the cluster, as well as determining the extent to which the cluster forms new stars and moves through the region.  Additionally, a comparison of the rate of mass ejection to the mass of newly formed stars is needed for the region of Westerlund 2 and other similar regions in the galaxy.  Finally, a study of the movement and expansion of the cluster and its effect on the surrounding interstellar medium and gas content is necessary to understand the history of the region.  This research will contribute to a broader understanding of massive star formation and movement, as well as their effect on the surrounding interstellar medium and gas content in the galaxy.  Ultimately, a determination of the rate of mass ejection to the mass of newly formed stars in the region

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current document analysis algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative method utilizing a combination of Deep Neural Networks to restore and enhance the readability of handwritten documents. This pioneering approach draws from previous work in natural scene enhancement, yet differs by incorporating specific text-based regularization techniques to preserve the unique characteristics of handwritten text. To facilitate training, we constructed a vast dataset of 774 handwritten text images, obtained through deliberate degradation to simulate real-world ageing processes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our model, we employed a comprehensive set of performance metrics applied to both clean and degraded text images. Our experiments successfully demonstrated the superiority of our model in maintaining the unique features of handwritten text, while also significantly enhancing readability and achieving remarkable results for compound semantic recognition tasks. Furthermore, we successfully restored and enhanced over 500 extremely damaged handwritten documents from the 16th to early 20th centuries, yielding an impressive 80% improvement in overall recognition accuracy. These remarkable outcomes position our model as an invaluable resource for preserving and conserving critically important historical documents. Additionally, we publicly release our project source code, dataset, and restored and enhanced document collections to inspire future innovation in the field. In particular, we invite the research community to build upon our work in two key areas: scaling up our model for massive-scale document analysis and incorporating artificial intelligence to facilitate automatic, low-cost restoration and conservation of handwritten documents. To access these valuable resources, please visit our project website at: https://hdc.readme.io/.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel estimation, ultimately hindering data transmission. To mitigate these issues, the IEEE 802.11p standard's pilot symbols can be optimized by allocating them dynamically, and the resulting practical algorithms can be implemented efficiently using conventional hardware components. By leveraging these optimized pilot allocation algorithms, the performance of IEEE 802.11p systems can be steadily improved, and the best achievable outcomes can be accurately determined through numerical analysis. For instance, assigning more pilot symbols to longer IEEE 802.11p frames using the maximal derivation algorithm yields high channel estimation accuracy in high-speed vehicular environments, and this algorithm can be implemented on hardware with a negligible computational complexity overhead. Furthermore, this algorithm's effectiveness has been found to be insensitive to the speed of vehicles. Another successful approach involves embedding IEEE 802.11p pilot symbols into frames using the pseudo-orthogonal localizing and tracking method, achieving high channel estimation accuracy even when the vehicle's speed is as high as 180 km/h and with negligible overhead. Different allocation methods exhibit varying levels of effectiveness, and the best choice depends on the specific scenario. In particular, the max-pilot allocation method is suitable for applications requiring large datasets, whereas the embedding method is more practical in scenarios with limited pilot symbols available for use. These optimized pilot allocation algorithms provide steady improvements in channel estimation accuracy and are easily implementable on hardware, offering promising alternatives to current IEEE 802.11p systems. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Synthesis-by-Association (SbA), a technique used to generate visual content based on existing images by remodeling the color relationships within a set of training data. Although effective approaches have been developed for supervised colorization and SbA, these methods are often marred by a single, critical limitation - they are heavily reliant on the quality of the input images. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new approach, AutoColor, which leverages an iterative process incorporating both robust low-level image analysis and high-level artistic direction from human artists. Our approach has two primary components: the augmentation of training data to capture diverse artistic intentions and a novel optimization technique that produces a single, unified color scheme. To evaluate AutoColor, we present a comprehensive dataset consisting of 1000 unlabeled images, along with 1000 associated guidance signals from human artists, making our dataset relevant to the task and representative of real-world image data. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on this dataset, as well as on two commonly used benchmarks for colorization tasks. Furthermore, we have found that our method yields valuable artistic insights, including suggested color schemes and potential image transformations, which can be utilized to enhance the quality of the images. To facilitate future research, we provide a comprehensive implementation of our approach, along with the dataset of image and guidance pairs, for the benefit of the research community. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our method rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. With inherent overfitting prevention, our method provides reproducible results that are also easily interpretable. With respect to observations and features, our method's computational complexity lies in the P class and has a specific running time expressed in terms of these variables. Conversely, traditional ANN training algorithms fall into the NP-Complete class. Its outstanding generalization capability allows our method to effectively handle datasets that are either small or large in size, and its remarkable performance on image classification tasks surpasses that of other deep neural networks such as ResNet, a CNN. A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on local edge computing and AI-driven processes at multiple robotic platforms to generate a unified, AI-driven global model that is shared across the network, and utilizes human-robot interaction instances to inform learning. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. To our surprise, we discovered that this
cross-sentence predictive task plays a crucial role in enhancing the models'
accuracy and often yields notable improvements, particularly in instances
involving long-tail relations. In addition, we observed that models trained with
this approach tend to generate more natural-sounding artificial negative pairs,
highlighting the importance of the predicted subject-object structure in
characterizing a relation's semantic definition. Lastly, we propose a novel
evaluation metric to assess the effectiveness of a relation extractor, one that
compares test set predictions to hypothetical scenarios in which an extracted
subject-object relationship is replaced with an alternate object, this change
being detected through the use of a knowledge graph link predictor. This
evaluation metric allows for a more comprehensive assessment of an extractor's
performance as it incorporates data from the entire knowledge graph rather than
just individual sentences. Using this metric, along with traditional F1 score
metrics, we evaluated the performance of existing models and discovered that the
multi-task approach yields substantial improvements, in some instances doubling
F1 scores and exceeding our proposed evaluation metric's baseline performance. In
addition, knowledge graph link prediction scores and the proposed ConNLL score
indicate that the multi-task approach allows for a more harmonious balance
between these separate objectives, as scores for each individual task surpass
the baseline when calculated separately. Complete code and model reproductions
are available on GitHub at the link https://github.com/glibg/MultiTask_RE_KGLP. In
the knowledge graph link prediction section of the GitHub repository, you will
also find the code for the proposed ConNLL score metric. Currently, the code
does not support the generation of artificial negative pairs as predicted by
relation extractors. We intend to incorporate this capability in future updates
to the repository. In the relation extraction section of the GitHub

Energy eigenvalues have been calculated in N-dimensional space for any n, l state. These findings have been used to investigate the characteristics of quarkonium states bound by Debye screening in the N=3-dimensional color-confined medium at finite temperatures and baryonic chemical potentials. Results indicate that anisotropy significantly lowers the dissociation temperatures of quarkonia, and charmonium and bottomonium can be bound in the N=3-dimensional color-confined medium at the N=0=Tc for certain quark flavors but not others. Furthermore, approximating the Analytical Exact Iteration Method in the N=3-dimensional space reveals that certain properties of quarkonium states can be accurately reproduced using perturbation theory, and this technique can be utilized to investigate quarkonium states bound by Debee screening in the N=3-dimensional space for any n, l state. Lastly, energy eigenvalue spectra have been calculated for quarkonium states bound by Debee screening in the N=3-dimensional space for any n, l state. These findings have various applications in the fields of quantum chromodynamics, cosmology, and condensed matter physics. Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space and a reference vector, and a mapping network that
produces the reference vector given the input data. We craft highly modular
designs for both networks, and demonstrate the exceptional quality of our
representations through applications in two-dimensional image representation,
three-dimensional shape representation, and multi-channel light field
representation. We note a notable improvement in fidelity when comparing our
approach to other methods, and observe a $10\%$ increase following our
evaluation of numerous examples. Our implementation details are provided to
facilitate replication, and the generated representations as well as source
code are available online for reference. We anticipate our work generalizing
neural representation learning will inspire future innovation in the field. 

Here are the key improvements over the current approaches in representation
learning for general data:

  1. A new dual-MLP network design achieves generalization, outperforming the
  competition in fidelity. Compared to Light-Field-Network, this new design
  achieves $10\%$ increase in fidelity with images, $6.9\%$ increase with
  three-dimensional shapes, and $14.6\%$ increase with light fields.

  2. A highly modular synthesis network is crafted with periodic equivariance
  using Fourier features, achieving a $4.6\%$ increase in fidelity with 2D
  images and $6.1\%$ increase with 3D shapes.

  3. A novel mapping network is introduced with a linearization of positional
  encoding, yielding $4.2\%$ increase in fidelity with 2D images and $2.1\%$
  increase with 3D shapes.

  4. Dual-MLP representation learning surpasses state-of-the-art methods in
  fidelity with 2D images, 3D shapes, and light fields, and generalizes well
  across these example datasets in representation quality

Our model and related algorithms can be applied to a broad range of theories suffering from a sign problem, offering a promising direction for future research. This study seeks to stimulate conversation on VPPM ethics and encourage the development of safer and more transparent VR experiences. Additionally, we propose an evaluation method to assess the physical safety of VPPMs. While our focus lies in haptics and walking, this methodology can be applied to other VR interactions, such as gaze and audio manipulation. Nevertheless, this investigation highlights the need for a thorough and concrete ethical framework for VPPMs, encouraging researchers to delve into this significant area of ethics. This research's interviews with experts provided input on our findings and provided valuable insights into the existing perceptions of VPPM exploitation. Our study identifies a significant gap between current research and the practical implications of VPPM safety, as well as the potential for exploitation, calling for significant attention from the Ethics of VR community. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can be deciphered, and their underlying arguments clarified. To achieve this, we outline a conditional generation strategy using a unified model that combines both conditional and unconditional language generation. By using this approach, the narratives can be summarized, and the transient rumors and content can be monitored. Our model also enables the creation of narrative graphs, furnishing fine-grained control over the production of social media posts. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach by evaluating our method on a dataset of 670k Twitter posts, resulting in the identification of 21k distinct narrative graphs, and our findings are now available on our project repository: https://github.com/salehmon/narrative_social_media. We anticipate this methodology to foster advanced social media understanding, facilitating real-time monitoring of prominent social issues such as election campaigns, product promotions, and public health awareness. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal point process model built upon neural network technology for capturing complex underlying patterns in social media data. The model leverages multiple deep neural network components to estimate the event density function, spatial expansion, and duration of the event. Comprehensive experiments using multiple years of Twitter data for eight locations in the United States demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in accurately recognizing and mapping events, compared to traditional methods. Results indicate the proposed model's capacity to detect anomalies with high accuracy, outperforming existing approaches, when the anomaly prevalence is relatively low (one percent). New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum as an optimal estimator of angular bispectrum amplitude in extracting non-Gaussian information on both galaxy bias and cosmological parameters, achieved by analyzing bispectra derived from galaxies and CMB lensing data simultaneously, resulting in significantly faster computation times. We found that combining the Planck satellite and DESI will potentially reduce biases in galaxy bias parameters by almost two orders over assuming a perfect bias parameter. We also compare our results with current approaches and finally discuss how our analysis may impact future cosmic structure experiments. \\

Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but are less accurate in classification, while deep learning-based methods (AE and DAE) offer better trade-offs between compression rates and reconstruction errors without compromising classification performance. Moreover, our investigation sheds light on the suitability of each method for a range of compression rates and highlights the importance of considering both compression rates and reconstruction errors when selecting dimensionality reduction methods for hyperspectral pixel classification. Based on our findings, we provide practical guidance on how to utilize these methods effectively. Ultimately, our research identifies the most effective dimensionality reduction methods for hyperspectral image classification and provides a framework that can be applied to other remote sensing tasks, including land cover classification. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing sparse networks that can be trained to replicate the same results is a potential solution. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor smaller, sparse sub-networks that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our goal is to explore the existence of this ideal, sparse sub-network in the realm of natural language models, specifically within the context of the HyperNYU-CSD dataset. Our findings show that such a sub-network does indeed exist and we have successfully identified a sparse sub-network within the ComplEx model, resulting in a substantial reduction from 98.53% to 98.34% in accuracy with just 0.22% of original weights. We also discovered that more modest reductions in parameters are sufficient for comparable results with less time required for training. Our analysis through attention mechanics explains these observations, highlighting the differing roles of various attention mechanisms within the ComplEx model. Our work also marks the first instance of applying the lottery ticket hypothesis to knowledge graph completion methods, potentially revolutionizing the way sparse learning techniques are utilized within this domain. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to reconsider the prevailing consensus. Additionally, we develop a systematic approach to evaluating loss function performance, which we employ to inform our selection of loss function in a real-world scenario. Moreover, we highlight the inherent connections between loss function and the characteristics of the data being attempted to classify, as well as the implications of our findings for the development of new loss functions. Ultimately, we advocate for a more meticulous approach to loss function selection, grounded in empirical evaluation and informed by the inherent properties of the data in question. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. This discovery confirms that exciton condensation is responsible for the charge-density-wave state in TiSe2, indicating the developed approach is versatile and could be applied to searching for potential excitonic insulators in naturally occurring materials. Additionally, the method was used to investigate how certain factors, such as external stress and chemical doping, influence the excitonic gap in TiSe2 and found that it could be effectively controlled through lattice compression. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, as our results show that the curvature of the Fermi surface dictates its overall structure. Based on our computational findings, we conclude that nematic and chiral superconducting states exhibit distinct behaviors in terms of their magnetization properties. Ultimately, our analysis predicts that a linearly varying superconducting gap, coupled with strong electron-phonon coupling, can yield a higher critical temperature for the doped topological insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$. Our study also indicates that the incorporation of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave component into the superconducting gap can further enhance the critical temperature by optimizing the superconducting energy gap. As an added note, our analysis also identifies distinct differences between the superconducting properties of time-reversal symmetric and nematic/chiral states. A significant outcome of this analysis is the prediction of reduced electron-phonon coupling $\Lambda$ in the vicinity of the Dirac point compared to that observed at larger doping levels. Specifically, our results show that $\Lambda$ can be approximated as $-\mu$ (with $\mu$ representing the doping level), assuming a time-reversal symmetric state. Nevertheless, our computational findings also underscore the intricacies associated with calculating $\Lambda$ using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near the Dirac point. Moreover, our analysis shows that nematic and chiral superconducting states can be distinguished from their conventional $s$-wave counterparts via measurements of magnetic susceptibility and superconducting gap topology. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method integrates a network to estimate example probabilities with a clustering objective guided by a variational autoencoder. By optimizing this framework, we can select samples that are both uncertain and informative, leading to improved performance in classification tasks. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results on small to medium-scale datasets and competitive results on large-scale datasets. Our code and models are available for reproduction.

This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Specifically, it relates to a condition defined as cut-free redundancy and two alternative notions of harmony in relation to ordered and unordered deduction systems. Ultimately, this study serves as a testament to the versatility of the Computational Ludics framework in tackling proof-theoretic literature arguments. Inversion and recovery have been replaced with a more unified requirement, harbouring both meanings. Furthermore, this new requirement holds the key to understanding arguments previously presented in the proof-theoretic literature as contingent rather than necessarily intuitive. Most notably, this study argues against the necessity of inversion and recovery through a counter-example rather than dismissing their underlying logic. These estimators are based on Fourier series expansions and can be efficiently computed via neural networks. By analyzing the properties of these estimators, such as bias, variance, and coverage, we find that AIPW and nAIPW have similar characteristics. Building on this finding, we investigate a relaxed version of the ATE, the Relative Intensity Causal Parameter (RICP), and its estimators, the Relaxed AIPW (RAIPW) and Neural Relaxed AIPW (nRAIPW). By examining the properties of RAIPW and nRAIPW, such as bias, variance, and coverage, we discover that they exhibit similar traits to AIPW and nAIPW. Additionally, we find that RAIPW and nRAIPW yield more accurate predictions compared to AIPW and nAIPW, especially for sensitive causal parameters. As a result, we propose a simple regularization approach that can improve the performance of these estimators while maintaining their robust causal estimates. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining the robustness of linear RL in a tabular setting and its application to the benchmark of hardest first. It reveals that even with the most advanced techniques, the problem is still cast as a min-max minimization optimization and becomes infeasible as the adversary's share increases. Nonetheless, we find that when the adversary’s share remains under 1/20, multiple existing RL methods are robust. Moving forward to the general model setting, characterized by large action spaces, we find that robustness becomes significantly more difficult and introduce a new approach comprising multiple stages of adaptation. Our experiments in both the linear and general model settings highlight the importance and correctness of our minimax bounds. Moreover, our novel robust learning method outperforms the current best methods, with the most notable improvement seen when the adversary’s share is lower than 1/20. For the general model setting, the gains are less pronounced but still evident when the adversary’s share is lower than 1/5. Notably, when the adversary’s share is very low at 1/80, our method exhibits nearly optimal performance in the offline setting. Our study also showcases the value of analyzing the most challenging data in RL via the benchmark of hardest first. It confirms the problem’s correctness and highlights the problem’s applicability to robustness as well as when the data distribution shifts in RL. This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step analysis of a control problem for a related equation featuring a time-dependent coefficient affecting the diffusion term, which builds upon existing work in linear control theory and applies to both finite and infinite-time horizons. Key aspects of our findings include the integration of harmonic analysis and a unique growth condition for the coefficient, as well as the application of logarithmic convexity for optimal control and direct control problems. Specifically, we address several subcases of the original problem, such as controlling from a single point, which is a well-established result. Our approaches to these challenges involve distinct strategies and new ideas. For example, in the case of controlling a time-dependent equation, we leverage the rapid decay of Fourier coefficients and a key result in harmonic analysis, as well as a crucial extension of the Helmholtz decomposition. Ultimately, our research showcases the interconnectedness of these control strategies and provides a framework for applying these methods to other problems within this domain. To facilitate understanding, we include detailed proofs and highly detailed estimates for specific cases, as well as introducing new concepts and techniques throughout the text. Notably, we introduce the concept of a "pseudomotion" and its associated Fourier series, as well as a unique decomposition of functions relative to a compact set, which could hold value even in the absence of the specific mathematical challenge that inspired this approach. Additionally, we establish a fundamental result in the analysis of second-order nonlinear equations, as well as a significant extension to a result by Carleman and Littman in the context of approximate controllability with impulse controls. This research not only addresses the original question but also yields a range of new and valuable findings. Although we primarily focus on controlling from a single point, our methods and strategies have broader applications and can be adapted to various related problems. Furthermore, our work opens up avenues for future research, such as exploring the feasibility of controlling impulsive effects using point controls and extending our results to models of coupled phase transitions. In conclusion, this study showcases the power of combining geometric and analytic methods in controlling dynamic systems through the use of precise regularity estimates and the strategic application of variational approaches, as well as highlighting the potential for impulse control to serve as a tool to address nondegeneracy

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of electric currents. The analysis shows that while non-conservative forces might play a significant role under certain conditions, they appear to be unimportant in the specific case at hand. However, conservative forces stemming from these electric currents could substantially impact the system's dynamics. By extending our model, we also predict outcomes for systems where a motor molecule interacts with a thermal bath of particles, where we anticipate the emergence of remarkable phenomena. Ultimately, our work highlights the efficacy of combining experimental and theoretical methods to uncover the intricacies of these complex systems and may pave the way for innovative motor design through computation. Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, similar deviations are explored in two-way transducers, examining whether there are transducers for which determining acceptance or rejection is computationally difficult, even with limited automaton variations. Despite initial findings indicating no major discrepancies, this study reveals a significant divide between two-way transducer theory and its one-way counterpart. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours, occurring every 7.7 days when it's closest to it. Observations using JWST and Spitzer have confirmed that even in the depths of HD80606b's long, dark periods, there is a residual heat remaining that treks the planet up to 800K even when it's far from its star. This means the planet continues to emit a faint light observable from Earth, but only under specific conditions. Notably, this emitted light is insufficient to support the presence of any atmosphere that might surround HD80606b, according to models. Analysis of the planet's light has revealed that its atmosphere is extremely thin and likely composed mainly of gas that would be expected in a rocky planet, with no evidence to suggest the presence of water or other substances that might surround a rocky planet at this distance from its star. This finding is particularly significant in the search for planets with similar characteristics. Most of the known exoplanets with similar features fail to demonstrate similar levels of temperature fluctuations, instead possessing more stable and regular patterns. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.

We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance both in small-scale real-world environments and large-scale simulated worlds.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By exploring SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, we gain a deeper understanding of operator growth dynamics and entanglement properties, including correlations among various eigenvalues of the density matrix. Finally, our work converges by demonstrating that certain Lie-symmetric systems can be used to replicate the operator growth curves of non-symmetric systems, thereby shedding light on the fundamental quantum nature of operator growth phenomenon. In this spirit, we outline future research directions that could lead to a universal understanding of quantum chaos and operator growth, potentially uncovering inherent connections between the underlying Lie symmetry of the systems and their underlying geometric structures of their Hilbert space. Furthermore, our work is expected to stimulate the development of new methods for extracting information from quantum systems utilizing their inherent Lie symmetry, which may offer advantages in quantum information processing applications. In this context, we illustrate how SU(2) symmetric systems can be employed for enhancing quantum teleportation of matter and energy within the Bell channel, thereby potentially amplifying the teleportation success probability from 0.25 to 0.5 for certain states like the SU(2) coherent state. Lastly, our work is anticipated to inspire the creation of Lie-symmetric quantum optimization problems, opening up avenues for tuning quantum sensor precision and improving estimated parameter accuracy. In this vein, we outline a feasible scenario for SU(2) coherent state optimization in order to enhance the precision of quantum measurements in quantum sensing applications. This study offers a comprehensive quantum information framework for extracting information from Lie-symmetric systems, thereby offering novel approaches for handling quantum uncertainty. In this spirit, we convey the extensive reach of Lie symmetry in the quantum information sector. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ via the Texas Active Target Time Projection Chamber, a highly sensitive measurement of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio can be made without interference from overlapping events. The analysis using a Bayesian approach reveals that the direct decay fraction is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level. This value is in line with previous studies and the present findings suggest a minor non-sequential component with a decay fraction of approximately $10^{-4}$. The measurement of the non-sequential component of the Hoyle state decay without a medium is performed for the first time and the derived upper limit agrees with previous studies.
