Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also occurs in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending on the dissipation mechanism, (ii) It may appear in 3D, but with more complex features, (iii) It can be activated by slight softness or dissipation irregularities. Based on these results, we suggest developing higher-order numerical methods to accurately capture oscillations and improve the computation of fracture problems. Additionally, we propose an effective approach to determine the minimum threshold for a dissipation parameter representing a dissipation length scale. The results from the phase-field models match those from explicit simulations of elastic materials with a fixed dissipation length scale, confirming the robustness of the approach. The determined length scales can be employed to predict the onset of oscillations in experiments, offering further insight into the fracture process. The minimum threshold for a dissipation length scale obtained in this study may serve as a boundary, beyond which oscillations do not emerge, even with increased crack speeds. Conversely, this threshold could be crossed if the dissipation length scale were diminished. The found length scales are comparable to those observed in previous experiments, which were conducted at lower speeds for 2D dynamic fracture in brittle materials, thus confirming that oscillations can occur at even higher speeds, awaiting verification through experiments. Finally, we explore the possibility of controlling crack propagation oscillations by adjusting a dissipation length scale with an applied magnetic field, presenting an innovative pathway for fracture dynamics research and experimentation. The discovered mechanism may be applicable to other type-II threshold phenomena in dynamic fracture. Conversely, this understanding could be used to induce oscillations in other type-II threshold phenomena, which could be crucial for practical fracture control. This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each involving a grid convergence study to determine the optimal number of discrete light sources for maximum performance. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of residence time and reactor size on SO2 removal. Ultimately, under optimized conditions, the results show that an ozone-UV light system can be a suitable solution for sustainable air pollution control applications. The model developed in this study can be used for designing and sizing such reactors, and the approach presented can be applied to other pollutants and removal processes as well as other reactive gas-phase reactions. Additionally, the work has potential implications for understanding certain atmospheric reactions. For example, SO2 can form sulfur trioxide SO3, which contributes to acid rain; and SO3 can condense onto particles, increasing their mass and affecting their gravitational behavior. Finally, the work has implications for certain health hazards associated with air pollution, including respiratory issues and premature mortality. Therefore, improving air quality using innovative pollution control technologies is crucial for mitigating climate change and protecting public health. As part of these efforts, there is growing interest in emerging technologies for air pollution control, and the work presented here is distinct due to its focus on the integrated use of ozone O3 and UV light for gas-phase pollutant oxidation. Other air pollution control technologies using UV light typically involve oxidation reactions with water H2O, which is not the case here; and most studies on sulfur compounds in the atmosphere focus on the chemistry of sulfurous gases, not their destruction. Therefore, the work is original and contributes to our understanding of certain atmospheric reactions, including the destruction of SO2 using an ozone-UV light system. Such a system has potential implications for designing innovative and sustainable air pollution control technologies, and the work presented here is a crucial step towards realizing these opportunities. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches. The results show substantial time savings of up to 95% during the application testing phase and the distribution of tasks can be optimized to counterbalance potential bottlenecks in the simulation workflow. The proposed solution serves as a foundation for evaluating various architecture designs and facilitating the development of software drivers for the accelerators, thus streamlining the overall simulation process. The developed model and benchmark code are made available for the community to ensure ease of replication and extensibility. Furthermore, the integration of the multi-core simulation environment with VIVADO toolsets enables the seamless conversion of sequential designs into parallel architectures, enhancing the efficiency of future hardware implementations. The proposed solution has the added benefit of being applicable to different architecture designs, hosts, and applications, thus ensuring broad adaptability and applicability. Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from user uncertainty about the model's input or output.
Existing solutions attempt to alleviate this issue, yet require substantial modifications
to the original models, resulting in reduced efficiency. This study proposes
a new framework known as Indecision Trees, capable of handling uncertainty
with minimal impact on performance. Indecision Trees are an adaptation of Decision
Trees, designed to incorporate uncertainty and output distributions. This
study evaluates the effectiveness of Indecision Trees through comparative analyses
on sample datasets, as well as two larger-scale dataset collections from the
UCI repository, focusing on regression and classification tasks. Results demonstrate
strong performance for problems with limited input uncertainty and demonstrate
reasonable compromise in scenarios with extensive input uncertainty, while
maintaining compatibility with original models. Furthermore, this study outlines
possible applications of Indecision Trees, highlighting potential benefits in
domains with measurement errors, validation uncertainties, or qualitative factors. 
Ultimately, Indecision Trees present an appealing alternative to more complex
models, offering efficient handling of uncertainty with minimal modifications. 
An open-source implementation of Indecision Trees is accessible via the GitHub
platform at the address https://github.com/apolc/IndecisionTrees. This project
is continuously updated to integrate new features and test cases. Additionally, a
technical report detailing the theory and results of this study is available at
the address https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05844. All data employed in his research

To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it achieves faster abandoning times compared to previous versions. In experiments, we observed a notable improvement in EAPrunedDTW's computation efficiency during similarity searches on the UCR Suite, and it renders pre-calculated bounds unnecessary. In contrast to PrunedDTW, EAPrunedDTW shows more consistent results across different data sets, and it achieves better time complexity on certain datasets, but PrunedDTW still outperforms it in others. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, an educational tool that provides students with code analysis and diagnostic feedback on their testing practices. By using Testing Tutor in conjunction with modern testing technology, we have developed a model to evaluate a student's testing skills, guide them through the learning process, and provide personalized feedback. Our assessment of this approach demonstrates that we can accurately determine a student's testing level and that Teaching Tutor enhances students' testing methodologies, thereby preparing them for a professional testing environment. Our results indicate that students can become proficient in testing with a high level of accuracy without needing extensive training, and by using Testing Tutor, students can improve their testing practices and increase their accuracy in identifying issues from code reviews and test case analysis. Additionally, we have introduced an open competition challenge to evaluate other educational tools and methodologies in the area of testing education. You can find more information about Testing Tutor at https://testing-tutor.github.io. Additionally, the tool's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Testing-Tutor/testing-tutor for possible integration with other educational tools. We are excited to collaborate with other educational researchers in order to further improve teaching and learning effective testing practices. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning models, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing intrinsic network features, we create a comprehensive, descriptive verbal explanation of a DNN's decision rationale through an analysis of learned features, associated human-interpretable concepts, and an ILP approach resulting in logical rules that faithfully mirror the behavior of a well-trained CNN. We've applied this method to classify tasks such as detecting diseased skin conditions and synthesizing synthetic images, finding that on various benchmark datasets, the derived logical rules can be translated into straightforward image processing operations, thus making the model more understandable. Moreover, by implementing these rules in an ensemble of simple image filters, we've achieved precise image-to-class predictions, thus "opening the black box" of a CNN. This groundbreaking approach, though computationally intensive, offers a groundbreaking understanding of how image features interact and enables more efficient application of logical rule-based models by leveraging more sophisticated learning methods. Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it. Moreover, this research proposes a novel framework to systematically evaluate and compare the over-smoothing phenomenon and its prevention methods across multiple graph convolutional architectures. The framework also enables the creation of a comprehensive benchmark to assess the impact of over-smoothing on task performance and evaluate the efficacy of countermeasures on theoretical and practical levels. The benchmark is comprised of over 1800 experiments on 7 datasets, utilizing 12 methods to prevent over-smoothing and addressing 9 tasks. The research demonstrates that selecting an appropriate countermeasure depends on the specific problem at hand, highlighting the significance of balancing the constraints imposed by over-smoothing and performance. Empirical evidence shows that several methods are susceptible to over-smoothing and fail to achieve state-of-the-art performance when removing the smoothing component from the network's spectral decomposition. Notably, this research reveals that LGCN, an iterative graph convolutional network, is the most resistant to over-smoothing among all the evaluated methods, achieving a 9.5% improvement in performance on tasks affected by over-smoothing. Moreover, two key factors were identified as primary contributors to over-smoothing: the properties of the graph, affecting 54.6% of tasks; and the initial network parameters, accounting for 40.9% of tasks. These insights provide valuable guidance for developers when selecting methods to mitigate over-smoothing and designing new approaches to prevent it. Lastly, this research highlights the necessity for further research into the composition of the network's spectral decomposition and its dynamic processes during training, emphasizing the current lack of understanding of these processes in deep graph convolutional networks. Based on these findings, multiple promising research directions are proposed at the end of this research. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found, with earlier studies suggesting that materials grow via traditional techniques that necessitate direct contact with the substrate. This study investigates the growth of the Heusler compound GdPtSb on graphene using low-energy electron microscopy and reveals that fragments of this material can adhere to graphene at energies corresponding to minimal kinetic constraints. Furthermore, atomic force microscopy shows large domains of GdPtSb grown on top of graphene through a process involving in-situ heat treatment. This finding suggests that a novel, remote epitaxy process is occurring, allowing the deposition of this Heusler compound onto graphene without direct contact. The domain sizes achieved in this study are comparable to those obtained with a substrate, paving the way for the development of efficient spin injectors and other innovative devices utilizing this epitaxial process. We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using recent advancements in stochastic estimation and influence function theory, we can show that this analysis becomes more accurate as we collect more data, even in cases where the data distribution changes over time. A practical implementation of this method is available in the R package stt. It includes tools for simulating data that includes hidden patterns, assessing the reliability of these models, and using them to detect changes in data series over time. Additionally, we discuss how to extend these models to include variables that appear in multiple time series data sets, which was a challenge to overcome. Two case studies illustrate the effectiveness of these methods. First, analyzing the daily price fluctuations of Bitcoin and seven other cryptocurrencies from 2016 to 2021 reveals consistent underlying trends despite significant price fluctuations. Second, analyzing monthly data from 2016 to 2021 of various economic indicators including inflation rates and stock market performance across various countries fails to reveal common underlying patterns, which aligns with expectations. Both analyses used a recent expansion of these methods for time series data sets to include variables that appear in multiple groups of time series data sets, which was a challenge to overcome. Our primary objectives are to derive highly efficient computational methods, evaluate multiple backtesting metrics, and provide practical solutions for common issues like missing data and the heavy-tailed properties of certain assets. The combination of techniques presents a promising solution for accurate cardiac condition diagnosis using cardiac auscultation.  The authors anticipate this solution to contribute to various applications of cardiac auscultation analysis. This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences. We conclude that auction format integrity has a substantial impact on bidding and that integrating credible and uncredible auctions does not yield beneficial outcomes for sellers. This research has implications for situations such as online advertising, public procurement, and auctions in social media, where the integrity of auction formats can be compromised. Additionally, this study sheds light on the broader topic of the impact of uncertainty in economic experiments. Despite its importance, this area remains understudied, as evident from our findings and existing literature. In particular, we address the question of how to apply our results to online advertising when facing challenges such as lack of data availability and human misperception. In light of our findings, we propose that when human agents are involved, uncertainty regarding the auction format credibility should be considered a key factor in bidding, as its impact surpasses that of other uncertainties. We also highlight the necessity of designing protective mechanisms to safeguard online transactions involving human agents and large sums of money, as exemplified by our experiment's high-stakes conditions. Lastly, we reflect on the limitations of our study and the potential avenues for further investigation. These could include examining (i) how to determine the intensity of penalties for rule breaches, (ii) whether protective mechanisms for large bidders can coexist with breaching opportunities for small bidders, and (iii) whether the market for online advertising auctions can be segregated into credible and uncredible segments. In light of our results, we speculate that such segmentation could lead to a loss of revenue. In contrast, we envision possibilities where the integration of both credible and uncredible auctions results in increased profits for sellers. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters. These interior fixed points give rise to three distinct epidemic scenarios, and we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the discrete-time model for various parameter combinations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a constant stable equilibrium for a specific set of parameters and leverage this to understand the discrete-time model's dynamics when it is non-stochastic. To evaluate the discrete-time model's asymptotic behavior, we derive a system of ordinary differential equations (ODE) corresponding to the non-stochastic model and identify its corresponding singular perturbation system using two time scales. Ultimately, we analyze a discrete-time stochastic epidemic model, exploring the same model parameters and examining the convergence of the stochastic model to the corresponding non-stochastic model. Our key findings indicate the convergence of the stochastic model to a constant stable equilibrium, thereby validating the discrete-time model's asymptotic behavior. These analyses provide fresh insights into understanding epidemic dynamics while highlighting the significance of 'The Big Freeze' phenomenon. To facilitate readability, we include an appendix detailing various limiting processes and a discussion on the discrete-time model's relationship to its continuous-time counterpart. Additionally, we provide an overview of the 'The Big Freeze' phenomenon, along with an introduction to the proposed discrete-time epidemic model and its distinction from existing epidemic models. Crucially, our work offers a novel argument for estimating the COVID-19 mortality rate and existing epidemic model parameters using widely accessible data such as population size, daily new cases, and total deaths. By applying this approach to pandemic monitoring, we can gain vital insights into epidemic progression and progression towards herd immunity. Ultimately, our work serves as a foundation for developing more sophisticated discrete-time epidemic models, thereby expanding the arsenal of statistical tools for such applications. Key methodologies employed include stochastic and deterministic epidemic model analysis, singular perturbation, Taylor expansion, Newton-Raphson method, matrix perturbation theory, Lyapunov function identification, and Stratonovich-Ito SDE techniques. Alternatively, our work contributes to the broader fields of epidemic dynamics, population dynamics, and mathematical epidemiology. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases with widely recognized meanings, closely tied to understanding context. Failing to recognize them results in diminished reading speed and comprehension. This study examines how effective machine learning models are at identifying and interpreting acronyms within written content, including their explicit definitions and contextual usage within texts. We develop and distribute two innovative datasets comprising 9,597 annotated English acronyms, one focused on definitions and the other on contextual usage. By analyzing these datasets through a combined analysis of classifier performance and human evaluations, we determine the feasibility and effectiveness of using machine learning models to identify and interpret acronyms. Despite the uncertainty surrounding the first dataset, our research indicates that machine learning models can successfully identify and interpret acronyms with reasonable accuracy, relying on the integration of natural language processing techniques and advanced models like BERT. It becomes evident that the utilization of deep learning models can aid in automatically generating definitions and improving acronym identification and interpretation. This work marks the first attempt to employ machine learning models for acronym identification and interpretation, paving the way for the development of effective solutions to the complex issues of definition ambiguity and unclear contextual application. Potential avenues for further research involve incorporating additional information such as author intent, semantic patterns, and the interconnectedness of domains. Additionally, our findings may find applications in developing tools to aid readers who struggle to understand acronym-based texts. We have made our code and dataset available for other researchers to build upon our work. https://github.com/asharmon/AcronymML. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We discovered that, although there are limitations to the variety of index sequences given the limited alphabet size of twenty base PCR primers, their vast combination total far exceeds the capacity of conventional storage systems. Our design leverages this abundance of index sequences and incorporates novel indexing techniques, allowing for a highly scalable and adaptable DNA-based storage system with multiple uses. Furthermore, we developed several refinement techniques for updating data in DNA-based storage systems, including extending data and adding new files to existing ones, and showed both through theoretical analysis and experimental proof that our proposed DNA-storage system offers significant benefits in terms of data organization and updates, and has the potential for extremely high data storage capacities. Experimental outcomes confirming the feasibility of writing large datasets to DNA and verifying the robustness of our DNA-storage system through the retrieval of multiple files from multiple storage segments are discussed. The potential for extremely high data storage capacities and substantial increases in overall computing power also make this DNA-storage system a promising means of significantly boosting overall computing power and storing vast datasets. Our study on DNA-based storage systems, the largest and most intricate structures built from DNA to date, involved constructing 32 distinct storage segments, combining 11 different primer pairs, and recording over 35 terabytes of various files and data objects. We demonstrated the robustness of our DNA-storage system, confirming its capacity and reliability through the successful retrieval of nearly all data from the stored files, and observed an overall recovery rate of approximately 99.8%. All experimental outcomes concurred with the predictions made by the theoretical data recovery analysis. The robustness of our DNA-storage system, and the confirmation of our theoretical data recovery analysis, demonstrate the feasibility and reliability of our DNA-storage system. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Lastly, it highlights potential future research directions, including the application of nodal lines in quantum computation and the development of a theoretical framework for nodal lines in systems with symmetry protection.

These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information at a constant speed over extended distances. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore the determinants of wave velocity, focusing specifically on singular perturbation and phase reduction techniques in the context of two distinct types of oscillators, one built on bistability and the other featuring time delay in negative feedback mechanisms. We examine how temporal separation of oscillatory scales impacts resulting wave speeds and assess the influence of pacemaker size and oscillation frequency. Our analytical findings are further validated by numerical simulations described previously, which were designed to model this phenomenon. Ultimately, our investigation reveals the complex interplay between temporal separation, pacemaker characteristics, and synchronization across system scales. This research has far-reaching implications for understanding pacemaker-generated wave dynamics in biological and chemical systems. A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The essential question is how many queries to unitary operators are needed to achieve such approximations. The results show a transition from polynomial queries to exponential queries, depending on $\gamma$, and these findings have implications for the field of quantum algorithms. A key result concerns the sample complexity of the von Neumann entropy estimator introduced by Alevinston et al., demonstrating that $O(\log^3 N)$ quantum samples and capacity estimates suffice, where $N$ represents the number of basis states. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to both encode medical classifications and derive meaningful insights from their content. One such method, known as ICD coding, helps track and understand diseases' distribution and patterns across populations, thus contributing to epidemiological research. Another approach, Clinical Note Summarization, focuses on extracting essential information from CTNs, primarily for time-saving purposes in the medical profession. Although both ICD coding and Clinical Note Summarization share the same goal of extracting relevant information from CTNs, they tackle the task in distinct ways, necessitating an investigation into their mutual benefits and potential integrations. This paper marks the first step in this endeavor, with the goal of combining ICD coding and Clinical Note Summarization to create a hybrid framework that not only encodes medical classifications but also derives insights from CTNs while minimizing the risk of errors. To achieve this, we proposed an algorithm called Summary-Infer encoder (SIE), which utilizes a deep neural network to encode both clinical observations and interviews, thereby enhancing the accuracy of ICD coding and reducing the error rate by 35% compared to the current top-performing method. Furthermore, our proposed SIE algorithm also successfully derived meaningful insights from CTNs, thus paving the way for a potential integration of ICD coding and Clinical Note Summarization. This study's findings were confirmed through experiments using data from 193 general medicine clinics in East China, containing the de-identified medical data and observations of 405 physicians, amounting to a total of 1,958,112 CTNs. Our experiments were conducted in accordance with regulations governing the protection of personal data, specifically the GDPR and HIPAA. Our method may hold implications for other classification tasks, as evidenced by its superior performance compared to other methods using information from medical classifications and clinical observations. This study's results demonstrate the potential of a hybrid framework combining ICD coding and Clinical Note Summarization to derive both medical classifications and meaningful insights from CTNs while minimizing the risk of errors. This hybrid framework can be adapted across various classification systems by replacing the current ICD coding labels with alternative labels as needed. Our code is available for reproduction and modification at the following link: https://github.com/StanleyBoxer/SIE. Our dataset is also available for reproduction and modification at the following link: https://oakiddatabase.org/. This study's findings have been submitted for review to relevant medical and clinical conferences

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth in data processing requirements. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially leverage up to 100,000 qubits, potentially resolving this issue. However, widespread adoption of quantum machine learning depends on the development of suitable algorithms and efficient qubit models for large-scale data processing. Researchers have proposed both quantum-based models for machine learning algorithms, as well as the application of classical models on a quantum platform. This study aims to examine the current state of quantum machine learning algorithms and the diverse range of efficient qubit models with the potential to process increasingly large datasets. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed analysis of seven practical applications, evaluating the efficacy of existing models in comparison to their conventional counterparts. Our key finding is that many current applications can be effectively addressed using both quantum and classical methods, albeit with some tasks better suited to a quantum platform due to significantly enhanced performance. These underappreciated quantum algorithms possess the potential to play a pivotal role in widespread adoption of quantum machine learning, thereby empowering researchers to tackle increasingly complex problems with large datasets. Here, we delve into specific challenges, outcomes, and future prospects, identifying potential avenues for further research to accelerate quantum machine learning advancement. Additionally, a comprehensive codebase is available on GitHub for reproducibility and future research. https://github.com/qm-lab/qml_paper/tree/main/qml_paper.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and provide reliable gradients. However, the standard fully differentiable rendering approach is too slow for large-scale inverse problems. Hybrid rendering, which combines accurate but non-differentiable and approximate but differentiable rendering techniques, is considered to address performance issues. Despite the speed boost, using Hybrid Rendering leads to stale gradients during optimization due to the substitution of renderers mid-process. Our study is the first to investigate the application of Hybrid Rendering in inverse problems, and we significantly improve its speed while achieving comparable results to standard Differentiable Rendering methods by introducing an innovative technique: gradient recalculation of layer masks. Our research is demonstrated through the practical application of image-based rendering for the restoration of paintings and the reconstruction of faces. Our results show that using Hybrid Rendering results in a 5 times faster convergence than standard Differentiable Rendering, and we also introduce an innovative method for determining when to switch between renderers at optimal times. Our theoretical analysis and experimental results validate the effectiveness of this new technique. Our research is implemented in an open-source framework called HyDR, which is available on GitHub. Our HyDR framework is designed to speed up standard Differentiable Rendering-based inverse problems by utilizing advanced techniques such as GPU optimization and accurate but efficient renderer approximation. HyDR also has the capacity to handle complex 3D surfaces through the application of multi-layer masks, and our research demonstrates its versatility by achieving significant speedups in painting restoration and face reconstruction while maintaining accurate results. Our HyDR framework is distinct from the standard Differentiable Rendering approaches in that it can handle large-scale inverse problems due to its increased robustness to noise and fast convergence properties. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where global phase coherence is shown to be less likely than in the full system. The observed global phase coherence in the full system is attributed to the infrequent occurrence of resonance amplification due to the random nature of the oscillators' frequencies. Furthermore, it is observed that increasing the nonlinearity in the system leads to global phase coherence becoming less likely. The obtained results may be applicable to understanding the global dynamics of biological oscillators due to the conserved nature of the interactions. The system studied is also reminiscent of the complex electrical activity observed in the heart. The presented work is in line with recent findings on nearly conservative systems as well as the study on the effects of nonlinearity and randomness in coupled oscillator systems. The global phase coherence in the studied system is distinct from that typically observed in self-organized synchronization where the interacting components are not strictly conservative. Additionally, it is possible that the studied global phase coherence could have implications for the understanding of electromagnetic interactions within the heart. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia items. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of unified representations across multimodal data points. Comprising sheet-music images, lyrical text, and synthesized audio, the dataset is comprised of three modalities, each represented by advanced models. This paper outlines the development of our music dataset and showcases the process behind our data collection, as well as initial methods applied to cross-modal retrieval tasks using MusicTM-Dataset. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/crcrcrc/MusicTM-Dataset. Additionally, our code for reproducing the demo can be found at https://github.com/crcrcrc/CrossModalMusicReproduction. Both links offer the possibility to fork the repo for further reference. This potential expansion will grant us insight into the capabilities of four-modal datasets and cross-modal retrieval methods. One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration. Moreover, the integration of natural language processing complements the existing Ontodia drag-and-drop interface, accommodating users who communicate through natural language and requiring minimal technical expertise. We've achieved this by dividing the exploration process into distinct phases: (1) the initial phase entails identifying core properties related to the user's query entity; (2) the secondary phase involves finding secondary properties related to those core properties; and (3) dynamic adaptation adjusts the results according to the properties of the target entity as users drill down into the data. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this process through quantitative evaluation of our implementation's accuracy, alongside qualitative assessments of user experience and performance. Furthermore, the system's flexibility allows it to seamlessly integrate with the current Ontodia interface, reinforcing our argument that this fusion of natural language and visual exploration enhances user experience and facilitates effective data exploration and visualization. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume. By prioritizing quasisymmetry and volume, we show that stellarator design can be optimized to meet specific scientific objectives while accommodating various rotational transform range requirements. Furthermore, we observed that stellarator design is inherently linked to the lambda diagram, and to maximize flexibility, quasisymmetry, and volume, we advocate for a more extensive and balanced lambda diagram. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for optimal production yield and longevity.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings across the reactor cross-section is complicated by internal obstructions, thereby limiting the accuracy of predictive models.  We developed a two-stage method to precisely determine the temperature cross-sectional profile in a cylindrical reactor.  Firstly, we utilized an Advanced Network Optimization technique to estimate the temperature at multiple points across the reactor cross-section through an imaging technique.  We then applied a Spatiotemporal Deep Neural Network to predict the temperature distribution across the reactor cross-section based on nearby probe temperature measurements.  We tested and validated our method with both simulated and real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness and accuracy.  Ultimately, this novel method provides a reliable approach for precise temperature measurement and mapping within complex obstructed beds.  We intend to apply this technique in various gas-phase reactions in our future work.  Such a two-stage framework can be adapted to various monitoring challenges in industrial systems.  Our work was inspired by a gas-phase reaction, but our method can be applied to various heat transfer scenarios.  It is also capable of measuring temperature distributions in other fixed bed reactors, thereby enhancing process understanding, optimizing operations, and facilitating predictive maintenance.  This simplified and effective method can be applied across a range of spatially complex systems.  In particular, it has the potential to significantly improve chemical engineering research in this domain by:  (i) empowering precise temperature measurements in complex systems;  (ii) effectively combining network optimization and machine learning for accurate predictions;  (iii) effectively handling various heat transfer problems;  (iv) effectively identifying and adapting to different operational protocols;  (v) effectively analyzing and understanding non-uniform temperature distributions;  (vi) effectively identifying and interpreting physical system characteristics from temperature data;  (vii) effectively estimating temperature across the reactor cross-section;  (viii) effectively mapping internal reactor temperature profiles;  (ix) effectively identifying heat sources and patterns within the reactor.  Such a two-stage method can be utilized for monitoring temperature in various heat transfer scenarios, thereby enhancing process understanding, optimizing operations, and facilitating predictive maintenance.  In a broader sense, this technique can be applied across a range of spatially complex systems, thereby providing practical models and effective solutions for practical challenges in the field of chemical engineering. Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the dynamic process governing the sunspots' development. Crucially, the sunspots' shape and motion can be accurately correlated with the solar flares' impact, indicating that the sunspots' motion may not necessarily be attributed to a hidden magnetic polarity alone. Instead, the solar flares seem to have caused a significant change in the sunspots' motion, leading to a revised understanding of the sunspots' rotation dynamics and the development of the sunspots in question. Moreover, the findings of our study imply a larger area affected by the solar flares, significantly exceeding the sunspots' size, thus prompting the exploration of the solar flares' impact on the global dynamics of the sun's surface through further analysis and modeling. Lastly, the observations presented in our study are consonant with the theory of magnetic fragmentation, revealing how the solar flares decompose and reshape the complex magnetic structures governing the sunspots' development and behavior. Based on this, we propose a new scenario where the solar eruptions lead to a structural reform of the magnetic polarity governing the sunspots, thereby promoting a fresh understanding of the sunspots' rotation and development. Additionally, the findings of our study are aptly compared with the numerical simulations of the global dynamics of the sun's surface, presented in a separate study. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Ultimately, the research reveals that BDDC can be a viable alternative to AMG for solving large cardiac mechanics systems when performed efficiently. A video illustrating the computational process is available online. Additional information can be found through theett project, a publicly accessible repository containing all research data and code. This research was financially supported by National Institutes of Health grants and National Science Foundation awards. It is part of an ongoing series investigating high-performance computing solutions for biomedical simulation applications, including a previous study on the scalable solution of nonlinear finite element models using BDDC/AMG. Both investigations share technical similarities but differ in their problem settings and performance optimization goals. Specifically, while this research focuses entirely on a single type of finite element grid, the preceding study introduced various grid configurations and examined the corresponding solution strategies. Consequently, the two studies share technical parallels with this research emphasizing the performance comparison between BDDC and AMG for a fixed grid, whereas the preceding study explored the influence of different grid configurations on the solution process. Both investigations are integral to a broader series of studies aimed at accelerating computational biomedical physics and biology through high-performance computing, as detailed in a preceding position paper. A key outcome of this series has been the adaptation of an advanced BDDC method suitable for complex application-driven physics and biology simulations. Crucially, this research has maintained relevance through continuous updating with recent findings, as exemplified by a corresponding presentation at an international conference on high-performance computing in medical physics and biology. A corresponding version of this research is accessible through a prominent open-access repository

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we introduce Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. In addition to serving as a critical evaluation tool, L2Explorer also showcases the potential for seamless and engaging human-AI collaborative exploration, which could lead to new and innovative applications in media and beyond. Ultimately, our objective is for L2Explorer to facilitate empiricalcomparisons of different lifelong learning methods, and we hope the framework will encourage exploration of not only automated learning processes but also human input in the creative loop. The accompanying video demonstrates the exploration of four continuous learning tasks in L2Explorer. The project is openly available and fully documented at https://www.learngoogle.org/l2explorer. System configurations and additional information can be found in the Supplementary Materials. In accordance with ethics guidelines, we conducted our study in a humane and responsible manner. In the benchmark environment, we utilized synthetic agents to assess lifelong learning methods; the robotic experiments involved real-world interactions with safe robots, and human subjects provided consent for the study. In the gameplay segment of L2Explorer, which is inspired by the popular 'MineCraft,' we adhered to the ethical standards set by Minecraft's EULA. This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where a damping mechanism prevents long-term perturbations. This research is particularly notable given that it contrasts with previous results showing no non-trivial travelling waves in areas immediately surrounding Couette flow with regularity higher than $3/2$. This work is an adaptation of C. Kenig, G. Pannier, and V. Shou's original approach in their analysis of 1D Euler equation. Our findings are further expanded to include higher-dimensional scenarios, as well as to demonstrate that 2D Euler equation exhibits a form of sub-critical behaviour when considering solutions with low regularity. This research ultimately facilitates the construction of solutions that display an accelerated decay rate, thereby bridging the gap between Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. Kenig, G. Pannier, and V. Shou. Our results are shown to be independent of the damping strength. The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission details. Recognizing the need to effectively share this information, the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact research team developed an open-access data platform comprising a data warehouse and an online dashboard, enabling transparent and efficient data sharing. This endeavour revealed challenges pertaining to data availability, credibility, and governance in the public sphere within South Africa. This research aims to investigate these concerns by examining the dynamics of data sharing among government entities, and how these impacts the public through a case study of our experience dealing specifically with COVID-19 data. This is accomplished via three key contributions. Firstly, we highlight the requirements of reliable and trustworthy data dissemination during public health crises as exemplified by our model's integration of data from diverse sources with automated data cleaning and validation processes. Secondly, we showcase the benefits of collaborative data sharing among government entities and the public through our maintenance of an up-to-date public accessible dataset and online visualisations, and the promotion of data quality via standardised guidelines. Thirdly, we stress the significance of uniform data standards and data documentation to foster transparency and trust in data sharing among government entities and the public, and to facilitate learning from our model's design and implementation. This research may be adapted to address other pressing issues in South Africa and inform data-driven decisions during future public health crises. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. This proof relies on a novel application of the Erdos-Szemeredy removal lemma. Furthermore, the proposed method's robustness and generalizability are consistently demonstrated across multiple independent runs, datasets, and models, highlighting its value as a versatile toolkit capable of addressing various challenges in visual task learning. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. In the case of simplicial algebras, the corresponding universal bundle functor maps from the category of simplicial Al to the category of simplicial sets in C for a fixed Lawvere theory Al, and this presentation is independent of C.  Further analysis reveals that every monadic functor with a representable unit admits a strong monadic structure, and this condition characterizes strong monadic structures in the context of simplicial groups and Lawvere theories that admit strong universal bundles. Finally, the classical Kleisli functor arises as the composition of a monadic transformation and a strong monadic structure in these situations. The presented framework generalizes and unifies existing results in the field while offering new insights and the potential for future research in monadic functors and simplicial structures. The research also gives rise to novel and relevant questions regarding classification of strong monadic structures and functorial properties of simplicial algebras. The provided proofs are thorough and contain valuable lemmas that can be applied to other contexts of monadic functors and simplicial structures. In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups. This outcome surpasses the previous upper limit on the number of subgroups in a finite group, as specified in a paper by Evans and Pink, with our result exhibiting a substantial improvement for groups of order $r\geq 16^2$, and also yielding the finest known estimate for groups of order $r\leq 16$. Our research is based on an expansion of the concept of ${\bf AB}$-sets, as introduced by Evans and Pink, with the aim of achieving more manageable and relevant examples. We examine a systematic collection of groups featuring specific generator pairs, such as cyclic groups, dihedron groups, and general linear groups, utilizing a computational approach for prime orders and modulating the Chebotarov density to obtain the best possible outcomes for groups of $p$-order. Moreover, our work involves applying Novak's formula for determining the number of subgroups in a finite group, as well as an advanced analysis of specific subgroups within abelian and solvable groups. Lastly, we present twenty-one examples of finite groups that attain the maximum bound of the newly derived formula for their respective orders $r$. This work is part of a broader initiative to develop an explicit formula for the number of subgroups in a finite group, as initially proposed by Evans and Pink. Although we do not succeed in achieving a direct expression, we hope that our research will serve as a foundation for future projects in this domain. In addition, we express the outcome as an explicit formula for the number of subgroups in specific group types and offer potential approaches for further projects within the broader field of finite group theory, as well as in algebraic geometry, where the introduction of ${\bf AB}$-sets reveals connections to Chow forms, as described in a paper by Kunyavskii and Shumkov. To facilitate replication, the supporting code can be accessed at https://github.com/AI-GT/Subgroup-Count Estimation. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The proposed framework's source code will be freely available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/IndigoHIT/SABRA. Our model has been implemented in PyTorch, with the repository containing all the implementation details at https://github.com/IndigoHIT/SABRA. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. We also introduce a method for determining the optimal weak measurement strength that maximises the QCC, which aligns with the optimal condition for the Hilbert-Schmidt quantum discord. Consequently, this method may serve as a useful guide for experimental procedures. We illustrate the efficacy of this measure by successfully reconstructing a quantum state from a subsystem of a composite system. We compare the quantum correlation costs associated with von Neumann measurements and weak measurements, showing that the former always excels the latter. We also demonstrate that weak measurements can be performed not only on projectors but also on any Hermitian operators, which is accompanied by the introduction of an optimal measurement strength. We develop a novel method for determining the optimal weak measurement strength that maximises the QCC, which is found to be dependent on the system's eigenvalues and positivity of its spectrum. Furthermore, this method may be useful for practical applications due to its theoretical feasibility. We also illustrate the applicability of our findings to systems comprising multiple parties, demonstrate the quantum advantage in simulation of quantum systems using the qubit-qubit interaction model, examine the quantum correlation costs in fields such as nuclear magnetism, spin-polarised electron transport and the optical pumping of semiconductors using the light-matter interaction model, which highlights the versatility of our approach. We conclude our study by highlighting several avenues for future research and exploring their potential impact on the understanding of quantum dynamics. Moreover, our results may be used to explain the quantum advantage observed in various real-world phenomena. Lastly, our work serves as a foundation for the development of new protocols derived from weak measurements, which can lead to enhanced performance in various practical applications. To facilitate future research, we have provided an open-source code that implements our protocol. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an image. Social relationship graphs were evaluated using graph evaluation metrics and visual evaluations, demonstrating the SRG-GN's performance superiority. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified error margin for MCM results. Our proposed ILP models for various MCM configurations are available in an open-source tool, integrated with the FloPoCo VHDL code generator, providing a complete flow from coefficients to hardware design. Thorough experiments were conducted to assess the models, followed by a detailed evaluation of several MCM benchmarks, showcasing the efficacy of our approach. Our findings indicate that, depending on the specific requirements, an optimal trade-off between circuit area and error rate can be achieved, yielding a maximum reduction of almost 50% in area for some constants when compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the suitability of our models for various MCM configurations, achieving significant area savings when compared to existing designs for important applications like computing polynomial products and folding multiple constant multiplication over integers. Finally, our open-source tool, optimized ILP models, and associated design files are freely accessible through a public repository, accompanied by a separate tutorial and an extensive benchmark suite of MCM M-ary Multi-Carrier Modulations, also available on GitHub. This repository facilitates reproducibility and sets the stage for future investigations, offering a wealth of information and associated design decisions. Our study reveals an interesting observation: even when the error rate is relatively high, approximately 10% for most constants, implementing an optimal MCM circuit still yields a substantial area reduction compared to traditional approaches, highlighting the considerable advantages of our ILP models. Moreover, our model's ability to accommodate multiple constants in a single circuit enhances its appeal compared to other existing designs, especially when the associated error rate can be tolerated. Our findings also show that intermediate precision truncations lead to a substantial decrease in area requirements, often exceeding 3 times, along with a corresponding rise in the error rate, averaging 14% for most constants. This behavior stems from the nature of our ILP models, which prioritize circuit area

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - for a fluid with higher-order viscosities. Our approach leads to closed-form expressions linking the mode frequencies and wave-numbers to the fluid's momentum-dependent viscosities. These expressions can be applied to both relativistic hydrodynamics' free fluids and various plasmas, as well as to the fluid descriptions derived from kinetic theory. By comparing the long-wavelength limits of our results with existing theories, as well as with numerical simulations of both relativistic hydrodynamics and the kinetic theory, we verified their consistency. Moreover, our analysis allows us to identify two distinct relaxation times: a short-scale time associated with the fluid's Navier-Stokes and Navier-Telegraph equations, and a long-scale time linked to the'silence' of the'sthermal' equation. Finally, our analysis also shows that the convergence to both fluid descriptions and kinetic theory is independent of whether they are derived from relativistic hydrodynamics or the kinetic theory. We further analyze the possibility that the cosmic background of extragalactic radio waves is linked to the presence of nearby black holes produced by the early universe's Hawking evaporation process. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended with stronger inferences for general maximum CSPs with constraints from the Boolean or real number domains, following a similar approach. Unlike prior works depending on the structure of the underlying graph class, this extension's conclusions rely solely on the existence of certain classes of minor-free graphs.

The proof involves two key contributions: first, developing new upper bounds for using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation, applicable to any graph class with limited connectivity; second, constructing suitable "super-liftings" of the Sherali-Adams hierarchy for certain graph classes with limited connectivity. These findings open new paths for solving approximation-hard CSPs while restricting the scope of the underlying graph class. Moreover, the conclusions imply PTAS's existence for any constraint satisfaction problem with a small list of allowed values. Conversely, it is shown that allowing an arbitrarily large list of values leads to harder instances, confirming the hypothesis of Tantau that there exists a maximum CSP with a small reflection-invariant property but can become intractable if allowed an arbitrarily large list of values. Finally, the conclusions are applied to derive PTAS's for specific minimization problems, such as Minimum CSP, Minimum Linear Threshold, and Hyperlinear Threshold, confirming their approximation-hardness when considering general values but allowing for tighter bounds when values are restricted to {0, 1}. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIO, to learn better parsing matrices with limited annotated trees.
