High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application, specifically employing hyperspectral images for cityscape object segmentation using an unsupervised learning approach that circumvents the need for manual object classification. This method capitalizes on the rich spectral data inherent in HSI images, which facilitates efficient object segmentation within complex urban environments. By analyzing the inherent properties of HSI images and developing a corresponding segmentation framework, we demonstrate how these images can improve low-quality labels, ultimately leading to higher accuracy in object segmentation. Our results demonstrate that this technique produces competitive results and outperforms manually refined labels in certain scenarios. Moreover, the refined labels derived from HSI images contribute significantly to the improvement of object segmentation. This research validates the significant potential of HSI images in semantic segmentation and showcases their utility in complex urban environments. Moreover, the employed hyperspectral object segmentation framework can be adapted to various camera platforms, enabling automatic object detection and segmentation in diverse settings. In addition to its inherent benefits, this technique also offers a promising solution for semantic segmentation in areas where object classification can be partially or fully inhaled. In conclusion, this research highlights the considerable value of HSI images in semantic segmentation and object detection, demonstrating their immense potential to improve robotic object segmentation within complex urban environments. Our developed hyperspectral object segmentation framework can be adapted to various camera platforms, offering a promising solution for semantic segmentation in areas where object classification can be partially or fully inhaled. This research is an extension of our previous work in "HSI-Object: A Study of Hyperspectral Images for Object Segmentation" [1]. In this updated version, additional details have been included to enhance understanding of the proposed framework, along with new results for object segmentation using the Hyperspectral Object Segmentation (HiOS) method. Moreover, the HiOS code has been made accessible on our website to facilitate reproducibility and future development of the technique. In particular, the improved version includes the evaluation of the proposed framework with multiple cityscape datasets such as NYU-2D, PascalS Segments, and Semantc Segments, as well as the introduction of a novel performance metric to gauge segmentation performance at the object level. In addition, comparative studies with prominent deep learning-based object segmentation algorithms have been conducted, confirming the unique advantages of the proposed hyperspectral object segmentation approach. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation system within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, as these stars advance to the giant stage, we anticipate discovering slower rotation speeds near the core compared to the surface. Our research focuses on the rotation profile of $ars$ 12479, a less massive ($0.187 M_\odot$) star in the metal-rich galaxy ($[Fe/H] = 0.03$), using cutting-edge observational techniques. To model the data, we integrated cutting-edge 3D congestion and radiation transport calculations into the ASTEC stellar code. Our findings show noticeable differences in the internal rotation rates, with a core rotation speed of $4.8  \pm$ 1.5 km/s and a surface rotation speed of $42.4  \pm$ 1 km/s. To explain this peculiar pattern, we considered various scenarios involving the star's interaction with its surrounding disc and the effectiveness of tidal forces in slowing it down. Our findings show that the star is likely undergoing this unusual internal rotation pattern due to its proximity to the boundary between the spiral arm and the Canopus Stream at about 2 kpc. This encounter with the stream may have caused the star to absorb rotational energy from the disk, resulting in slower core rotation and a more preserved surface rotation speed. This close encounter may have caused the star to absorb rotational energy from the disk, resulting in slower core rotation and a more preserved surface rotation speed. As a result, $ars$ 12479 serves as a compelling argument for further exploring internal rotation patterns in low-mass giant stars and the presence of congestion within these stars.  Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of incorporating 3D congestion and radiation transport modelling in the ASTEC stellar code to accurately model rotation profiles in these low-mass giant stars.  In the future, we intend to expand our modelling to incorporate extrstellar dynamical interactions and the effect of congestion on these stars.  Additionally, we plan to apply these advancements in the modelling code to a larger sample of 44 low-mass giant stars selected in the K2 programme.  Our ultimate aim is to investigate internal rotation patterns in a larger sample of low-mass giant stars and to determine whether the star $ars$ 12479, shown here to have an unusual rotation profile, is an outlier or whether other low-mass giant stars exhibit similar internal rotation

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation. A key issue arises from the RAM model's ability to perform arbitrary operations on uninitialized variables. This leads to considerable difficulty in developing efficient algorithms. In an effort to address this challenge, we can view the RAM model as an instance of the LIN class, a specific class of models characterized by having only linear independent variables. The LIN class is notable for its robust algorithmic properties. By recognizing the RAM model within the LIN class, we can leverage a wide range of established algorithmic tools. Additionally, this recognition enables us to develop a new, efficient randomized compiler that efficiently translates RAM algorithms to linear time algorithms. Our compiler can accommodate RAM algorithms featuring arbitrary operations on uninitialized variables, thus effectively resolving a long-standing open problem in algorithmic literature. A key insight behind the compiler's efficiency is the realization that randomization can effectively mitigate the complications arising from the RAM model's lack of initialization mechanisms. By leveraging randomization, we can ensure that each RAM variable is initialized, thus preserving the underlying algorithm's correctness. Furthermore, we can ensure that the compiler's time complexity scales linearly with the input size, thus effectively preserving the underlying algorithm's time complexity. Additionally, we leverage a novel application of the Moser's disdisjointness theorem to efficiently handle cases of conflicting assignments to RAM variables, thus further enhancing the compiler's efficiency and utility. By leveraging the above insights and ideas, we can develop a new family of efficient draw-and-tableau algorithms that efficiently solve fundamental graph problems such as finding a minimum spanning forest and a minimum-cost flow. A key hallmark of these algorithms is their ability to scale linearly with the input size while maintaining a linear-time complexity. Furthermore, we can leverage the randomized compiler to efficiently translate a wide range of RAM algorithms, thus effectively resolving a long-standing open problem in algorithmic literature. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as graph-specific functions. Our integrals lack the analytic nature one might initially expect. We establish that they are precise measures of the graph's Euler characteristic, its number of edges, and its barycentric spanning tree count. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  Additionally, our findings indicate that under low visual interference, these auxiliary variables can be efficiently compressed and stored in a compact manner within the RNN.  We further found that under high visual interference, RNNs exhibit distinct characteristics such as increased recurrence among auxiliary variables and enhanced sparsity in temporal context summation for object size, which together contribute to better performance.  Interestingly, our study reveals a novel mechanism by which recurrence in RNNs facilitates object categorization in visually complex conditions. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena. In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay. Pairs of dopants in close proximity exhibit unique behavior in terms of exchange interactions and quantum tunneling, leading to a hybridization of states. This research focuses on the electronic structure of two closely spaced phosphorus dopants in a silicon box, oriented in a vertical plane, with their positions varied to observe the quantum tunneling effect. Calculations incorporating the effects of spin-orbit interactions, vertical disorder, and random nuclear scattering show that the energy levels of the dopants become entangled through a common finite tunneling amplitude. In the scenario of negligible tunneling, the wave functions of the dopants remain separate, whereas, with nonzero tunneling, these wave functions get coupled by a common finite overlap integral. This coupling results in related but distinct states with energy splits of a few microelectronvolts. Moreover, the dipolelike characteristics of the coupled dopant chain give rise to a magnetic polarizability, thereby generating local magnetic fields upon the injection of spin currents. This instance of quantum tunneling has potential implications for the operations of quantum bits in silicon, particularly in relation to the generation of magnetic fields and polarization, thereby offering opportunities for improved device performance in silicon-based quantum computing. Additionally, the research shows that the spin-orbit interaction has a subtle but substantial impact on the coupled dopant chain. Finally, the research also highlights that the consequences of quantum tunneling can be identified in experiments on silicon modules by analyzing heating effects associated with spin interactions and fluorescence, thereby offering a new approach to the understanding of spin interactions in silicon. This research is expected to open new avenues in the theoretical prediction of quantum phenomena in silicon, coupled with innovative experimental methods for their identification. Moreover, the research may also be adapted for the prediction of quantum phenomena in other group IV semiconductors such as germanium and carbon. Additionally, the research can be extended for predicting quantum phenomena in silicon-germanium materials with varied silicon and germanium compositions. Lastly, the research may also be utilized in the prediction of quantum phenomena in nanostructures such as silicon nanowires and quantum wells. This research can also be extended for predicting the electronic and transport properties of nanoscaled semiconductor devices operating at the quantum level. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related concepts and examining key mathematical proofs in detail. Specifically, we demonstrate that if X is a quasi-affine toric variety that is not a torus, then its transitivity degree is infinite, unless it is a linear space. Additionally, we establish the transitivity degree for any homogeneous space of the form X / G, where X is a toric variety and G is a subgroup of Aut(X). Finally, we provide a generalized criterion for determining the transitivity degree of algebraic varieties with specific properties, including those that are complete or non-complete. This includes determinations for a range of diagonalizable varieties and imprimitive hypertorics. Ultimately, we outline unresolved problems and potential areas for further research. These results contribute to a broader understanding of the geometric and algebraic properties of these varieties, revealing connections between their arithmetic and geometric aspects. Specifically, we may deduce information about the arithmetic of Aut(X) from the dimensional structure of X. By studying the complexity of Aut(X), we can gain insight into the mixed rationality of X, as well as the degenerate rationality of its secant varieties, without directly applying algebraic geometry techniques. Specific instances include the Segre embedding of P^1 x P^1 x P^1, the Salomone cupola, the Ferrar cyclic imprimitive hypertoric, and the Roman cyclic imprimitive hypertoric. Furthermore, we may use the geometric properties of these varieties to infer rational properties of their automorphism groups. For example, if X is a hypertoric with transitivity degree m, then m is its largest invariant degree, implying the variety has no degenerate rationality. Similarly, the variety P^1 x P^1 x P^1 has four invariant degrees, but its degenerate rational properties lie beyond current understanding. Our solution paves the way for a new category of wavefunction representations, paving the way for a fresh understanding of multi-particle systems in non-commutative space-time. Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$. The cancellations of these Eisenstein series then leads to partial confirmations of a conjecture regarding the local unfolding of the archimedean part of the Asymptotic Siegel Formula. Additionally, the result is that the (ordinary) local contributions are precisely the Speh local components as described in Langlands' paper, specifically regarding the second term of the analytic Siegel formula. It is also noted that the methods employed and outcomes obtained are compatible with prior works of Muić and L. Feng. The document also includes a description of nonarchimedean local contributions and their calculation, resolving a conjecture proposed by Dickey and Muić, and specifying the support of the Whittaker function of the Speh local component, all for various values of $m$ and $n$, and $s_1,s_2$ in the set $\{0,-\frac{1}{2}\}$. The results provided are particularly specific and factored with respect to the prime number $2$. Lastly, all results have been rigorously established under the condition that $m$ is greater than or equal to $n$, and the case where the opposite holds can be obtained through a simple operation of permutation. The authors of this document confirm that the composition of the two Speh representations $\Delta(\tau,m)$ and $\Delta(\tau,n)$ results in a degenerate Eisenstein series that is indeed cancelled, and this outcome holds true for any possible combination of the two representations. Further still, it has been determined that the same pattern holds true for any number of Speh representations when combined in pairs, and this pattern can be seen in the calculation of asymptotic Siegel formulas for classical and classical-like motives, and in the local contributions at places that are nonarchimedean. Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Additionally, we examine the limitations of our method in handling multiple geometric constraints and its potential applications in navigating complex environments. Further research is needed to optimize performance in such environments. 
Ultimately, we believe this approach holds potential for implementing safe navigation systems in complex robotic configurations.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity. To enhance the accuracy of the editor distance metric, edit distance based on the Levenshtein algorithm has been utilized. Two distinct approaches were adopted for overlap-based similarity: firstly, a basic approach relying on generated graphs and secondly, a more intricate method involving multiple graphs and an integrated model, both to calculate sentence similarity. For the task of text summarization, an integrated model combining overlap-based similarity with the Levenshtein edit distance metric on undirected graphs was also explored. To tackle the issue of highly computed similarities, a novel approach involving a threshold-based filter has been proposed. Furthermore, a novel filter named Minimum Bounded Minimum Cut (MBMC) has been designed for fine-tuning the selected sentences containing vital information. Demonstrations and evaluations of the methods were performed using the widely-used DUC datasets, accompanied by a presentation highlighting the effects of the methods on text summarization, available online at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?time_of_day=34&size=large&video_id=6vpxpYElXHQ. In addition, the source code and datasets have been made available online at: https://github.com/GraphBasedSummarization. Our studies indicate that an integrated model combining the overlap-based similarity with the Levenshtein edit distance metric, accompanied by the MBMC filter, produces the most effective results. In line with this, the method has been implemented in the form of an open-source tool named Graph-Based Summarizer (GBS), designed to facilitate selective text summarization via graph-based analysis. This tool caters to both researchers and practitioners, offering an easy-to-use interface for gauging sentence similarity and generating high-quality abstracts. Moreover, the method has significant practical implications, having been validated in a wide range of applications including condensed transcripts, blogs, and real-time news updates on micro-blogging platforms such as Twitter. Ultimately, the tool has facilitated a profound understanding of text summarization via graphical analysis, empowering automatic summarization and feature extraction on a large scale. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics, effectively applying it to interferometry and information processing. \textbf{Highlights}: Our study lays out the quantum dynamics of a nonlinear Bose-Einstein condensate, resolving existing descriptions in the literature. Furthermore, we successfully developed a nonlinear version of the Hadamard gate, making it the most sophisticated gate implemented in a quantum system governed by nonlinear quantum mechanics. Moreover, we introduced a method to sample nonlinear quantum states efficiently, and this method became a key tool in generating various nonlinear quantum gates. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing is the most advanced application of nonlinear quantum mechanics in interferometry and information processing. \textbf{Capabilities}: Our developed nonlinear gate can be implemented with f-number $10^4$ and coherence time $0.1\mu$s, adequate for numerous applications including nonlinear quantum computing and interferometry. This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration. To achieve these objectives, the paper utilizes a novel approach based on the following key techniques. 1) It formulates a unique solution to a certain functional equation involving hypersurfaces and a associated capacity function. 2) This solution is shown to have properties of continuity and continuity at infinity. 3) The paper applies a specialized version of the Bernstein-Wolfmann theorem to establish the desired mapping. This method may be considered innovative and worth noting. Additionally, the paper offers a corollary based on a previous work by other authors, achieving a unicity theorem for a certain class of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share 2k hypersurfaces. This result is shown to be equivalent to a celebrated theorem by Yang-Zhang under specified conditions. Finally, the paper concludes with an examination of the limit of a complete Kähler manifold as its dimension tends to zero, resulting in a unicity theorem for a certain class of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share 2k hypersurfaces in the special case of a complete Kähler manifold with arbitrary dimension. This result is shown to be consistent with a corresponding theorem for the case of a projective space. This work is partially based on previous research by other authors, combining and synthesizing their outcomes. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation. The proposed method applies to finite-dimensional situations, whereas the Gröbner basis algorithms often encounter infinitesimal obstructions. The method involves a Gröbner basis computation for an associated linear system modulated by obstructions from the polynomial system's Newton decomposition. The Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure computes the Gröbner basis for the infinitesimal obstructions' ideal, thereby sidestepping degeneration points. A key limitation of this method involves efficiency, as it is significantly slower compared to other methods for relatively low-dimensional degeneration points. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a post-completion strategy utilizing Gröbner basis characteristics to filter out degeneration, thereby speeding up the computation. The proposed methods have been implemented in the software system GröbnerBasiscpp, showcasing promising results for various scientific vision applications. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess over hadronic contributions, we found a photon excess that increases with $N_{\text{part}}$, the number of participant nucleons, and at low $p_T$ values it exceeds that of binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ collisions by about 35%. Data from Cu$+$Cu collisions follows the trend of earlier measured Au$+$Au collisions and deviates from $J/\psi$ observed in Pb$+$Pb collisions, indicating an increasing influence of collective phenomena on direct photon production with increasing nucleon density. Furthermore, we found that Au$+$Au and Cu$+$Cu collisions yield similar photon excess ratios despite the variation in charge density, suggesting that processes other than thermalization and chemical freeze-out are responsible for the collective effects on direct photon production. Models such as $3N$-$J$ and $2J$/$k_{\perp}$ reactions, involving nucleon and quark jets interacting with nucleons and quarks in the medium, respectively, were proposed to explain the data. Finally, we evaluated the interaction of quark and antiquark producing a hard photon with charged hadrons, but it failed to account for the observed collective behavior of direct photons. Model calculations incorporating $3N$-$J$ and $2J$/$k_{\perp}$ processes for Au$+$Au, Cu$+$Cu, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions were done to verify these hypotheses. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up. The study of exco2(n,H) and related properties, including codegree patterns and distribution, could provide valuable insights into hypergraph extremality and stability. Near-optimal estimates for the Turan tetrahedron problem's asymptotic extremal function are obtained through our analysis, bringing us closer to the conjectured threshold of 7/9. Turan's tetrahedron problem's resilience to proof methodologies is also highlighted, as well as potential future directions and the beauty of this problem. Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the human visual perception of line joins. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet effective algorithm for spatial anti-aliasing, utilizing the alpha channel and texture lookup operations via a pixel shader, which results in an enhancement of the line rendering quality for maps. According to our findings, this novel technique outperforms previously established methods in terms of aesthetic appeal and efficiency. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough analysis of different filtering patterns in relation to their impact on the line width, a parameter that plays a crucial role in the visualization of vector maps. Ultimately, we establish a best practice guide for spatial anti-aliasing in line rendering, which includes an optimized phi-filter pattern suited for maps. In addition, we compare the performance of this anti-aliasing technique against other commonly used line rendering methods, providing concrete performance metrics and illustrative examples to support our claims and promote effective map visualization and fast rendering results. In particular, our study shows that this anti-aliasing technique coupled with poly-line rendering outperforms all other line rendering methods in terms of system performance and visual experience. Details of our experimental results are presented in Section 5. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of our proposed algorithm is provided to facilitate its adoption by the map visualization community. Specifically, the demo code can be accessed via the GitHub repository https://github.com/qqang/holomap, which utilizes the holomap library to generate beautiful map visualizations with spatial anti-aliasing effect. Similarly, the quasi-mc and holomap-d3 versions of this algorithm can be found respectively at https://github.com/qqang/quimc and https://github.com/qqang/holomap-d3. The multivariate interpolation operator is subjected to examination in this paper, specifically in relation to its approximation property. Researchers have found that this operator, derived from a radial basis function (RBF) with L-shaped cells, can approximate any continuous function within a specified domain at a rate of O(N^-1/2), where N represents the number of data points. In this paper, we present a new, efficient RBF based on the hyperbolic tangent, and demonstrate that it surpasses the multiquadric due to its smoother appearance. Furthermore, we prove that this new function results in faster convergence when approximating continuous functions. Additionally, our study highlights the benefits of combining the hyperbolic tangent RBF with a localized least squares algorithm, yielding superior results compared to the multiquadric with a least squares algorithm. To validate our findings, we put our methods to test using both synthetic and real-world data. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering new pulsar haloes and places where the diffusion is unusually slow.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. The dataset and source code are accessible via a public repository for the purpose of facilitating further research on robust weather detection. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model for each country, which we then apply to forecast future interests of various groups in relation to one another in Europe and the US. Interestingly, our results indicate a resurgence of public interest in climate change in both regions, albeit through different pathways. In the US, our predictions show a continued increase in general public interest but a decline among scientists, whereas in Europe, we anticipate a rise in public interest but a decrease among policymakers. We also identify several groups whose interests in climate change are mirroring each other, such as media outlets and the general public in both regions, and discover novel cross-links, including a correlation between climate change interest in Germany and investors in renewable energy. This comprehensive framework can be adapted to track the individual interests in other key issues and help in informed decision-making. Moreover, our forecasts indicate a significant shift from manual to automated forecasting by analyzing historical data of various indicators. For instance, we have calculated that analyzing climate change interest in Germany can forecast temperature changes with a mean absolute error of $0.58^{\circ}C$, a relative error of $0.14\%$. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and the non-linearity of their interaction with object surfaces make classic control approaches difficult to implement. In this study, we introduce a novel algorithm that combines online process learning with model predictive control to effectively control soft grippers. The algorithm uses data collected during the learning process to create a dynamic oral surface estimator, which is based on a time-varying kernel elastic map (KEM). The results of our simulations are very encouraging and demonstrate the feasibility of our approach. The development of this algorithm is expected to facilitate the adoption of soft grippers in various real-world applications. For example, our method could potentially enable the successful grasping of cytoplasmic components during the development of soft biomedicine. The algorithm is also suitable for use in soft/gelatinous sampling tasks and may contribute to a major advancement in soft robotics technology. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. We tested this approach in various tasks, including a neural network and a 2D physical system, where our method showed promise of matching NGD's performance and overcoming its limitations. Since our method is linked to NGD, but operates on a chosen manifold, we refer to it as the Generalized Natural Gradient Descent method. Furthermore, we discovered that GNGD can be broken down into two distinct methods, characterized by a flat or projective manifolds, each offering a new perspective on optimizing large datasets. We investigated these ideas through the lens of statistical physics, analyzing the computational complexity and efficiency of these methods. By developing an effective and efficient optimization tool, we hope to contribute to future research in this domain. In addition to its potential impact on optimization, our work also aims to promote inter-disciplinary collaboration between physics and applied sciences. As such, we included six additional sections with relevant information and promotional content to showcase the prowess of statistical physics in applying theoretical concepts to practical challenges in science and technology. These segments cover the intersection of physics and machine learning, the role of entropy in optimizing systems, the connection between quantum and classical gradients, the applicability of statistical mechanics to modern algorithms, the future prospects of this field, and the promotional benefits for researchers and readers in this domain. In contrast to a typical conference paper, our work presents six novel sections, totaling 86 pages, and 20 new figures, as well as 18 existing ones, to showcase the potential and impact of statistical mechanics on modern algorithm design. This chapter serves as a bridge between physics and applied sciences, highlighting the prowess of statistical mechanics in optimizing large datasets through actual implementation of these concepts. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxies. To address this, we're proposing a new method that uses simulated data and Delaunay triangulation to improve the accuracy of detecting prototypical "high-energy monsters" at high redshift. Our results show that using this method, we can significantly increase the accuracy of identifying distant galaxies with misaligned jets, especially when we consider the constraints of future telescope capabilities. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions that leverage multimodal clinical data. Our major contribution is AdLung, a multimodal lung cancer analysis model that combines text-based clinical information and high-resolution imaging to determine patient survival times. This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators. We conclude by investigating similar problems for gl(2) and its module of free actions. Our analysis partially answers questions posed in [Kor11] and extends results from [AW10] on the irreducibility of tensor products between highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$ to a broader class of modules. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain a desired persona, style, or safety profile. To achieve this, we've
introduced a new role-constrained dialogue generation framework that uses two
components: (1) a role encoder that converts a role specification into a
latent representation, and (2) a conditional dialogue generator that produces
responses based on this encoding in conjunction with the input context. Our
model's capabilities were demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations of
persona, style, and safety preservation across various roles and scenarios, 
showing our model's ability to effectively maintain these characteristics
consistent across multiple conversations. Furthermore, our model's overall
performance compares favorably to a leading open-domain dialogue model in
our dataset of conventional dialogue scenarios but still maintains a notable
improvement in maintaining role-consistent responses. The entire model has been
made available for public use at https://github.com/aiyanei/RCDD. Dialogue
datasets utilized in this study can be accessed via https://github.com/aiyanei/

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory. Researchers are equipped with tools to analytically both generate and detect SGWMB, and are able to gauge its strength and distribution across various scenarios. The concept of SGWMB also holds great promise for further exploration into its non-Gaussian properties and potential applications, such as being used to estimate the occurrence rate of binary black hole mergers. For instance, analyzing the summation of certain harmonic components can help establish the average temporal fluctuation. Researchers also discovered an unexpected non-zero average spatial fluctuation, and that the correlation between these fluctuations is significant. In addition, the temporal-spatial entanglement present in SGWMB is not merely a theoretical concept, but rather a real phenomenon that requires further examination. In order to better understand gravity theory, and unlock the potential of future gravitational wave observatories, researchers must thoroughly study and characterize the stochastic gravitational wave memory background. Doing so will necessarily involve collaboration with researchers from diverse backgrounds, and therefore such efforts should be inclusive and adaptive to meet the diverse needs of participants. Furthermore, the study of SGWMB offers an ideal setting in which to implement such a inclusive and responsive research approach, and therefore it serves as an excellent example for future scientists. On a broader scale, the SGWMB offers an opportunity for researchers to delve into the broader social implications of their work, and therefore it presents a valuable case study for evaluating the impact of research findings on the community. Consequently, the successful completion of this research will necessarily involve examining the dynamics of research production, and therefore it can potentially lead to improvements in research quality. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either static or dynamic methods to extract word features. In contrast, existing approaches have often overlooked the inherent structure of text, failing to account for multiple possible readings of a sentence. To address this limitation, this study proposes a novel framework, incorporating both static and dynamic features, coupled with a novel paragraph-aware recurrent neural network model to leverage the text's inherent meaning. Our study assesses the efficacy of this model against established benchmarks, using datasets compiled from the Wikipedia's full content and semantic frames. Moreover, this study showcases the potential of a new semantic resource, called Rogers, which consists of precomputed vector representations of words, their associations, and their expected neighbors. Our results indicate that the integration of Rogers achieves a new benchmark on the SEMCOR dataset, while the paragraph-aware RNN model outperforms existing approaches on the Wikipedia datasets, thereby establishing a new benchmark for word prediction tasks. Furthermore, this study validates the efficacy of Rogers in generating accurate word predictions, validating its utility as a valuable resource for Natural Language Processing applications. In conclusion, this study achieves new benchmarks for word prediction using a paragraph-aware RNN model, and showcases the ELEGS and Rogers resources, which proved to be indispensable in achieving these successes. To facilitate future research, these datasets and models have been made publicly available for further investigation into the word prediction problem. Our study confirms the exceptional performance of Rogers, while highlighting its potential to enable numerous applications in Natural Language Processing, from sentiment analysis to machine translation. Ultimately, this study marks the beginning of several promising research directions, one of which involves using Rogers to handle out-of Vocabulary words, another involves incorporating it into existing frameworks for information retrieval and generation, and lastly, utilizing it for frame-based semantic analysis. To achieve this, we propose a novel joint model for predicting words, leveraging the inherent structure of text, and estimating the likelihood of word associations based on existing knowledge graphs, thereby marking the first application of a neural network to the word prediction problem using a paragraph-aware RNN model, and showcasing the utility of the Rogers resource in achieving this success. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly eliminate disturbances, thus minimizing the time required for the swarm to reach its destination and ultimately lowering the energy consumption of this process. To quantify the extent of formation disturbance triggered by collision avoidance, deviation in the centroid of the swarm formation is measured, drawing inspiration from the concept of center of mass in classical mechanics. The study's experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed technique in terms of performance and energy efficiency. It is notable that this technique can be applied to obstacle avoidance situations as well. For instance, in a recent application of this kind, a group of drones were able to bypass an obstacle by adopting a U-shape formation (see the attached video). Video at https://youtu.be/4RJhocPFUCw. The key innovation of this study lies in the integration of point set registration and cellular automata to address the issues of collision avoidance and swarm formation reformation, presenting novel approaches to these problems. The work is preaced by a chapter on formation reformation strategy design featuring multiple techniques such as sequence optimization, depth-first search, depth-first search with reversal, and coastal traversal, explaining the fundamental concepts of collision avoidance and formation reformation in drone swarms through a unified strategy. A thorough literary review is presented in Chapter 5 of the doctoral study. The presented study was initially submitted as part of doctoral studies in the field of computer science. The primary contributions of this study reside in the automated design of formation reformation strategies using the depth-first search approach with reversal and the integration of point set registration for optimal reformation. The implementation of these ideas is showcased through a simulation platform built using C++, featuring a drone-related library that allows the creation of arbitrary shuttle graphs, selection of arbitrary nodes for reformation, and calibration of the reformation process to minimize the time required for the swarm formation to reach its destination. This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions. Furthermore, our study extends the findings to non-chain graphs. We establish a condition to determine when the Seidel matrix of a graph is circulant and examine the properties of the latter. We investigate various spectral characteristics, including eigenvalues, multiplicity, energy, and irreducibility of the matrix in question. Additionally, our work delves into the properties of the Levay matrix associated with chain graphs, presenting an inequality that outdoes a previously proposed one by Haemers in the process. Our investigations shed light on various closed problems and introduce new ones, along with providing a comprehensive comparison of the Levay and Seidel matrices through their respective powers, eigenvalues, multiplicity, energy, and irreducibility, as well as their distinctabilities in terms of matrix structure and spectral characteristics. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of leveraging Wikipedia's inherent structure and editor behavior to enhance article quality through machine learning. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. A highly efficient reinforcement learning algorithm has been developed that accelerates the training process. By imitating expert behavior, our method leverages previously gained knowledge to minimize unnecessary reinforcement learning trials. However, conventional imitation learning techniques are inefficient when the agent and expert employ different action spaces: the agent cannot directly learn from the expert's actions. To overcome this challenge, our method utilizes a technique known as action embedding, converting expert actions into a format that can be learned by the agent. Action embeddings can be acquired through various means, such as by decoding a latent space or translating the expert's actions into a comparable space. The effectiveness of our approach has been demonstrated on two complex tasks: Retro Game Controller and Continuous Control Benchmark. Retro Game Controller involves training a controller using expert gameplay data, while the Continuous Control Benchmark requires training agents using reinforcement learning and expert guidance. Our method surpasses the efficiency of conventional reinforcement learning and expert imitation learning techniques, achieving impressive results. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate of the underlying convolutional code, we can design PAC codes with superior error-correction performance and near-optimal compression ratio. We also investigate several metrics that facilitate rapid code design and illustrate the advantages of our approach by comparing it to existing PAC code designs. To validate our findings, we conducted extensive experiments and observed that our proposed metric function achieves superior performance with reduced computations compared to previous approaches. Moreover, our results suggest that the gap between the maximum mutual information and coded compression rate converges to zero for PAC codes with the proposed metric function. To facilitate the design of superior PAC codes, we created an open-source tool that designs PAC codes using our approach, which is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/AU-NTL/PAC-Decoder. This tool significantly outperforms the conventional PAC code design methods in terms of error-correction performance, compression ratio, and list Decoding computations. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the proposed metric function yields superior performance when combined with climbing staircase arithmetic coding. We also investigated the application of our approach to convolutional codes with multiple trellis structures and observed that our results remain comparable to the existing state-of-the-art convolutional codes with optimal trellis structure. Moreover, our results suggest that our approach yields superior performance for low-rate convolutional codes with the hexagonal trellis structure. Furthermore, we developed a low-complexity approximation of the proposed metric function, which maintains near-optimal performance with significantly reduced computations. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A key feature of our approach is its ability to train and deploy on various systems without needing specialized software, as long as depth camera data is available. For a range of 6-DoF kinematic systems, the method can accurately determine pose parameters with high precision. Moreover, the system requires minimal setup, as calibrating the network involves simply moving the end-effector to touch a sphere in front of the camera. Our study shows that when compared to established methods using fiducial markers, our approach is more flexible and robust, with faster calculation times and greater generalizability across different systems. For example, fiducial-based methods were found to consistently make the same mistake when using the same data, suggesting a limitation in their dependability. In contrast, our learning-based method is more trustworthy, as it uses real-world data to train and can account for potential positional and procedural variations in the training data. As a result, the method is seen as more reliable and versatile, making it ideal for use in range-based depth sensors, as well as fiducial-based systems where look-up tables for pose estimation are impractical. With this in mind, the method presents significant value to users of calibration methods, as well as potential applications in robotics, as evidenced by its effective use in vision-based robotics tasks such as object recognition, rotation prediction, and real-world project implementation. Additionally, the code and models for the method have been made publicly available. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within the network. 
The impact of treatment on other units' responses is random and independent, 
along with the interference affecting a unit's own response being different from this random effect. 
Conditions are established under which inference on treatment interference can be accurately made. 
The model allows for both homogeneous and heterogeneous treatments interdependencies. 
The latter is represented by a subgroups structure, 
enabling the identification of interference within specific groups through data-driven clustering methods or pre-defined categories. 
The impact of treatment on a network of units is tested using a permutation test, 
while confidence intervals for interference can be estimated using Bayesian methods. 
The approach is demonstrated on simulated data and real-world experiments across additivity and non-additivity scenarios. 
It is particularly useful when observing a unit's response may disturb the behavior of other units in the experiment. 
Examples of such experiments include neuroscientific studies of decision-making, 
as well as a range of other experiments such as those investigating the learning behaviors in artificial life and animation of strategic interactions in economics. 
A significant advantage of this method is the ability to perform cross-validation and assess the reliability of inferred interference. 
The approach is applied to an actual experiment involving the stimulation of a patient's premotor cortex using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), 
which is a renowned technique in neuroscientific research and is considered one of the safest procedures in neuroscience. 
In the experiment, nine patients underwent TMS at four different sites, resulting in a total of thirty-one experiments, 
with the resulting data suggesting a significant interference between two sites and the response of a third site. 
However, this effect could not be confirmed through subsequent repetitions, 
along with other experiments where the response was not affected by treatment interference. 
The proposed method proves to be an effective tool for detecting treatment interference in such experiments. 
A related R package is presented for performing computations, with example use cases and source code available at the following links: 
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/TreatmentInterference/index.html (for R) and https://github.com/alyemtzajtzi/TreatmentInterference (for GitHub). 
A related Python package can also be found at https://alyemtzajtzi.gitlab.io/TreatmentInterference/. 
Both versions provide an accurate representation of the concept.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The model's constraints are then formalized into relation sets that connect various observables of DM composition to one another. These constraints serve as a test for more comprehensive models attempting to explain multiple aspects of particle physics and cosmology within this framework. The model's capability to generate correct DM abundance is found to heavily depend on the model's parameter values, and thus we are unable to pinpoint a single set of values. However, we are able to identify several sets of values that result in the model being in compliance with observational limits of DM composition. The model's results are then compared against an alternate model, the MSNM model, in which neutrinos acquire mass through a different mechanism. The comparison is found to yield little to no discrepancy in this exchange of theoretical frameworks. The model's results are then subjected to scrutiny against a variety of astrophysical data, specifically that of cosmic microwave background, dwarf galaxies, and big buldy galaxies. The results of this examination yield no discrepancy with observational limits of this data. Moreover, we are also able to identify several regions within the model's parameter space in which anomalies in these data may manifest. This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges. A significant benefit of using larger molecular structures under 10 nm in length is that they can withstand various electrical and chemical alterations without compromising their performance as resistive switches. As such, they hold great promise for sustainable and efficient data storage in resistive memories and other emerging electrochemical devices. Lastly, alternative configurations for these molecular constructs have been proposed, incorporating electrode components that are formed into specific patterns and using a self-assembly technique to create monolayers with electrical properties that can be easily replicated and mass-produced. The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties. Our conclusions are validated by analyzing the electronic structure and how it differs from the bulk material. Lastly, we apply a generalized Ginzburg-Landau approach to determine the energy cost of various antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard ordering patterns and how this cost evolves with ultra-thin film thickness and orbital decorations. Our analysis reveals an intricate relationship between different orbital triplets, thin-film geometry, and material physics that govern the metal-insulator transition in ultra-thin strontium vanadate films. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of terminal cations, ultra-thin film reconstruction, and changes to coordination polyhedra, as well as the associated orbital degrees of freedom, in dictating the unusual metal-insulator transition in these films. Such an understanding can be applied to other transition-metal oxides to predict potential thickness-induced insulator-metal transitions in these materials. Additionally, this research may stimulate experimental measurements to verify our theoretical predictions and offer a broader perspective on ultra-thin film transition-metal oxides and their potential applications in advanced technology. Conversely, our study's focus on ultra-thin strontium vanadate films allows for a more in-depth examination of this particular material system, including its underlying physics and the interplay between electronic, magnetic, and orbital interactions that give rise to the thickness-induced insulator-metal transitions in this material. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread practices, including parameter regularization, dropout, and early exogenous termination, serve to control geometric complexity. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of our framework in constructing more efficient training pipelines for deep learning models. Our study is the first to our knowledge to link standard deep learning techniques to a controlled variation of model functions. Our method permits the development of more effective training protocols that balance model performance and generalization. Our empirical findings reveal that two distinct training approaches exist, each corresponding to varying degrees of geometric complexity: a dropout model and a residual network, each exemplifying a distinct level of geometric complexity. Our research also shows that early exogenous termination in dense models and parameter pruning in convolutional models both serve to reduce geometric complexity. Our analysis indicates that Naive Bayes Neural Networks, neural networks characterized by their lack of learnable parameters apart from their initial weights, exhibit the highest degree of geometric complexity. Our research poses important questions about the characteristics of geometric complexity in deep learning models, whether these arise from their architecture, their hyperparameters, or their training protocols. Our study also raises questions about the intercorrelation of different metrics used to control model complexity. Our research also serves to illustrate the effectiveness of our framework in constructing more efficient training pipelines, promoting further research into its applications to deep learning models. A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice. Furthermore, this technique can be applied to future single-top and triple-lepton production measurements at hadron colliders that may offer improved sensitivity to new physics. Although new challenges arise from dealing with experimental sidebands and radioactive contaminants, the direct detection method remains attractive due to its relative simplicity and computational efficiency compared to traditional Bayesian techniques. However, this approach requires careful radioactivity control to prevent background from radioactive decay in the detector's crystal, which might offer further improvement with radioactivity suppression. Finally, the direct detection method's sensitivity to new physics is tested against beyond Standard Model theories involving vector-like doublets and leptoquarks, exhibiting promising results that could potentially be verified with up to $20\%$ larger Wilson coefficients. This theoretical model's corresponding $R_{K^{(*)}}$ ratios could reach values as high as $0.112$, and various flavour-violating decay couplings including $\bar{B}^0\to \bar{K}^0 X" a_\mu$ and $\tau^+\tau^- X" a_\mu$ could reach levels as high as $10^{-2}$, offering unique insights into the structure of these leptoquark particles. Ultimately, the direct detection method's sensitivity could reach levels as low as $10^{-10}$ for certain leptoquark masses below $6.8\,{\text TeV}, 6.3\,{\text TeV}}$ for $X"$ type leptoquarks and $4.3\,{\text TeV}}$ for $Y"$ type leptoquarks, thus providing valuable particle mass bounds. This approach has far-reaching applications and can be adapted for various theoretical models and rare processes such as $b\to c \mu \mu$ transitions. Moreover, its versatility makes it suitable for use in a precision strategy for particle physics that could potentially offer sensitivity to new physics up to $10\,{\text TeV}}$ with future experiments and particle colliders. \\ \\ \\ \\ \\

Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile automated essay grading model across diverse topics.  Our key findings are as follows: (1) BERT and RoBERTa outperform an outstanding competitor model by a significant margin; (2) Pre-trained models excel over an RNN-based competitor model; (3) Several data augmentation methods substantially enhance model performance; (4) BERT achieves impressive results with minimal training times compared to a 3-layer LSTM model; (5) BERT's performance remains exceptional even with a substantial reduction in its training dataset.  Our study's findings have valuable research implications and practical applications in developing highly accurate automated essay grading models.  Our model code and supporting materials are freely accessible at https://github.com/jc-woods/MAVLE.
