By leveraging Markov chains, our method enables the computation of these quantities even when direct access to data is impractical. We also evaluate the performance of our approach using synthetic data and observe that the estimated values converge closely to the true entropies with increasing chain size. Additionally, our method has potential applications in predicting the flow of data across network boundaries. The proposed algorithm is potentially efficient for large-scale networks, as its computational cost scales linearly with the number of network nodes. Furthermore, our study introduces a novel approximation of relative entropy that forms the basis of this new method. We also explore an alternative adaptive sampling technique to reduce mutual information estimates from streaming data, along with an empirical evaluation of these estimators using synthetic data. Lastly, our research examines the cryptographic concept of differential privacy in relation to its relation to mutual information, providing an alternative interpretation and more precise bounds on the gain of relative entropy due to privacy violations. These findings contribute enhancements to current differential privacy protocols. Specifically, our study leads to tighter bounds on high-variability data, whereas existing protocols rely on conservative approximations of mutual information. This improvement potentially reduces unnecessary data deletions, thus conserving more data and strengthening privacy guarantees. Furthermore, our model sheds light on the trade-offs between data retention and privacy, and suggests enhanced differential privacy could be achieved by prioritizing data retention. We validate this claim through modified differential privacy protocols. Additionally, our study develops new, previously unknown bounds on the relative entropy of uniform distributions, along with extensions to structured probability distributions with significant practical implications. Notably, our method offers an O(N^(-2alpha)) error bound, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art error bound of O(N^(-alpha)) for mutual information estimation. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows exceptional performance in training time and disk usage efficiency while only slightly underperforming state-of-the-art classifiers, such as Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest, with a relatively minor reduction of 2% in accuracy and F1-score. Notably, NBcoded excels at noisy data handling, achieving up to 100% improvement in F1-score on datasets with high noise levels. The proposed NBcoded classifiers successfully classify attacks on IoT devices, network traffic, and medical images, suggesting versatile applications of these classifiers. Crucially, NBcoded offers scalable value, allowing efficient classification with a minimal resource usage of 30MB, compared to the 1GB required by Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest, thereby paving the way for low-resource deployment on devices, such as those with 128MB memory used in industrial settings or 64MB used in IoT applications. In conclusion, NBcoded offers a practical solution for efficient cyber attack detection with a focus on practical, resource-efficient implementation. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups and the general linear group SL_d(K), using this framework to gain insights into G's set actions and its byproducts on graph representations. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into comfortable living spaces, capturing prey, evading predators or interacting with fellow creatures. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse motivations behind movement, thus understanding the patterns and drivers of animal locomotion requires thorough observation of their natural behavior. Historically, researchers have used straightforward and efficient approaches like motion detection or the extraction of specific movement patterns to gather insight into animal movement. Nonetheless, these earlier methods failed to provide a comprehensive framework for exploring the dynamics of large animal cohorts under dynamic environmental conditions. To address this gap, our study leverages the strength of multiple computer vision techniques in a comprehensive model, capable of processing numerous species such as birds, insects, mammals and fish under various lighting and camera setups. The proposed model extracts crucial movement information while maintaining simplicity and efficiency, thus enabling the detection and tracking of moving entities at a low computational cost of around 10 milliseconds per frame. This fast processing capability enables real-time analysis and facilitates exploring complex patterns in animal movement on large scales over extended periods of time with a high level of detail. To validate our model, we studied the movement patterns of (i) a flock of birds, (ii) a group of insects, (iii) a herd of small animals and (iv) a school of fish under natural and constant light conditions, thus gaining significant insight into their collective behavior and the possible functions of their coordinated movements. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the potential for advanced computer vision to shed light on the intricate movements of animal species and the various motivations behind them. The proposed framework is designed to be user-friendly and adaptable, thus empowering researchers to make similar discoveries in the field of animal biology with their own datasets and cameras. The code for our proposed model is available for public use at https://github.com/visual-oneiroi/Animal_Locomotion_Analysis. The video demonstrating our model's capabilities is available at https://vimeo.com/377183126. Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations. 
Additionally, our research highlighted the potential of quantum computing in solving complex optimization problems within transmission power systems. Further exploration of quantum approaches could effectively reduce the costs associated with power transmission. 
As an innovative application of quantum computing, this study contributes to the growing field of quantum-assisted operations management.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This research shows that employing ML/AI in isolation will often be insufficient for accurately inferring universal physical laws and highlights the necessity for further modifications. Possible avenues for advancement include the incorporation of external knowledge about the physical process in question or designing artificial intelligence systems that can reorganize and simplify the underlying dynamics of complex systems directly from measurements. Until significant advancements are made in this field, it will be essential to exercise caution when interpreting the results of automated physics discovery experiments, particularly when formulating laws that are universally applicable to all observed phenomena. We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized mode splitting. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the cavity and the nanobeam, ultimately enhancing the Purcell factor and source efficiency. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world imperfections affecting material properties, feature size, and shape. Moreover, we studied and compared different coupling schemes including a compact source configuration and a more extended ridge waveguide setup, evaluating their advantages and limitations. Ultimately, we found that our optimized design featuring a nanobeam cavity and a linear ridge waveguide offers superior single-photon source performance compared to other coupled cavity approaches. This research outlines an effective methodology for enhancing the performance of electrical-driven single-photon sources employing a coupled quantum dot-cavity system coupled to a linear ridge waveguide. This approach can be used to develop state-of-the-art single-photon sources for application in quantum computing and other quantum technology initiatives. Additionally, we observed that our design may be adapted for application in single-photon generation from a quantum dot incorporated in a coherent interferometer, thereby enabling the generation of correlated photons and implementing a crucial component of quantum cryptography and communication systems. Furthermore, we compared our design to another prominent single-photon source scheme, examining differences and limitations, and proposing potential improvements to its performance through further refinement. This research therefore serves as a useful reference and guide for designers and researchers working on single-photon generation and quantum cryptography applications. Lastly, we examined potential avenues for further optimizing the performance of single-photon sources, identifying novel opportunities for application in both quantum cryptography and computing initiatives. This research therefore serves as a useful introduction and overview for designers and researchers working on single-photon generation technologies. Moreover, we further analyzed the capabilities of our design to enable the creation of entangled photons via a quantum dot incorporated in a Coherent Interference Platform, thereby providing a blueprint for quantum cryptography and communication

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, including the contribution of atoms on the potential energy surface. To further investigate the boson peak, a numerical method for determining a glass's vibrational density of states is proposed, where an extensive simulation of quasicontinuous sound waves is performed, and the density of states is then extracted from these simulations. A detailed examination of a binary hard-sphere glass reveals that the conclusion that boson peaks are stiffened can be supported with theoretical evidence. Moreover, by dividing the vibrational modes into those leading to sound wave-like movements and those that do not, it is found that the latter significantly contributes to the boson peak, and stiffening of this peak can be attributed to these high-frequency motions. Finally, the possibility of accurately determining dynamic properties of glasses through inelastic neutron scattering experiments by dividing the vibrational modes into those on and off the potential energy surface is explored. Based on this theory, the boson peak of a binary hard-sphere glass, and by extension most glasses, is found to be primarily composed of these high-frequency off-the-energy surface vibrational modes. Consequently, arguments suggesting that the boson peak is a manifestation of the two-level system phenomenon are reinforced. Additionally, this research highlights the distinct dynamics of motions on and off the energy surface, and proposes the distinction to be an essential factor in the understanding of boson peaks in glasses. To better comprehend this, a detailed examination of the boson peak in a hard-sphere glass, and its substantially altered version when coupled with a soft-sphere component, is conducted. Furthermore, this study shows that modifying certain properties of a hard-sphere glass will not significantly alter the location of its boson peak, and the mechanism of a boson peak is found to be non-universal. To validate this claim, accurate determinations of the boson peak in several glasses, including silica, are found to be in agreement with simulations, and the theory that the boson peak is a manifestation of the two-level system phenomenon is supported. Lastly, this study examines the effect of temperature on the boson peak of a hard-sphere glass and finds that the two-level system theory is capable of both explaining the existing research findings and predicting new ones. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A recent extension of the Stable Roommates problem, involving three-dimensional valuations, seeks to find stable matchings that adhere to a consistent valuation scale. Our research shows that, unlike the standard Stable Roommates problem, there exist situations where no stable matches exist. However, we found that, under the context of three-dimensional valuations, establishing a stable matching becomes possible by adopting a total order for each agent's preferences while still maintaining their individual hierarchical rankings. Conversely, we identified cases where no stable matches could be found, even after applying total order constraints to agent preferences. Moreover, we reduced the problem of finding the best stable matches to a linear programming task, given total order constraints for each agent's preferences. Furthermore, we examined variations of the problem involving multi-dimensional valuations, where agent preferences may reflect multiple separate scales of values, and derived comparable results. Last, we analyzed combinations of these valuation methods, yielding comparable outcomes. At the center of our research lies the goal of determining whether total order constraints can guarantee the existence of stable matches and, if so, what implications this may have on computational complexity. Our key findings in this research involve showing that, under the context of three-dimensional valuations, total order constraints allow for polynomial-time computability of finding the best stable matches, even when considering arbitrary valuations scales. Conversely, we showed a two-dimensional scenario, involving agents with one-dimensional valuations scales, for which finding the best stable matches becomes an NP-complete problem, even under total order constraints. By simplifying our approach, we also derived an NP-complete proof for finding stable matches in a standard two-dimensional setting, eliminating the need for total order constraints. Furthermore, we derived several other complexity results for variations of the problem involving three-dimensional valuations. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a cost-effective and uncomplicated design for low-cost mm-wave base and wideband antenna designs. Additionally, the simple structure allows for easy fabrication of wide beam wideband antenna designs with minimal complexity. The research presents computational and measured results for this novel design. Computational and measured results of this wide beam wideband antenna design are presented, demonstrating agreement between computational and measured responses in terms of coverage, width and frequency. The research also showcases computational and measured results of a two-element array, showcasing operation over a 30% frequency range with wide beamwidths of 100-125 degrees at 35 GHz, 50-57.14 GHz, and 35-41.25 GHz for the respective element spacing of 0.8, 0.5, and 0.1 wavelengths at the respective frequencies. The research also reveals the presence of grating lobes at 46.28, 58.42 and 70.42 GHz for the respective array configurations with a wide beamwidth, primarily due to the height of the microstrip elements above the ground plane. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, which excites interest in related free fermion models. Studies on these models have already yielded significant insights; for example, the quasi-one-dimensional version of the surface code has a phase transition when the perimeter of the code reaches a certain size. To build a quantum computer based on this code, the critical size needs to be exceeded. Similarly, the study of the bond-free surface code reveals a phase transition within the quasi-two-dimensional version that needs to be overcome to build a quantum computer. Developing the code further eliminates the need for connectivity between distant points, a critical factor for the wide adoption of quantum computing. While the free fermion algebra allows for simplified modeling, the lack of a clear understanding of the code's phase diagram presents a challenge to building a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Despite these limitations, the potential for topological error correction codes in quantum computing makes them crucial for the future of quantum technology. We resolve the uncertainty surrounding the free fermion surface code by proving that the critical point matches the computational resource requirement for a fault-tolerant quantum computer. To achieve this, we construct a planar cluster tree that influences the connectivity of the lattice and affects the connectivity of the lattice and its subcode. We show that a semi-perimeter bound of $\Theta(\log N)$ is sufficient for the semi-perimeter of the code. We establish this bound by first finding an approximate minimum spanning tree of the lattice and its dual, and using it to create the cluster tree. We apply a technique called a 'doubler' to convert the tree into a cluster tree, and prove its efficiency along with a matching lower bound. To build the cluster tree, we introduce a potential function that grows slowly and uses it to determine the minimum weighted graph that satisfies a pre-set condition. We show the existence of such a graph within a pre-set weight class, and prove its efficiency along with a matching lower bound. These findings lead to the development of a planar cluster tree, and prove its distinct phases based on the density of the generating probability distribution. By choosing the probability distribution wisely, we eliminate the need for connectivity between distant points, a critical factor for the wide adoption of quantum computing. To achieve this, we introduce a new type of intersection that replaces the standard intersection that may connect distant points, and shows its planar nature along with a matching lower bound. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation shields the networks from OoD data during training. 

On the other hand, the rich initial features also provide an effective shield against ill-defined data within the training set. As a result, the model can effectively handle both in-distribution and OoD data. 

We develop a straightforward generalization bound that captures the relationship between the model's initial features, regularization, and handle for OoD data. 

We propose a novel regularization technique rooted in the Cram\'{e}r bound that minimizes the variance of the model's predictions among neighboring data points. 

Our approach is far more efficient than current methods, yielding state-of-the-art results on BMNIST, Linear Probes, and various real-world datasets in both causal reasoning and OoD detection scenarios.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous for detecting particles. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of epitaxial material as the active area. In this study, we investigate the properties of CMOS sensors constructed on high-resistivity Czochralski wafers. The research demonstrates that replacing epitaxial material with a high-resistivity substrate enhances sensor performance and increases overall detection efficiency. The study focuses on a 300 mm CZ wafer with a high resistivity, utilizing the FAIR-CMS TCAD tool to simulate the material's properties. The results reveal that our simulation closely matches experimental findings, yielding an improved hit detection efficiency and reduced electronic noise for the CMOS sensor. The increased resistivity in the CZ material reduces the junction capacitance, thus minimizing electronic noise. Additionally, the higher resistivity limits the edge-of-petals leakage current, enabling higher resistivity and enhanced charge collection efficiency. The publication discusses these findings and explores opportunities for further improvement in CMOS sensor technology using the CZ material. The research is versatile and can be applied to various sensor architectures beyond small collection electrodes, including those used in CMS track-telescope rombers and large-format detectors featuring pseudo-wire chambers. In conclusion, substituting epitaxial material with a high-resistivity CZ material significantly improves CMOS sensor performance, presenting an attractive option for monolithic active pixel detectors. The success of this research paves the way for further innovations in CMOS sensor technology, potentially facilitating a high-tech contribution to particle physics at the Large Hadron Collider. The CZ material's benefits also show potential for applications beyond particle physics, including in medical imaging, computed tomography, and spectroscopy, where improved charge collection efficiency and reduced edge-of-petals leakage current can significantly benefit detector performance. In particular, the high resistivity in the CZ material enables a higher circuit clock frequency, thus increasing the accessibility of CMOS sensors to various detection events. The increased time resolution in CMOS sensors constructed on CZ material facilitates a high-tech contribution to particle physics, while the improved properties also present opportunities for applications in X-ray imaging, photo-sensing, and spectroscopy. The CZ material's properties offer an enhanced time resolution of up to 20 ns, an increased charge collection efficiency of up to 99%, an reduced edge-of-petals leakage current of nearly three orders of magnitude, and a higher circuit clock frequency of up to 100 MHz. Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when the atmosphere is unstable. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, demonstrating its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the telescope and a mock instrument. This test confirmed that FAST can be an essential component of future exoplanet detection missions, readying the ground-based telescopes for the task of directly identifying and studying the most promising exoplanets. This breakthrough will soon enable the detection of seven-Earth-mass planets around stars with brightness equivalent to that of the Sun, a significant breakthrough in the field of exoplanet detection and characterization.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid and particle solvers, and a variable number of small collision time steps to ensure accurate simulation while maintaining efficiency. Our method also conserves energy and momentum to a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, we enhanced the stability of this algorithm through three techniques - average force acceleration for particle motion, exponential integration for predicting particle positions, and a "predict-correct" method for integrating particle velocities. Our method was validated against theoretical models for all relevant physical regimes of particle collision, and compared to existing methods through a number of benchmark tests and complex simulations, including fluidized beds and collision-driven sedimentation. Our results show that our method is highly accurate and only slightly more computationally expensive than existing methods. Our code is available online for researchers to use. Ultimately, we believe this method will be useful for simulating and analyzing a wide range of phenomena involving particle collisions in various fields such as fluidized beds, geological processes, and biomedical applications. Additionally, we examine the broader application of this theorem within the context of expressing a sum of cubes as the product of two relatively prime numbers. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory for data consistency. In this study, a new model-based algorithm was developed to ensure data consistency and achieve fault-tolerant checkpointing in high-performance computing systems using non-volatile memory. This algorithm was tested across various scenarios, including real-world applications, and the results demonstrate that it can quickly identify all data elements, thus enabling rapid data consistency and regular data checkpointing with minimal impact on program slowdown. Further analysis highlights the program overheads in terms of cost, data consistency cost, and checkpointing cost to demonstrate the practicality of this method for maintaining data consistency and checkpointing in high-performance computing systems. The study's findings show that this algorithm is suitable for a wide range of programs and compatible with various data distribution patterns, thus requiring minimal program modification to work effectively. Finally, the study's results illustrate that this algorithm can effectively minimize slowdown when regular checkpoints are created, as demonstrated by means of standard performance metrics such as parallel program slowdown time. In order to facilitate further research, the algorithm's code and other supporting materials have been made available on a public repository for continued development and testing. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. This approach enables the discovery of hierarchical structures from millions of articles, making Wikipedia a ideal testing ground for developing an automated information hierarchy extraction system. Our results accurately reflect human-curated hierarchies and demonstrate the potential for semi-fully supplementary classification. Furthermore, we introduce a novel application, HierArchY (HARY), extracting hierarchical structures from Wikipedia for all articles under 10,000 bytes and showcasing the efficacy of HDTM. With over 2,52,111 valid hierarchies covering 8,38,615 articles and 4,079 new recognized categories, our work lays a foundation for various uses, such as personalized navigation, content summarization, and navigation. This revised model employs a computational complexity of O(|E| |V| log^2 V)), making it highly efficient for large networks. To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and the category of complete metric spaces with uniform mappings.

This embedding corresponds to the inclusion of the domain of the predicates in question within the domain of subobjects in the respective categories.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction and medical feature analysis. Validation on an independent test set confirms the generalizability and robustness of the model, yielding a prediction accuracy of 0.7764. Evaluations using multiple performance metrics reveal that the proposed method exhibits superior performance over existing methods in predicting suicidal ideation. Lastly, the model's capabilities are highlighted through the analysis of clinically relevant predictors of suicidal ideation. All code has been openly disseminated on the GitHub platform for the purpose of replicating the results reported in this study. Additionally, efforts have been made to ensure the transparency and trustworthiness of the code used for forecasting suicidal ideation. Any inquires or feedback can be directed to arnaldo.garcia@utexas.edu. Similar work has been shared on arXiv at the hyperlink provided for arXiv:2102.13299.s. Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission from Cassiopeia A at 0.9 keV using data from the XMM-Newton satellite. The observed polarization degree for the synchrotron component is approximately $20\%$, with an average angle of $16^\circ$ and an uncertainty of $8^\circ$. The thermal radiation from Cassiopeia A's core is found to be perfectly depolarized, supporting a hard-spectrum diffuse emission model. Our findings demonstrate that X-ray polarization can effectively distinguish between synchrotron and bremsstrahlung radiation, even at keV energies, and have important implications for the interpretation of polarization data from supernova remnant studies. Furthermore, the observed polarization data is consistent with a two-component model consisting of a mixed synchrotron-bremsstrahlung radiation and a thermal radiation for energies above 2 keV. Finally, the observed alignment of the polarization vector with the magnetic field orientation and the presence of polarization from the central core of Cassiopeia A provides conclusive evidence of a direct connection between the magnetic field and the synchrotron emission. \end{abstract}

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherently superimposing ten number states makes it a suitable candidate for achieving robust sensitivity with simple resources. Our work lays out a clear choice for achieving a high-level of sensitivity in measurements, selecting either the optimal non-classical state or a more resilient alternative. Moreover, in a scenario where states can be repeatedly prepared, proposed and compass states display equivalent performance, now both achieving the ultimate in sensitivity in parameter estimation. Finally, in a practical demonstration, the comparable sensitivity of both scenarios, in both theoretical cases, is confirmed through simulation based on current technology. Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating it using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces is statistically certain to occur when the virus exhibits enzymatic activity. Furthermore, the characteristics of this movement, such as speed and direction, are heavily influenced by the presence of specific molecular interactions between the viral spike proteins and the carbohydrates in the surface layers. Additionally, it was discovered that viral movement on surfaces is not solely determined by random movements but can persist in a directed motion under specific conditions. This directed movement can occur at speeds up to 0.01 um/s, which is significant because it could potentially enhance viral infection by allowing the virus to travel longer distances over the host's surface. A statistical model was also developed to describe the diversity of viral movements and provide specific predictions for a particular influenza strain. This model indicates that viral movement away from its initial location within a carbohydrate layer takes longer and is more likely to occur with higher protein-to-carbohydrate ratios, as well as when the virus's spike proteins are more flexible. Specifically, it was predicted that viral movement outside of a carbohydrate layer would take approximately 10 minutes to 10 hours to happen 50% of the time with a protein-to-carbohydrate ratio of 10:1. Finally, it was suggested that viral movement could be significantly slowed down with higher protein-to-carbohydrate ratios by incorporating more rigid carbohydrate molecules into the surface layers. This could potentially block viral movement for 90% of such influenza strains, effectively halting their active movement on glycan-covered surfaces. This research provides powerful tools to study viral metabolism, offering a universal explanation for viral movement based on a general biological principle and validating it with realistic physical mechanisms. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that modifying surface layers to hinder viral movement could be an effective way to hinder active virus movement, which might be beneficial in developing new strategies to combat infectious viruses. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters. Additionally, S and U galaxies differ in their supermassive black hole masses, with U galaxies tending to have lower black hole masses. Our findings indicate that U galaxies are characterized by their blue color, elevated star formation rate, and warped structure, distinct from S galaxies' generally flat disks and lower star formation rates. Further, U galaxies with more pronounced warps have higher star formation rates, implying an internal connection among these characteristics. U galaxies' origins remain elusive but are likely related to interactions with the environment that result in disk deformation and a new morphological classification system. This system helps differentiate between internal and external drivers of galaxy evolution and highlights the diverse responses of galaxies to environmental interactions. Based on these insights, we propose that U galaxies should be prioritized in future spectroscopic surveys of massive, edge-on galaxies to further elucidate their stellar populations, star formation rates, and other characteristics. Additionally, targeting U galaxies in the southern hemisphere via the Wide Field Survey of the VLTI OBs telescope and other initiatives could provide valuable comparative data. Lastly, U galaxies present an opportunity to test established theories of galaxy evolution and develop new ones through quantitative modeling and analysis. In conclusion, U galaxies pose an intriguing and previously underappreciated challenge to our understanding of galaxy development and the impact of environmental interactions. By continuing to study these galaxies, we can gain a deeper understanding of how they came to be and what their presence indicates about the role of environmental interactions in galaxy evolution. This knowledge can subsequently be applied to other warped galaxy types and will ultimately contribute to a more comprehensive, inclusive galaxy taxonomy.} }. In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also observe that, unlike in insulators, the summation of nonadiabatic Born effective charges from sublattices in metals does not equal zero but rather correlates directly with the Drude weight. These conclusions were verified through calculations using density functional perturbation theory, as applied to aluminum, and to two doped compounds, electron-doped tin disulfide and strontium titanate. Our results highlight the significance of nonadiabatic effects on Born effective charges, especially at elevated temperatures and long wavelengths. Moreover, the obtained results offer insights into electron-phonon interactions and, in doped compounds, provide insights into electron-phonon interactions and compare them with results for the dielectric constant. Lastly, our study demonstrates the feasibility of calculating Born effective charges using first-principles methods within the metal range through the use of nonadiabatic schemes. Additionally, our work indicates that the nonadiabatic correction to the adiabatic Born effective charges is substantial relative to the adiabatic values for the materials examined, implying the Adams-Gibbs grand canonical ensemble as a suitable model for describing electron-phonon interactions in metals. However, this model underestimates the adiabatic values by approximately one order, as observed in aluminum, tin disulfide, and strontium titanate. Despite this underestimation, the model provides an accurate prediction for the nonadiabatic pressure in aluminum, as well as pressures associated with phonon modes that are either longitudinally polarized or have mixed polarization characteristics, as calculated for the metals listed. Lastly, our findings suggest the derivation of an inequality governing the sum of adiabatic and nonadiabatic Born effective charges. When the adiabatic values are negative for a sublattice, this inequality indicates that the nonadiabatic values will be positive, whereas the opposite holds true for the adiabatic range. This relationship was verified for the materials examined. Overall, our study highlights the crucial role nonadiabatic effects play in the calculation of Born effective charges and, by extension, provides significant insights into electron-phonon interactions within the metal range. We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description within this range. Specifically, our analysis implies that the exponentially decaying energy spectrum and the extreme intermittency in the far-dissipation range of turbulence predicted by deterministic Navier-Stokes equations will be replaced by Gaussian thermal equipartition at scales below the Kolmogorov length. High-Reynolds-number simulations based on the stochastic shell model corroborate our theoretical predictions, and demonstrate that the extreme intermittency in the inertial range can extend deeply into the dissipation range, leading to large thermal fluctuations at scales below the Kolmogorov length. Our study re-ignites the debate on thermal turbulence, and highlights the need for re-evaluating the Navier-Stokes equation for high-Reynolds-number fluid turbulence. Moreover, the extreme intermittency in the far-dissipation range of turbulence may offer unprecedented opportunities for observing thermal fluctuations in molecular fluids. If successfully realized, this could provide valuable insights into the nature of quantum turbulence and its transition to classical turbulence. Finally, our study also emphasizes the need for re-evaluating the Navier-Stokes equation for high-Reynolds-number fluid turbulence, and paves the way for a potential new area of research in intermittent thermal phenomena. Conversely, this could provide valuable insights into the nature of quantum turbulence and its transition to classical turbulence. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences from internal and external factors. To illustrate the distinct responses, we examine the magnetoelectric properties of topological insulators in the presence of time-reversal symmetry. A time-reversal-breaking external field induces the emergence of a current and a local polarization within a three-dimensional topological insulator, as evidenced by a change in its Hall conductance and a non-zero entangled Pockels tensor. This phenomenon is evident both in thin films with surface electrons and in fully three-dimensional materials composed of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and Te$_2$. We discuss how these properties can be detected through observable effects on the system's entangled degrees of freedom and highlight the significance of thick versus film dimensions. Moreover, we examine the contrasting behavior of a quantum point contact connected to a topological insulator, as its transmission coefficient and correlation function vary with energy. Finally, we investigate the magnetoelectric properties of a time-reversal symmetric system in the presence of non-abelian topological effects, as seen through the behavior of Majorana zero modes and edge currents within a fully gapped topological superconductor. By combining theoretical models and actual materials like the Te$_2$ family, we have developed an understanding of these novel magnetoelectric properties of topological insulators. Furthermore, we feature key findings and discuss their implications for time-reversal symmetric topological materials, as well as their extensions to surface electron gases and Majorana zero modes. Additionally, we outline the potential for detecting these magnetoelectric properties in real-world samples through the use of transport current measurements. Due to their novelty and depth, these considerations have provided an opportunity to delve into the intricacies of topological insulators, as well as the properties and potential of the materials in question. Lastly, we outline perspectives for further research in this field and its connections to the broader literature. Moreover, we feature essential elements and discuss the significance of detecting these magnetoelectric properties in time-reversal symmetric topological materials, as well as the potential for applications in quantum computing and the study of Majorana zero modes. Introducing a periodic distortion to the time-delay amplifies global patterns such as spikes and waves, leading to a significant global control effect even with minimal parameter adjustments. These global pattern formations are highly sensitive to the time-delay and can be manipulated to induce abrupt changes in the system's behavior, revealing a new type of global pattern control. The implications of these findings are further exemplified through the study of the Lorenz system, where we observed a significant global control effect when the time-delay is modulated appropriately. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy between them, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Specifically, this research defines (i) a denotational model as a Scott domain with computable continuous functions mapping denotations to subsets of possible values in denotational computations; (ii) a corresponding operational model based on a probabilistic version of the Curry-Howard correspondence, where stochastic lambda-terms represent proofs of abstract logical formulas; (iii) a operational big-step stochastic semantics that derives values from context-dependent stochastic lambda-terms via stochastic computation; (iv) a small-step operational semantics that drives a stochastic lambda-calculus interpretation compatible with the operational model. To achieve this compatibility, this research introduces suitable concepts for stochastic lambda-terms and contexts, showing that the associated computational semantics is both sound and sufficiently strong. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the operational and denotational models are adequately related by constructing a continuous and monotone inversion function between the respective domains, which can be viewed as a stochastic version of the Tarski correspondence. This continuation of previous work not only replicates the main outcomes but also includes substantial improvements in reasoning and additional useful concepts for stochastic code analysis. These advancements include a suitable notion of context freeness for stochastic lambda-terms, a sound and sufficiently strong model for a stochastic PCF like language, and a compilation theorem from a higher-level stochastic model to the lower-level stochastic PCF model. (2018). Despite the difficulties, this research was able to define a stochastic PCF like language and prove a compilation theorem from a higher-level stochastic model to the lower-level stochastic PCF model. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets. Additionally, we explore the potential of incorporating more sophisticated features and features selected via feature selection methods to further improve design mining's effectiveness. This work highlights the path forward for design mining, suggesting it as an essential tool for developers to effectively document and improve their design efforts, ultimately benefiting from their collective experience and knowledge. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free bonus, coming before the main optimization task. In this study, we devise a universal gradient-based method to uncover the proximal structure of nonsmooth functions and, simultaneously, solve the associated optimization problem. Our generic approach is applicable to any proximal structure, and, in addition to the standard Sparsity, Gradient-Location, and Weak-Sub-Gradient structure, we illustrate its effectiveness for discovering the Proximal-Structure and Rank-Proximal-Structure. Our novel approach relies on a non-smooth convex optimization task that uncover the desired structure, and, interestingly, its gradient at the optimal point corresponds to the desired proximal structure. We rigorously analyze the convergence rate of our algorithm, demonstrating linear convergence for sparse cases and logarithmic convergence for non-sparse cases. Moreover, our results are supported by extensive numerical experiments, showcasing the efficacy of our algorithm even in the presence of noise. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. Additionally, its low-cost and custom-built feature makes it an ideal device for schools and universities, enabling students to participate in hands-on research in astrophysics. Moreover, its high sensitivity enables detection of exoplanets orbiting closest to the host star, a capability that can significantly enhance our understanding of exoplanet formation and development. Lastly, its custom-built nature means that the limitations can be tailored to meet specific requirements, a characteristic we believe to be particularly beneficial for the educational community. This research is thus a pivotal moment in the progression of optical technology, marking the shift from computation to on-device processing and execution. Moreover, the findings prove that photonic technology can effectively revolutionize the field of spectroscopy, opening up new avenues for research and rendering the technique more accessible to a broader community. Nonetheless, there remains a pressing need to further simplify the manufacturing of photonic devices, thereby reducing their cost and paving the way for widespread practical applications of photonic technology in astronomy. Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible technology for road inspection,
its adoption has been primarily limited to Japanese manufacturers. Our research
aims to address the needs of local authorities by developing an advanced yet
affordable solution for road damage detection. Our proposed method leverages
modern deep learning techniques using the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and
Transfer Learning (TT), incorporating pre-trained models to optimize performance. 
Evaluation on three data sets reveals that our approach excels at detecting
damage, achieving success rates of 97.60%, 95.20%, and 93.60% respectively. 
Notably, our results demonstrate that modern architectures can effectively
contribute to cost-effective automated road damage evaluation without requiring
specialized hardware, making it suitable for widespread adoption. Our research
encourages local authorities to utilize automated road damage evaluation, thus
enabling more efficient and productive municipal operations. Our source code is
available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/gauthierghar/DeepRoad.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Furthermore, it integrates multiple correspondences to enable the learning of both the imitation policy and the domain-specific action mapping.  Demonstrations of the method's effectiveness are provided through successful imitations in two challenging domain generalization scenarios involving simulation-based training, and the method is shown to surpass current performance benchmarks.  The code and corresponding data can be accessed via https://github.com/alexrame/ImitationWithoutEnv-Embeddings.  A supporting project page is available at https://www.alexrame.com/iwae/.  The work was presented at the International Conference on Learning, Augmented and Mixed Reality 2020.  The paper received the DLR Award for outstanding contribution to the conference. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was influenced by magnetic effects in a cosmological setting with existing magnetic fields. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. To represent the protostars and their magnetic field structures, we utilized a stiff equation of state approach instead of the conventional sink particle technique. Ten years after the initial protostar formation, we observed an amplification in magnetic field strength from picogauss to kilogauss in the region around protostars, resulting in separation of secondary protostars in all our simulations regardless of initial field strength. We found that a significant decline in the merging rate of secondary protostars occurred when the initial magnetic field strength exceeded 1 picogauss. This shift led to a mass range for pre-sink particles in a range between 0.1 to 40 solar masses. In scenarios where the initial field strength is extremely low, even massive (above 10 solar masses) secondary protostars can still merge due to viscous effects in a high alpha_SS value environment. However, under such an alpha_SS regime, we notice that pre-sink particles in a range between 0.1 to 0.9 solar masses are produced as a result of magnetic wind stripping. In a cosmological setting, we see that Population III stars typically have a high mass range, extending from 100 to 10,000 solar masses. This is a direct result of the accretion process either from magnetic or viscous effects in a high alpha_SS value environment, resulting in a lack of low-mass (below 10 solar masses) secondary protostars in a highly amplifying magnetic field situation. This leads to a prediction that the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars should be modified to reflect this change. Additionally, we see that low-mass (below 10 solar masses) secondary protostars can still form in a low alpha_SS value environment with an extremely low initial field strength. This leads to a range of possible initial mass functions of the first (Population III) stars depending on magnetic effects and accretion processes, implying significant uncertainties in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars based on cosmological simulations alone.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Further investigation is necessary to confirm these findings' validity and examine the extent to which they apply to diverse populations within the criminal justice system.  The data also suggests mental health treatment's impact on reducing future crime may be attributed to treating less severe disorders more effectively than more severe ones.  More research into the characteristics of offenders who benefit from treatment and the role that severity of mental health disorders plays in determining effectiveness is necessary.  Additionally, the data suggests that utilizing probationary terms that incorporate mental health treatment may serve as a more effective and cost-efficient method of reducing future crime than incarceration alone.  This effect appears to be consistent across various groups as evidenced by the lack of significant interactions between treatment status and different demographic characteristics.  An individual-level financial analysis indicates that providing mental health treatment as part of probationary terms could cover the initial treatment expenses and lead to significant savings on law enforcement and court costs throughout the life of the offender.  Further examination into the potential for reduced future crime by incarceration is necessary to confirm these findings' general applicability and validity.  A primary limitation of this research involves its reliance on a single state's data which may experience a selection bias due to variations in crime rates and incarceration rates across different states. This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and decision tree ensemble methods. At its core lies the optimization of a Bayesian decision criterion, where the goal is to minimize the likelihood of observing anomalous data given the observed series. By applying the Bayesian Normal Approximation and maximizing the posterior distribution using the message passing algorithm, time series segments can be mapped to hidden states, which are then classified via a decision tree based classifier. Our method performs consistently well across multiple metrics, including classification metrics and measures of prediction uncertainty. Furthermore, the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art error rates when compared to established methods of anomaly detection, such as One-Class SVM and AutoEncoders, across multiple benchmark datasets. Additionally, the study highlights the advantages of using time series segments, rather than fixed-length windows, to improve detection accuracy and robustness. The associated source code and Pretrained Models can be accessed via the GitHub repository https://github.com/indigozar/GenerativeLearningAlgorithm. By evaluating the system through the lens of reliability theory, the analysis shows that the uncertainty of the model's predictions can serve as a strong indicator of anomalousity. As such, the study suggests utilizing the predictive uncertainty to refine the detection of unusual patterns, yielding an overall improvement in accuracy. In particular, the method excels in the detection of unusual patterns in the consumption patterns of historical datasets, as well as in the analysis of sleep patterns recorded over extended periods of time. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. This work builds on a previous paper (Cheng, Zhang and Li, 2021). Additional information can be found in the provided thesis. Recently, Li, Cheng and Zhang (2021) developed a unified approach for estimating the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on the classical and Bayesian methods along with their GMLE and empirical Bayes estimators. This work extends their research by providing a comprehensive framework that includes key estimators and their associated methods.  It is worth noting that the primary contribution of this thesis lies in providing a flexible and extensive framework for mixed data estimation by incorporating various classical and Bayesian estimation methods. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the GMLE can be closely approximated by the empirical Bayes estimator when the sample size is large enough. This finding implies that the GMLE can be seen as an improved version of the empirical Bayes estimator, especially for large sample sizes. Consequently, the GMLE can be viewed as a powerful tool for handling mixed data estimation. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy has been developed. It determines sensitivity on an individual-data-item basis rather than relying on aggregate measurements typical in traditional differential privacy approaches. By doing so, OSDP is more adaptable to scenarios where collecting total utility measurements for each data item is feasible and computationally efficient. Furthermore, OSDP is suitable for applications that require releasing detailed datasets or training accurate machine learning models. This paper presents an algorithmic framework for implementing OSDP from a general perspective and applies it to specific scenarios such as publishing count data and training linear regression models, achieving the highest possible data utility while maintaining dependable data privacy. An experimental analysis using real-world datasets reveals that OSDP is capable of providing more accurate data than Delimited Differential Privacy, the current state-of-the-art approach, across various metrics such as mean squared error, cross-validated classification, and total publication utility. Notably, OSDP achieves this by introducing new privacy parameters that reflect an inherent trade-off between data utility and privacy, offering a superior balance through an improved definition of total cross-entropy loss for private stochastic gradient descent. This new definition results in an almost identical convergence rate to its non-private counterpart, further highlighting the capabilities of OSDP. Overall, OSDP offers a versatile framework for achieving high utility while maintaining dependable data privacy. An empirical study confirms its superiority to existing approaches, demonstrating its potential to effectively address real-world data privacy challenges from a theoretical standpoint. This research presents a new approach to achieving dependable data privacy and provides a reliable solution for private machine learning in various applications. An experimental analysis confirms its effectiveness and superiority to existing methods. Furthermore, this research makes several key contributions to the state-of-the-art: achieves the highest data utility with dependable data privacy; provides an improved definition of total cross-entropy loss for private stochastic gradient descent that converges at the same rate as its non-private counterpart; and offers a versatile framework for achieving dependable data privacy with high utility. These contributions result in total publication utility up to $e^{0.00624p}$ and mean squared error up to $e^{0.00416p}$, depending on the total data items, making OSDP suitable for a wide range of applications. Ultimately, OSDP offers a versatile framework for achieving dependable data privacy with high utility, offering flexible options for various privacy and utility metrics. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust at very large scales that defy straightforward models of steady-state disk evolution. Gas and dust emissions have been detected in a significant number of systems in the molecular umbrella of the Taurus star-forming region, and one of these systems in particular, Taurus Disk (TD) 51, has been found to have two distinct substructures at 100 AU and 350 AU from its center that rotate at different speeds. Given that the gas permeates the disk, it is inevitable that certain non-uniform characteristics such as dust grains' varying sizes and efficiencies of radiative transfer would lead to localized self-absorption, creating complicated patterns that are observable. Additionally, it has been found that the gas in TD 51 is not at equilibrium, and it is likely that gas and dust are attached to a massive, unseen planet that is at a distance of approximately 14 stellar radii from the star, supporting the notion that the gas substructures are a direct result of the planet's gravitational influence. Localized cooling in the disk, possibly brought about by the presence of a planet, could further contribute to the observed gas substructures, although a planet is not the only possible explanation for the observed gas substructures as other factors such as magnetic winds and thermal instability could also play a role. Further study is needed to better understand the underlying causes of the gas substructures in TD 51 and their detectable effects on the system. Ultimately, it is hoped that a comprehensive understanding of the system will be achieved through concurrent observations and modeling of the system in the future. For example, a model based on a hydrodynamic disk model that takes into account the effects of a planet with a particular mass and distance, as well as the effects of thermal conduction, found that the gas at 100 AU is moving at the right speed, and it is predicted that certain signs of the planet will be visible in the CO and continuum data that is expected to be collected in the future. However, it is predicted that the gas at 350 AU is moving too quickly, and therefore it is suggested that other factors such as a second planet are necessary to explain the observed gas substructures at this distance from the star. On a broader scale, it is hoped that a better understanding of TD 51 will contribute to our understanding of the general evolution of the gas and dust in the gas and dust in protoplanetary disks. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint on state control cost. These'mild solutions' encompass both parts of the state and control dynamics. The existence of these solutions is shown using a unique solution path approach, by deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for solving the problem in a sequential manner. This method involves analyzing critical points of the Lagrangian and utilizing tools from non-smooth analysis, such as Clarke normals and bifurcation theory. By establishing a correspondence between solutions to the mean field game and critical points of the Lagrangian, we demonstrate that any solution can be expressed as the result of multiple successive bifurcations. Furthermore, we extend our methods to address a related problem of state constraint control. Our work is motivated by examples involving a robot arm subject to soft constraints, as well as a fluid dynamics model of a double pendulum. In particular, we study the emergence of periodic solutions, solutions constrained to lower-dimensional subspaces, and the formation of singular structures in the robot arm example, as well as the formation of shock waves in the double pendulum example.
