Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar strings. Research on these objects has initially presented them as compact, filamentary formations originating within the Milky Way's bulge. However, our findings provide compelling evidence that these structures are not physically connected entities but rather individual stars that share precise spatial and kinematic characteristics. By utilizing the Extended Sky Model, a statistical model of the Galactic distribution of stars, we isolated the'stellar strings' pattern as a result of noise reduction techniques applied to the data. Our research indicates that these'stellar strings' are an artifact stemming from the application of a certain noise filtering method, specifically the Sanchez-Blazquez et al. (2018) algorithm, used to derive the line-of-sight velocity distribution of stars across the bulge region. We discovered that these'stellar strings' are merely isolated stars that exhibit coincidental spatial and kinematic connections, while their projected shapes are entirely attributed to the volume completion effect inherent in the 3D distribution of stars across the bulge. Our research highlights the necessity of adopting a coherent and consistent statistical model, encompassing all celestial objects and processes, to facilitate accurate understanding and mapping of the Milky Way's structure and composition. Additionally, our findings underscore the importance of utilizing a variety of statistical tools to validate and cross-check the results derived from the analysis of Gaia data for the purpose of mapping the Galactic distribution of stars. Despite these'stellar strings' being an artifact, their widespread discussion in scientific literature and public outreach initiatives is an example of the effectiveness of multidisciplinary collaboration and science communication in furthering our understanding of the galaxy, though in this instance, their origin remains a subject of interest in the history of science misinterpreted by the general public.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their application in real-world contexts. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into 'free' and'resource' sets. Operations associated with free states emerge naturally from the system's constraints, whereas the potential or the value embedded in the'resource' states is determined by calculating its'resource quantity'. Recent breakthroughs in the field of quantum resource theory have generated immense interest among researchers. We now have an abundance of articles and reviews, which not only provide an in-depth analysis but also an extensive scope for further investigation. This article aims to unify and extend existing knowledge in the field of quantum resource theory by systematically examining its core principles and exploring its future prospects for extensive research. We commence with the fundamental aspects, such as the unification of various quantification methods for resource states and their relation to free states. We then delve into extensible frameworks for resource exchange and interconversion, culminating in an in-depth examination of the connection between the generation of resource and the geometric structure of the involved states. Lastly, we outline future research directions while highlighting their significant potential for further investigation. We hope this comprehensive review not only demonstrates our dedication to the field but also inspires future researchers to contribute to its ongoing evolution. We also incorporate an extensive collection of over 290 figures to facilitate in-depth understanding and make the content more approachable for diverse audiences. In this revised version, we have added novel insights, updated methodologies in the field of quantum resource theory, and also incorporated the emerging concepts of classically controlled quantum operations and related applications in order to ensure the accuracy and scope of the review. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This study offers a clear glimpse at how the dynamics of a material breakdown evolve and gives us deeper understanding of the causes behind the material's length-scale breakdown. Additionally, this research shows that a floating raft made of particles can serve as an ideal test subject for analyzing the breakdown of any material. A key advantage of this model is that we can measure its breakdown patterns very precisely while also controlling the expansion of its surface of support. This feature allows us to analyze how non-affine effects, which occur on a scale much smaller than the material itself, affect the general length-scale breakdown of any material. Beyond our specific study on a particle raft, this research can be applied to understanding the breakdown of various other materials such as polymers, crystals, and even the Earth's mantle. A key difference between our test subject, the particle raft, and these other materials lies in the time range over which the breakdown occurs. While a polymer's breakdown happens within a split second and a grain boundary occurs over days, the particle raft offers us a unique middle ground. A variation of this material, made of nearly touchable blue plastic beads, can be found in our study's supplementary materials. A version of the theoretical model has also been incorporated into a mobile app available for download in our study's supplementary materials. A paper discussing our findings has been published in Physical Review X, and the source code for the simulation model, as well as the template used to create the mobile app, can be found at https://github.com/jase-jt/Breaking_a_Raft. We show that, under these assumptions, $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We use this approximation to develop a Gaussian process that converges in distribution to $Z \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ and whose mean is given by the conditional mean of $Y$ given $X$. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our findings indicate that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and in addition, we identify issues with how static model performance on temporal data is typically evaluated, and provide two solutions to address these problems. This note revisits a theorem by Raeburn and Reynolds, demonstrating that for row-finite graphs and their associated C*-algebras, strong shift equivalence is equivalent to Morita equivalence. The proof relies on interpreting graph shift equivalences as unitary equivalences of weighted graphs, and subsequently establishing a weighted graph version of a theorem by Bates and Fu, which shows that strong shift equivalences are generated by self-isometries within weighted graph algebras. Our method also provides an alternative proof of the Reynolds-Sutherland theorem. Furthermore, strong shift equivalence has been found to be the intrinsic property that characterizes Morita equivalence among product-type graph algebras, and this generalizes to'semi-Product' graph algebras with possible additional ideals related to 'half-period' graphs. In addition, the concept of strong shift equivalence gives rise to'semi-Morita' equivalence, which is distinct from Morita equivalence, as illustrated using the graph Algebras associated with the hexagonal and double hexagonal graphs. The study of strong shift equivalence and its connection to Morita equivalence offers a new area of research in graph C*-algebras. The classification of graph C*-algebras that are strong shift equivalent or Morita equivalent is an area that requires further exploration. The relationship between Morita equivalence and partial isometries is another area for further research in this field. The classification of graph C*-algebras based on partial isometry classes of their subgraphs also merits additional investigation. The study of weighted graphs and their algebras, as well as the classification of 'half-period' graph algebras, presents another significant area of research. The continued and varied set of research topics in graph C*-algebras, as well as their applications and extensions to broader C*-algebra studies, is an area that requires further contribution. The classification of graph C*-algebras, in particular, is distinct from the classification of graphs, as evident from the hexagonal and double hexagonal graphs. The partial isometry classification is also non-trivial, as illustrated by the hexagonal graph, for which there are distinct isometry classes of partial isometries and graph shift equivalences. The C*-algebra generated by a single partial isometry also does not permit unique determination from its ideal associated with 'half-period' graphs. The study of strong shift equivalence and Morita equivalence in graph C*-algebras offers a new, broader area of research in inverse symmetry of C*-algebras.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the heavy quarkonium, specifically its dissociation, under conditions of high temperature and a strong magnetic field within a $3+1$ dimensional framework, utilizing the gauge invariant approach and the relativistic quark model with confining properties. By generating the confining potential from the Polyakov loop, we have developed a comprehensive approach to investigate the heavy quarkonium in a state of thermal equilibrium and a strong magnetic field, thereby including the influence of quantum Hall effects and heavy quark decay into D and \bar{D} mesons. Our computational method involves solving the Schrödinger equation for the heavy quarkonium, considering the complex nature of the bound state wave function. Furthermore, we have computed the complex binding energies of the heavy quarkonia ($\rm{J}/\psi$ and $\psi'$) in relation to the temperature and magnetic field strength, as well as how these energies vary with the orientation of the magnetic field with respect to the heavy quark momentum. Additionally, we have calculated the in-medium mass of the $\rm{J}/\psi$ in the quantum Hall regime at $T=0$ but at a finite magnetic field, thus allowing for comparisons with the LHC data involving Pb-Pb collisions at $2.76$ TeV. Our results demonstrate the heavy quarkonium dissociation at finite temperature and a strong magnetic field, incorporating the effects of the magnetic field on the complex binding energies and in-medium masses of the heavy quarkonia, thereby allowing for six possible orientational dependencies of the complex binding energies and in-medium masses of the heavy quarkonia in the quantum Hall regime. Our results show that the heavy quarkonium dissociation at finite temperature and a strong magnetic field can be accurately understood through the quantum Hall effect, thereby providing crucial insights into the interplay between the color screening and the orbital exclusion force in the heavy quarkonium in a strong magnetic field. To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and we've tested it by asking it over 300,000 questions about 8 different topics. The results show OREO-LM does just as well as models that have been specially trained to understand the structure of knowledge graphs, and leaves other methods that don't account for knowledge graph structure in the dust. What's more, OREO-LM helps to make predictions more accurate by learning to account for questions that are hard to answer and to reduce "over-shooting" when providing multiple answer options. By taking the best of what language models and knowledge graphs have to offer, OREO-LM sets a new standard in open-domain question answering. The code and knowledge graph configuration are available on GitHub at https://github.com/allenai/oreo-lm. The project has been successfully deployed in production on AllenAI's QASPELL system (https://qaspell.ai), which answers over 100 new questions every day. As a result of our investigation, we've come up with several important questions for future research (Section 7). Finally, our effort to bring the power of knowledge graphs to language models may also be useful for other tasks beyond question answering. To this end, we've released a new dataset called KGSamples (https://github.com/allenai/kgsamples), which consists of 1 million natural language statements that can help improve the accuracy of knowledge graph-based models. The standard benchmark for open-domain question answering is based on the Natural Questions dataset, which we've also updated to reflect the changes we made to the evaluation protocol to favor more accurate answers (see the analysis in Section 5). The updated dataset and evaluation protocol, as well as the new knowledge graph samples, can be found at https://github.com/allenai/ndq_v2. The repository contains information about our data source, the open-source implementation of our method, the configuration of our experiments, and the results of our investigation, including the reasons for our choices and analysis of the performance of our technique. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders.

Incorporating our methods also reveals a novel sparsification algorithm for high dimensional expanders, maintaining its key local spectral characteristics, offering an area of independent interest. Moreover, our results apply to approximate duality, preserving the dual to a high dimensional expander when given a sub-complex. Specifically, if X has a Pach's dual form, our algorithm generates a Pach's dual for Y as well, given certain conditions on X's links' size and alpha in X's group representation. The generated Y in turn has a Pach's dual form, offering an infinite family of Pach's dual forms to group representations. In the process, our methods offer an independent interest in determining Pach's dual conditions for graph expanders, giving the tightest known result to date. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. Further research is needed to confirm this hypothesis and explore its implications for understanding galaxy evolution and interaction. Additionally, UGC 8839 presents an intriguing case of "cosmic vandalism" where a chance collision could have a lasting impact on the galaxy's future development. The possibility of such events could be key in explaining various unusual galaxy characteristics and the demise of many dwarf galaxies in isolated environments. Nonetheless, the probability of this occurrence is low, and it's unlikely that UGC 8839 will experience another collision of the same magnitude in the near future. UGC 8839 is an essential subject for ongoing and future studies of its potential companions, including a newly discovered candidate named UGC 88382, which could be part of an larger structure hosting this unique spiral galaxy. UGC 88382 is an extremely faint, compact galaxy characterized by a very low surface brightness and a fast-moving velocity, which could indicate it's an dwarf galaxy in the process of being engulfed by UGC 8839. However, this hypothesis requires further verification through ongoing observations and a detailed analysis of available archival data. The data is essential in understanding various environmental, physical, and chemical properties of this unique spiral galaxy and its newly discovered potential companion UGC 88382. The research is part of a larger project aimed at mapping the local galaxy cluster using a novel, wide-area, deep imaging survey with a total area of 550 square arcminutes and a depth of AB magnitude 27, which is based on archival observations from CFHT, HST, Chandra, and VLA radio telescopes. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that energy deposition plays in driving the atmospheric variability observed. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the temperature of the background atmosphere. It is found that GWs of specific characteristics, including horizontal scales and speeds of propagation, exhibit more intense effects in the upper atmosphere due to the presence of a sharp temperature gradient at the CW boundary. Moreover, the data indicate that GWs of $10^{2}$ to $10^{3}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$ tend to lose energy as they ascend, whereas those with larger amplitudes appear to maintain their energy. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent Vector-Meson Photoproduction observations in proton-lead collisions at the LHC are examined, including data on forward vector-meson production in collisions of lead ions with photons. This analysis also discusses theoretical models and provides assessments of the influences of resonance decays and the choice of saturation scale in theoretical models, presenting results on the vector-meson spin density matrices and multiple geometric subchannels. Lastly, the study discusses the promise of new insights into the connections between photons, nucleons, and Regge trajectories, achievable through precise measurements of vector-meson photoproduction in EP collisions at the LHC. This involves identifying key areas of inquiry, discovering opportunities for making precise measurements, and applying these to understanding elastic $\gamma p$ scattering, nucleon Regge trajectories, and the links between photons and nucleons. To create more realistic sounds, a model is proposed that generates full-specification, high-quality audio directly from video by conditioning on a frame-by-frame mask. By utilizing a waveguide-based architecture, the model is able to produce high-fidelity, unlimited duration audio in real-time, while being constrained to a limited memory footprint. A significant advantage of this model is its ability to produce high-quality speech and non-verbal sounds such as human-like chirps and animal noises without being trained on actual audio data. When evaluated against other existing models, it is demonstrated that the generated sounds are more realistic and meet industry standards for quality, with a significant improvement in quality when the length of the input video increases from 10 frames to 64 frames. ASE is based on an architecture consisting of two components: AudioNet, a 2D convolutional neural network that learns the auditory patterns in a video, and WaveGuide, a probabilistic signal model that generates audio. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our IPO studio software. This module employs a fully recurrent neural network to maintain track history and update the internal state, allowing for the detection and monitoring of multiple objects. Validation results are presented for our approach, along with code samples and an intuitive visualization tool for recurrent networks, which facilitates the creation of highly effective models for a range of sequential data processing applications. The full source code is available on the IPO studio website at https://ipostudio.com/. A related video can be accessed via https://youtu.be/HzBayvM3Ilo. The vision for this work stems from our previous studies, including a 12-layer CNN for object recognition and a 4-layer RNN for multiple object tracking, which achieved impressive results. These studies motivated us to delve into the intricacies of recurrent neural networks, explore novel model architectures, and share our findings and the associated IPO studio software with the research community. This work aims to bridge the gap between deep learning researchers and practitioners, facilitated by the user-friendly, visual interface of IPO studio for recurrent neural networks, which streamlines the process of model construction, training, and testing. Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes the phenomenon of economic irreversibility to the interplay between infection spread and economic response patterns. By implementing a basic least-square method within a SEIR framework, researchers can quantify the thresholds above which stricter measures are necessary to combat the pandemic. Two real-world case studies, involving the COVID-19 outbreaks in China and South Korea, validate the theoretical findings and provide critical inference for decision-makers to strike a balance between pandemic control and economic sustainability. This research marks a pioneering effort in analyzing pandemic management by incorporating both epidemiological and economic perspectives, and offers a decision support tool to guide the formulation of effective policies. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, accounting for all stages and variables. DataScope's innovative approach allows it to reduce the high computational complexity associated with interacting Atlasi and ML model propagations, yielding an O(n log n) time complexity while maintaining scalability. DataScope's practical value lies in its ability to identify problematic training examples, reveal the impact of data preprocessing on model bias, and show the effectiveness of removing noisy samples during training. Experimentally, DataScope's efficient computation of the Shapley value for training examples within a complete machine learning pipeline has been validated. The remarkable outcome of these studies is the ability to remove up to 50% of training examples with little impact on model accuracy and fairness. This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices. Our research focuses on a fundamental question: how constraints on these matrices' eigenvalues influence their representability in projective space. This inquiry holds significant relevance in the fields of combinatorics, algebraic and topological statistics, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We introduce a novel combinatorial model that formalizes the concept of randomness for discrete algebraic models, which serves as the basis for a broad generalization of the Fourier decay theorem. This achievement is linked to the classical Bernstein inequality through a generalized Fourier decay theorem. We then apply this result to derive an inequality related to multivariate Hermite polynomials, which holds significant implications for algebraic and topological statistics. Our model of randomness is further utilized to establish the extremal symmetry of the Hilbert polynomial's fiber. This enables us to prove a generalized version of the Horn conjecture. Lastly, we explore the relationship between the determinant and Lorentzian polynomials under various constraint conditions on the eigenvalues of matrices in projective space, which involves the application of the Fourier method and a duality of intersection theory and Fourier approximation. This analysis holds significant importance for enumerative algebraic geometry due to its connection to the Jones polynomial and the topology of real solutions. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a novel geometric interpolation method, which enables the reconstruction of a continuous polynomial invariant from its discrete equivalent. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Furthermore, we expand upon a previous theorem established by Badan-Cortazar and Pascual-Ldezma by introducing more stringent conditions on the domain $\Omega_0$ and deriving a distinct approach to prove it. Our approach focuses on utilizing weighted integrability of eigenfunctions, both inside and outside the domain, to derive key inequalities and boundary estimates. Ultimately, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the first eigenvalue and obtain precise estimates for large $\beta$ and small $r$, as well as combining these results to investigate the interplay between $\beta$ and $r$. Notably, our analysis shows that the behavior of the eigenvalue often depends on whether $r$ is large or small, highlighting the significance of the Robin parameter $\beta$. Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between taut foliations and tight contact structures, this theory's rejection also means that tight contact structures in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a range limitation for their Euler classes, which is found to be between -12 and 0. Recently, David Jacobson discovered a new class of tight contact structures that were previously unknown and found that their Euler classes span the entire range from -18 to 0. Concurrently, researcher Mike Sullivan found another new class with Euler classes between -18 and -13. Collectively, these findings expand our understanding of the Euler classes for tight contact structures in hyperbolic 3-manifolds by showing that they can take any value within the range from -18 to 0. Researchers later found that the Euler classes can even be non-integral, which was previously unknown. Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and eight major stock market indices, including the S&P 500. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities between cryptocurrencies and reference assets, exceeding statistical significance levels in later years of our study, with some exceptions in 2016. Thirdly, our findings from the applied copula models reveal that the relationships between daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies and their reference assets have become more stable and symmetric over time, whereas the magnitude of total losses and gains in the cryptocurrency market remains greater than in more established financial systems. To further assess the reliability of our study, we employed 12 additional indices, including the MSCI Emerging Markets index and commodity futures, as well as conducting robust tests on the results, sharing code online to promote transparency and encourage replication studies. Our research confirms the growing stability of cryptocurrencies as a class, with some exceptions among individual assets. In 2016, the price fluctuations of cryptocurrencies exceeded those of reference assets, yet an analysis of daily returns in US dollars in later years indicates steady progress toward stability. The findings of this study can be viewed as temporal evidence for the growing reliability of cryptocurrencies as a class, reinforcing theories of convergence in the realm of currency and financial asset design. Cryptocurrencies' steady progress toward stability is pivotal in the development of digital currencies, showcasing their potential as trustworthy mediums of exchange. The code used for this study can be accessed online at https://github.com/ crypto-economics-gathering/2016-2020_cryptocurrencies_stability_time_warping. Additionally, the data behind the findings of this paper can be found at https://github.com/ crypto-economics-gathering/2016-2020_cryptocurrencies_stability_time_warping_data. For information on replicating the study, please see Section 6, "Replication Information," in the main paper

Additionally, we note that large deviation solutions of the KPZ equation can be represented through a nonlinear spectral problem. Lastly, we outline a possible extension of our methods to late time periods of the KPZ equation. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. These approximations lead to various approaches: using Stokes parameters, a uniform approximation; leveraging auto- LIABILITY operators, a Liouville-Green approximation; and applying WKB boundary conditions, a connection formula. Similarly, the principal and quasi-parallel approximations emerge when only the latter factor is considered. When the wave envelope's slow variation is at an incritical level, these approximations combine into a double-well potential singular phase solution, analogous to the Penetration, Non-Penetration or Intermediate Watering solutions observed in similar problems. Similar solutions for the more complex combination of factors include a double-well potential singular phase solution with a saddle-point connection to a modified Airy function solution, corresponding to an imaginary wave number representing exponential decay. Applying this theory to a specific geophysical example - a Bénard-Rayleigh dynamical system - the intermediate watering solution matches numerical simulations, whereas a modified Airy function solution matches both the simulations and an earlier, weaker evidence for such a solution. However, both this solution and the other extreme penetration and non-penetration solutions are found to diverge when the strain parameter is large. Instead, either a Stokes or Liouville-Green solution with a quasi-parallel approximation provides a more accurate description in these situations. Ultimately, a sparse reconstruction-based classifier determines the presence of defects within the given fabric image. To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. Our method demonstrates real-world efficacy through successful navigation in diverse environments, including unseen indoor spaces and continuous real-world settings. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our model shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can merge at high redshifts, potentially resulting in the formation of the 2.9 M_\\odot black hole detected in GW190521. Our model shows that 10-50% of nuclear star clusters host a Population III binary remnant and that these clusters have the potential to form the initially light black holes that go on to form supermassive black holes. These black holes can merge at cosmological timescales to form the 5 M_\\odot black holes seen in LIGO-O3_GXB-931. Our findings also show that these light black holes can form the second component of a system with a more massive black hole in a binary system, resulting in a merger event similar to that of GW190521 but with a lighter initial black hole. Our model predicts that 25-90% of nuclear star clusters can host a light black hole system such as this in a binary and that these events occur at z=2-6 with a rate of 0.1-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3, excluding those related to a massive black hole formation process. The implementation of this method would provide distribution system operators with enhanced monitoring capabilities and support data-driven diagnostic functions for smart devices. Most importantly, our method can be implemented without substantial infrastructure adjustments, and the addition of smart monitoring systems can be performed in conjunction with existing deployment plans. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our results show that the original games' reward schemes led to unfair advantages, with strategies built around game mechanics rather than genuine problem-solving skills.
To address this issue, we replaced the original rewards with more natural and moderate ones, creating a more challenging and genuine assessment of AI capabilities. 
Ultimately, the improved dataset and results serve as a foundation for advanced testing of AI capabilities in text-based games and encourage further advancements in robust, high-performance simulators.

A key concept in robot learning is mimicking familiar motion patterns, commonly seen in human behavior. To achieve this, robots utilize their full potential by controlling joint velocities that form an ellipsoidal shape, mapping to Cartesian motion as expected by a teacher. This study proposes an efficient method for teaching a robot the desired motion by specifying key positions along this ellipsoidal path, transforming the complex control issue into a simpler linear problem. Furthermore, the system can predict and adjust for minor discrepancies between the actual and intended motion, accounting for slight variation errors. To implement this, we introduce the concept of Manupat, an interactive tool allowing a human instructor to specify viable joint velocities that can be easily translated to Cartesian velocities, while providing real-time feedback through a simulated robot model. Manupat facilitates seamless teaching of novel tasks to robots by combining intuitive human input with accurate robotic modeling, thereby enhancing the accuracy of inferred joint velocities. A notable benefit is the system's ability to compensate for common errors in user input, ensuring effective robot learning. This approach was validated through a series of experiments, achieving impressive results where a mock robot was controlled with high precision, straight from Manupat. Specifically, our calculations showed an average reduction of 81.6% in the difference between planned and actual motion, across all tested samples. Ultimately, Manupat provides an easy-to-use, powerful tool for teaching robots the desired motion, paving the way for more efficient robot learning and paving the way for precise robotic control. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. car accidents, falls), yielding a high volume of raw video footage. After analyzing the rotation of objects within each video, accurate 3D pose annotations can be applied without necessitating multi-view geometry calculations often required for structured data. The proposed method leverages pose tracking and rotation estimation techniques to generate accurate annotations. Our approach demonstrates strong results on the newly developed ObjectPSN dataset for single-view 3D pose estimation, surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, the method demonstrates robustness on object categories lacking sufficient training footage by leveraging the tracked pose path to accommodate occlusions and misidentifications. Lastly, the method proves capable of estimating poses from unlabelled 'in-the-wild' video footage, demonstrating its practicality for real-world applications. Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, distinguishing between rejection, adoption, and neutral positions. To achieve this, a comprehensive Twitter dataset was created, containing over 2 million tweets, and the results demonstrate the framework's superiority over existing approaches, achieving a 90.43% accuracy rate. Furthermore, application scenarios reveal that neural networks and attitude consistency can be effectively applied to other domains, such as stances on vaccine efficacy, as evidenced by a 88.31% accuracy rate, thereby enhancing attorney-client communication and compliance with health regulations. Most importantly, a straightforward method to counteract the spread of misinformation has been implemented, demonstrating a 60% decrease in the propagation of one particularly pervasive COVID-19 vaccine misinformation on Twitter. Experiments confirm the significance of both social media features and application-dependent attributes in determining stances toward COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, underscoring the necessity of incorporating both social media propaganda analysis and attribute-based sentiment analysis to comprehend attitude adoption or rejection. This framework may serve as a model for detecting the dissemination of other health-related misinformation. Based on the insights gained, two potential counter-measures to mitigate the spread of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation have been proposed. First, a transition from a deficit-based to a surplus-based strategy for combating misinformation is advocated, focusing on promoting verified information rather than solely refuting misinformation. Second, initiatives to promote critical thinking and media literacy among social media users are being spearheaded in an effort to foster a healthier online environment and a more informed public. Finally, the design of a novel orientation-based surrogate loss function, called Attitude Clean Surrogate Loss (ACS), is presented. This loss function aims to remove attitude artifacts from the target variable in machine learning models, thereby allowing the generalization of attitudes across different domains while also maintaining a clean target variable for prediction tasks. Several experiments confirm the effectiveness of ACS in distinguishing stances toward COVID-19 vaccine misinformation and efficacy, as well as stances on vaccine efficacy and efficacy, despite minimal co-occurrence of these two topics on Twitter, with an accuracy rate of 86.19% for the latter classification task. This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and presents an innovative algorithm to identify vulnerability dissemination paths and scope. By conducting a comprehensive empirical study on Cargo's ecosystem, this research investigates vulnerability traits, propagation extent, and factors influencing vulnerability dissemination, revealing that Cargo's security vulnerabilities primarily stem from memory-related issues. Notably, 18% of libraries still harbor vulnerabilities even after updating to the latest version, while 19.78% of Cargo's ecosystem versions are affected by propagated vulnerabilities. This study's findings offer actionable insights for Cargo administrators, developers, and library owners to enhance ecosystem security and presents new concepts for bolstering Cargo's overall security posture. Furthermore, this research's methods serve as a point of departure for exploring vulnerability dissemination within other package ecosystems. In addition, this research's findings can be used to develop a recommendation system to facilitate more effective ecosystem governance. By analyzing vulnerability characteristics, this research suggests potential remediation tactics for Cargo's ecosystem, including encouraging developers to update to the latest versions of vulnerable libraries (especially those with high version counts) and prioritizing library maintenance for popular libraries exhibiting memory-related issues. To minimize vulnerability propagation, this research proposes increasing the version compatibility of Cargo components and implementing security policies that block usage of specific libraries with memory-related issues. Based on the results of this study, this research recommends performing regular checks on Cargo components and conducting more extensive security assessments to identify and address potential security vulnerabilities. Additionally, this research suggests developing training programs and implementing better security communication practices across the Cargo ecosystem to raise awareness of security governance and promote best practices in software development. Ultimately, this research emphasizes the necessity of adopting a comprehensive, ecosystem-wide security approach to bolster Cargo's security posture. To facilitate reproducibility, this research's methods, data, and findings have been made available on GitHub at the link provided. In accordance with Cargo's policies, this research only demonstrates the potential vulnerability propagation within the Cargo ecosystem rather than actually inducing vulnerabilities in libraries used within the ecosystem. This research seeks to explore vulnerability propagation within other package ecosystems and identify effective ecosystem governance strategies through a systematic examination of Cargo's security posture. Accurate quantitative determination of cosmic ray particle interactions is crucial to fine-tuning the model for further upgrades, including the inclusion of new particles and forces, with a special focus on connections between particle physics and cosmology. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively. A strong defense mechanism can slow down the model's accuracy decline, yet our proposed method still manages to evade it with a high success rate. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Atteno/Concept-Trojan.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size highlights the potential diversity of internal structures in terrestrial planets. By combining precise star abundances, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, our study advances understanding of terrestrial exoplanet interior structures, which are pivotal in grasping planetary evolution and dynamics. These findings have significant implications for missions like the James Webb Space Telescope, which will be observing the atmospheres of many transiting terrestrial planets in the coming years. Our analysis will guide these observations by suggesting which ones might be most comparable to the atmosphere of Earth. Furthermore, based on our internal structure models, we suggest potential targets for future radial velocity monitoring or future missions equipped with a coronagraph, which should prioritise planets with smaller differences between their planetary mass and the mass of the star, particularly those with masses lower than 1.5 times the mass of the Sun. Our analysis also includes new predictions for the magnetic field for each of the 13 stars in our sample, which is discussed in more detail in a companion paper. Overall, our study highlights the significant progress that can be made in understanding exoplanet interiors and diversity by combining precise stellar abundance analysis, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, which is essential for future high-resolution observational experiments on Earth and in space. In the long term, this is likely to contribute to the advancement of multiple astrobiological and planetary missions. Additionally, our study marks the first instance of a multi-observational effort that incorporates precise stellar abundance analysis, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, as well as the first simulation of terrestrial exoplanet interior structures and diversity. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN. The findings suggest that incorporating an attention mechanism with a deep learning architecture is an effective strategy for enhancing wireless localization accuracy in complex environments. The model's generalizability is demonstrated by testing it with unseen scenarios and training datasets with limited numbers of transfer cases. The attention mechanism is shown to focus on the most significant echoes for localization, thereby yielding a higher level of generalized performance with less training data needed. The proposed approach achieves higher localization accuracy in both scenarios, demonstrating an improvement of nearly 0.1 degrees for a limited dataset and about 0.3 degrees for an extended dataset, surpassing the conventional DNN method. Moreover, the attention maps show that the network has learned to prioritize non-line-of-sight echoes, specifically those related to human activity and background objects, suggesting that the attention mechanism can focus on pertinent signals for wireless localization tasks. The railway environments in which the model's effectiveness is assessed include the line between Munich and Vicq in Germany, outside a building in Vicq, and along a line connecting Berlin and Podszuhna in Germany. The line between Munich and Vicq, Berlin and Podszuhna, and Vicq and Podszuhna spans approximately 250, 100, and 50 kilometers. The model's ability to generalize is further demonstrated by testing it in other railway environments, as shown in Figure 11. When evaluating the model's performance in environments outside of railway scenarios, it achieves an average localization error of approximately 1.5 degrees for a 68 percent confidence interval. Despite its effectiveness, the proposed approach struggles with noise-intensive channels. In order to mitigate this limitation, the researchers suggest combining existing channel quality metrics with attention-based CSI to prevent the network from specializing in disturbance signals. This hybrid approach generalizes the potential of DNNs in wireless localization tasks and could potentially be applied to other machine learning techniques. Furthermore, the researchers discovered that the attention mechanism can focus on system disturbances to a limited degree

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI. Although initially designed to supplement COPASI, ShinyCOPASI has become a valuable resource for web-based biochemical network analysis and simulation. Furthermore, its modular structure and open-source code facilitate modifications and enhancements, making it possible to integrate other simulation tools for more comprehensive comparison and analysis. As a result, ShinyCOPASI has been utilized in multiple scientific studies. Additionally, based on its success, we developed other web-based versions for SBMLtools and SBMLvisualizer. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Although significant progress has been made in classification and regression tasks, no universal solution exists for solving this problem across different types of inference. Moreover, existing methods often rely on costly approximations to estimate uncertainties, leading to computationally burdensome processes, making them unsuitable for real-time applications involving high-data throughput. This study introduces a novel framework known as FAINN, for facilitating accurate inference with neural networks in various tasks, including classification, regression, and density estimation, while providing explicit error bars valid for both large and small data sets. FAINN represents a novel approach to hybrid uncertainty modeling, combining robust model approximations with refined error estimation. This framework's design ensures that error estimates can be computed quickly, even at high data throughput rates, making it ideal for real-time applications. FAINN's utility is verified through experiments on numerous problems, including classification, regression, and density estimation, where its error estimates demonstrate remarkable agreement with rigorous Monte-Carlo estimates, at both small and large data sizes. Furthermore, FAINN's error estimates prove informative for understanding various data-driven inference problems, including the role of data quantity, model specifications, optimization techniques, hyperparameters, and data quality, in contributing to uncertainty. This study's findings provide valuable generalizable insights into the role of uncertainty within neural network-based inference, at both small and large data scales. Ultimately, FAINN represents a potent solution for neural network-based inference, empirical law-establishing, and physical problem-solving with high data throughput rates, at rates comparable to those achieved with precise Monte-Carlo methods. FAINN's code is available online for reproduction purposes. Its recently released update on GitHub now supports inference with neural networks in various domains, including physics, engineering, and chemistry, in problems involving classification, regression, and density estimation with real and synthetic data sets. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP. Although inexact GMRES policy iteration assures convergence to the optimal policy, its complexity becomes computationally intensive for more than 10000 states. In response, a globally convergent version of inexact GMRES policy iteration was developed, which offers a 4.7 times speedup compared to inexact GMRES policy iteration on 10000-states MDPs while guaranteeing the existence of an optimal policy. Furthermore, two starting-point adaptation strategies were proposed, reducing the computational burden of both inexact GMRES policy iteration and its globally convergent variant by 2.2 times. In addition, a globally convergent variant of inexact Newton policy iteration was devised, assuring the existence of an optimal policy and offering a 2.2 times speedup compared to inexact GMRES policy iteration on 10000-states MDPs. These algorithms demonstrate the efficiency of inexact iteration methods for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees. Inspired by their success, inexact Newton method was also applied to large-scale nonsmooth optimization problems such as the linearly constrained nonsmooth optimization problem. This led to the development of a globally convergent variant of inexact Newton projectional methods, guaranteeing the existence of an optimal solution and assuring its convergence from any initial point with an arbitrary initial rate. This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to concentrate sampling efforts and then applying a specialized method to generate probability distributions for model parameters at those points. Ultimately, likelihood-based estimations are calculated at the chosen points. A proposed framework integrates these components to deliver a comprehensive solution. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy successfully mitigates the costly nature of simulator-based modeling, yielding accurate and efficient parameter estimations. Additionally, the selected points are marked with high predictive values. We anticipate this framework to be particularly useful in various fields where simulators play a crucial role. Furthermore, our study aligns with current trends in handling expensive optimization problems. We hope this work to be inspiring for future studies, and we will continue to develop new techniques to address this broad issue. A promising area for further research involves exploring other optimizers that could also benefit from our proposed framework. We intend to explore this direction in a future study. Another potential area for research is delving into the theoretical underpinnings of our proposed solver. We plan to develop a comprehensive theoretical explanation in a future study. Lastly, while our current study focused on probabilistic investigations, we plan to extend this study to uncertain hydrological modeling in the future. We will delve into the principles of modeling under uncertainty and how it compares to probabilistic investigations, then we will investigate various techniques for solving inverse problems in this domain. We will compare and explore new techniques in a future study. We will keep working on developing new techniques to address this broad issue, and we hope our study will encourage others to join in this endeavor. For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited increased yield of low-energy particles, combined with elevated rates of rare occurrences like three particles, relative to proton-proton collisions. This study offers the first evidence of parton cascade dynamics affecting jet fragmentation in collisions of large nuclei. Moreover, the observation that parton cascade dynamics become evident at lower energy (φ ∼ 1) in collisions of a lead nucleus with a large rapidity expansion, indicates that the collective cascade dynamics of particles can persist at rapidities exceeding that of 1 in collisions involving a large rapidity expansion. This discovery has far-reaching implications for understanding rapidity limitations of collective phenomena in collisions involving a large rapidity expansion. Based on theoretical models, it is estimated that the collective cascade dynamics of particles can survive beyond a rapidity of 5, in collisions involving a large rapidity expansion. Moreover, the observation that the rapidity at which collective cascade dynamics of particles can survive is much lower in collisions involving a large rapidity expansion, in comparison to collisions involving a large impact parameter. This discovery has far-reaching implications for understanding rapidity limitations of collective phenomena in collisions involving a large impact parameter. Based on theoretical models, it is estimated that the collective cascade dynamics of particles can survive up to a rapidity of 2, in collisions involving a large impact parameter. In summary, this study offers the first evidence of parton cascade dynamics affecting jet fragmentation in collisions of a large nucleus with a large impact parameter, in addition to a large rapidity expansion, at a lower rapidity than expected. Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts. Several key results can be derived from this solution, including an explicit expression for the hyperbolic analog of Apéry's original gamma function evaluation. This in turn enables the evaluation of hyperbolic Apéry binomial series and their basic summation counterparts. Furthermore, we establish a general formula for the hyperbolic analog of inverse binomial series of arbitrary degree, thereby providing an expressible formula for their standard version as well. Lastly, we investigate the behavior of all four types of hyperbolic Apéry binomial series in the limit as n approaches infinity. This research received partial motivation from a specific problem posed by Apéry himself in a 2017 paper. Additionally, our study found direct applications in the context of Feynman integrals, as exemplified by a specific example involving the master Ward scalar model. The key Feynman integral in question can be evaluated exactly using the standard version of Apéry's constant. Finally, we document several additional combinatorial identities related to division of the interval [0,1] that found no direct connection to Feynman integrals but rather served as the origin for many of our results. This is particularly evident for the alternating central version of Apéry-type inverse binomial series, where an explicit, combinatorial expression is presented equivalent to the level eight multiple zeta values it relates to, thereby offering an alternative to Feynman integral motivation for this series. The object's luminosity and coloration are most similar to that of ultra-cool stars, whereas its spectral type is better represented by late-type brown dwarfs. The object is one of the most unusual among ultra-cool stars and brown dwarfs. Further study of ultra-cool dwarfs is required to better understand the object's morphology and temperature distribution. We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching. The Chebyshev approximation maintains a high degree of accuracy for PDFs and DPDs through a low-order interpolation scheme, validating the results at the NNLO level with a relative error less than 1%. The Chebyshev DPDF is further applied to determine the double parton distribution for various processes such as $pp \to pp ZZ$ and $pp \to pp t\bar{t} t\bar{t}$ at the LHC. The calculations involve the evolution of doubled DPDFs up to $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2}$) and utilization of the saturation model to account for intrinsic parton saturation in the initial state, yielding suppressed cross-sections due to intrinsic saturation effects. The study reveals an impressive sensitivity to PDFs, emphasizing the need for further refinement. The corresponding code for DDINTERP and DDPINT evolution is available online for public use. The Chebyshev methods offer a practical solution for solving DDP evolution problems, empowering researchers to determine the impact of intrinsic saturation on double parton double DPDFs at the LHC. The investigated processes, $pp \to pp ZZ$ and $pp \to pp t\bar{t} t\bar{t}$, show expected sensitivities to PDFs. This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. It has been determined that the symmetries exhibited in this work encompass all non-trivial type II quantum subgroups of the specified categories, except for four exceptional instances which can be identified as specific quantum group analogues of the following four exceptional Lie algebras: $G_{2}$, $F_{4}$, $E_{6}$, and $D_{8}$. In the subsequent paper, we will utilize these classification results to derive the braided module categorization for the type II quantum subgroups of the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. This mathematical framework is based on the bosonic type II quantum group analogues of the free boson algebras, developed by Kauffman and Saleem.
