The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field. An interesting correlation exists between this solution and the first component of a Jack polynomial, as both share similar properties. Consequently, this connection gives rise to a distinctive solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, although unconventional, still holds significance. By comparing the approximate solution with the exact solution of the Fisher-KPP equation, which is known to be a smooth, analytic function, a surprising finding emerges. Both solutions share the same set of invariant manifolds, which are situated at the lowest and highest points of the given domain. An essential distinction arises, however, as the approximate solution's smoothness is only present up to the initial time and is non-smooth afterwards, in contrast to the exact solution, which maintains smoothness across all times. Notably, a similar behaviour of non-smoothness near the origin is observed in solutions to the parabolic Ginzburg-Landau equation, although the investigated solution exhibits an even more extreme form of non-smoothness. A crucial question remains whether a smooth solution to the Fisher-KPP equation actually exists or not. An attempt is made to provide an answer by assuming that a smooth solution does exist and proving, under this assumption, the existence of a smooth, analytic solution to a modified nonlinear equation, which is known to be well-posed. An essential distinction arises, however, as the proposed analytical solution fails to reach the boundary of the given domain, thus not being able to capture the solution behaviour near the origin. An alternative approach is proposed, where the unknown function is extended into the whole space by imposing continuous time and space smoothness on the solution, which results in a celebrated theorem by Nash in favour of smooth solution existence for compacts. An attempt is made to extend this approach to the whole space by using the finite dimensional approximations technique, which, however, faces the problem of selecting a suitable finite dimensional space that is capable of capturing the solution behaviour near the origin. This work addresses the UbiComp 2019 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction method is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy and performance in the challenge evaluation simulation with an average Levensthein Distance of 8, its overall efficiency and real-time capabilities still require improvement. One potential remedy is to replace the hybrid model with a fully Deep Neural Network for a more compact structure. Another suggestion involves incorporating more robust feature engineering to further enhance its robustness and adaptability. By integrating these techniques, the hope is to attain higher accuracy and reduce errors, and also achieve real-time performance capable of processing a flow of incoming images in real-time. To verify the feasibility of real-time processing, a simple Python application utilizing OpenCV is developed to display the recognition results in video streams in real-time with a minimum processing delay of around 2-3 frames per second. In theory, this should enable processing a flow of around 25 images per second. One possible area for further improvement is to refine the segmentation of the handwritten mathematical expressions into individual characters based on a more advanced method such as graph partitioning to achieve higher accuracy in single-character classification. Another suggestion involves using a more advanced technique such as Reinforcement Learning to select the most relevant features for classification, perhaps through a method like Feature Augmentation or saliency analysis, in an effort to further optimize the accuracy of the system. In conclusion, the proposed approach achieves an acceptable level of accuracy but still requires further refinement, and exploring other techniques and methods of feature engineering could lead to improved results in the future. Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functionalities for simulating data, testing models, verifying predictions, evaluating model performance, and making predictions on unseen data. Through a case study and a tutorial, this package demonstrates its capabilities by estimating species abundance in two distinct bird habitats: eastern USA's bird population and a forest ecosystem in New Hampshire, thereby providing a practical approach to address data inaccuracies and spatial relationships even for extensive datasets. Results demonstrate the accuracy of spOccupancy models due to their ability to effectively simplify complex spatial relationships, thereby reducing type I error rates and predicting species distribution with high precision. A comprehensive spOccupancy package documentation and relevant resources are available online for reference. A tutorial is also available to guide users in using this package effectively for practical applications. spOccupancy can be downloaded from CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=spOccupancy, and its source code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/mdobson/spOccupancy. A bug forum is also provided for users to submit questions or report any encountered issues. A Neo4j database is used to store results, especially for the New Hampshire forest ecosystem study, which allows users to visualize and evaluate model performance efficiently. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network has yielded an improved low-dimensional representation of SNe Ia. The middle layer's latent space variances for 16 SNe Ia spectra via visualization have distinguished explosions of differing Hubble types. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our model can generate spectral time series data which agrees with observations and mimics the overall spectral shape and intrinsic variability of SNe Ia, using pre-trained weights and a limited number of parameters. The reconstructed latent space is also informative about explosion parameters such as synthetic light curves and blackbody temperatures. The model's probabilistic output and ability to generate new spectra will aid in analyzing upcoming large datasets and planning follow-up spectroscopic observations for the next generation of SNe Ia experiments. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the size of the interaction group. Our findings indicate that this approach can predict the critical transmission rate more accurately than pair-based models and disclose how group size affects the emergence of sudden epidemic outbreaks. Furthermore, our models suggest that group meetings potentially contributed to the rapid spread of major pandemics, including the Black Death and the COVID-19 pandemic. Consequently, our study highlights the significance of group meetings in shaping the course of epidemic history and points to their importance in controlling future outbreaks. For example, our results suggest that imposing a 10-person gathering limit could have prevented over 50% of new cases in North America during the initial stage of the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study offers a framework for using hypergraphs to model infectious disease spread in networks and provides concrete examples of the impact of group meetings on public health. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified different rotational speed patterns, including differential rotation, which is further analyzed in relation to the Rossby number. This paper explores the rotational properties of solar-type stars across various stages of evolution, utilizing 3D simulations that model circular rotational migration. Specifically, it highlights how stars with higher Rossby numbers (Ng > 5) maintain nearly uniform coatings on their poles. Conversely, those with lower Rossby numbers (Ng < 5) exhibit rotational diffusion that affects their thermal interior and causes gradual changes in their rotational velocity. These simulations also predict the rotational characteristics of solar-type stars up to 10 billion years of age and provide theoretical foundations for the gyrochronology law. Furthermore, 3D modeling allows for the creation of synthetic observations that can be compared to actual data, focusing on rotational velocities and surface temperatures of moderately aged (500 Myars) and older (12.5 Myars) stars. Overall, these findings provide essential insights into the rotational properties of solar-type stars. They can be used to develop specific predictions about differential rotation and radial flow for nearly main-sequence stars, as well as about the overall rotational migration of these stars from the pre-main sequence to the late main sequence. These predictions can also be applied to solar-type stars that have not yet reached the main sequence or are in the post-main sequence stages of evolution. The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own set of thread operations and verify that the program's behavior conforms to established invariants during execution. By leveraging this mechanism, a series of fundamental thread operations have been defined, including access to structured data, which was previously difficult to verify with McMini. As a result, this mechanism has the potential to greatly expand the range of applications that can be effectively checked using McMini. In addition to its capabilities, efforts have been made to analyze the model checker's performance and determine the characteristics of programs that can be efficiently checked with limited memory. Ultimately, this has led to the development of StreamMcmini, a streamlined variant of Mcmini, which is suited for verifying data access in continuous, self-timing programs. The effectiveness of this tool has been demonstrated through its successful verification of the standard POSIX thread library, specifically for operations related to memory allocation and data blocking. The model checker's performance has also been evaluated while verifying real-world programs under various temporal constraints. The research behind this effort has produced two key performance metrics that can help guide the development of multi-threaded code with a focus on race-free design. Firstly, the minimum practical cycle size has been identified as a crucial factor, which represents the minimum number of execution cycles above which further optimizations become ineffective in reducing the model checker's memory footprint. Secondly, a relationship has been established between the maximum 0-cycles ratio and the model checker's performance, which indicates that programs with a higher ratio can be efficiently checked with little to no memory reduction. StreamMcmini has been shown to provide improved results relative to Mcmini for its supported thread operations, which include heap data access, mutex locking, and semaphore operations. The model checker's performance has been observed to be within the practical limit for a wide range of programs, which includes the testing of the POSIX thread library with various data access patterns. We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a constant rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. Specifically, we've identified three key attributes of AReLU that contribute to its effectiveness: 1) bivariate dependence between input features and attentions, 2) attenuation of non-biased inputs, and 3) biasing of attentions. Our experimental results demonstrate that utilizing AReLU, along with a corresponding attention mechanism, enhances the performance of our system by 14% when evaluating artificial alterations of speaker identity and by 17% when assessing speech synthesis-modeled artifacts. Our findings also reveal that AReLU's biased attentions constitute the primary contributor to its improved performance. Furthermore, we've successfully validated a transfer of our system to a real-world application, specifically a remote authentication system utilizing voice, which confirms the versatility of our approach. Valuable insights into how to effectively integrate attentive activation functions into speech processing systems, particularly those requiring artificial intelligence, are offered by our research. Additionally, we've made our codebase and model weights available to the public to facilitate future studies. Namely, we've released the follow-up repository, known as BasherNet, which can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/imdevkarush/BasherNet. Our primary hope is that this resource will inspire future research to surpass our current achievements. Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and the feasibility of the reheating process following inflation, often in conjunction with cosmic strings which provide unique observational signatures.  A comprehensive review of the developments in supergravity cosmology, focusing on inflation and related phenomena, including dark matter and non-thermal dark energy, strings, and black holes, is presented here.  Some promising avenues for further research, such as the connection between inflation and the axion sector, the constraints on inflationary models by recent observations, and the role of the KKLT construction in supergravity, are discussed.  A brief overview of alternative approaches to supergravity, such as the effective field theory of point-defect branes and the 6D supergravity, is also provided.  A woodcut of Albert Einstein is included in the introduction, while a brief introduction to general relativity and supersymmetry, including the benefits of the supergravity approach, appears in an appendix along with a list of abundant references. Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission. As a result, this research discovers a notable distinction between the coherence functions of photon pairs created before and after reflection, revealing a new aspect of nonreciprocity. This difference in coherence functions was quantified by measuring the relative coherence and finding a considerable ratio of greater to lesser coherence values. This ratio was measured at $10^2$ and demonstrated to be adjustable based on system design. This nonreciprocity of coherence functions presents an opportunity for enhanced data encoding in photon pair correlation experiments while simultaneously maintaining a strong signal for quantum optics research and communication. Furthermore, this work lays a foundation for developing various photonic circuits, transforming the field of quantum optics and communicating with coherence through the use of nonreciprocal optical systems. \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09238}{arXiv:2205.09238} \cite{Cheng_2022}

This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, our approach may be adapted for investigating other types of materials. This work illustrates the potential of SNOM in localizing loss mechanisms in quantum circuits and highlights its promise for advancing near-zero-loss quantum hardware. SNOM also holds potential for evaluating other material properties relevant to quantum technology. Additionally, our work indicates that an improvement of two orders of magnitude in Q-factor for specific resonators is achievable, bringing us closer to realizing this goal. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of quantum devices with enhanced coherence, thereby advancing the pursuit of practical quantum computation. Notably, our near-field terahertz investigations allow for the distinction between localized and widespread loss mechanisms, empowering us to design quantum circuits with minimal losses. This differentiates our approach from existing microwave investigations, which struggle to distinguish between systematic and statistical losses. In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be more likely than initially assumed. As a result, strategies based on the theory of adverse selection, which posits that higher-quality traders maintain lower levels of market participation, may be more pertinent to the interaction between CTA and SRT traders. Additionally, the research highlighted several key characteristics that effective SRTs display in order to boost CTA performance, including the ability to enter markets during volatility peaks and exit markets during periods of calmer market conditions. Ultimately, the study's findings suggest that the conventional view of SRTs as parasitic entities is misguided and that their impact on CTA success can be highly beneficial when certain conditions are met. Hence, efforts to develop both groups of traders in research and real-world environments are equally crucial. Moreover, further analysis is required to determine whether these models can provide a more accurate representation of market dynamics than existing theories. Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches have been developed for more precise identification. In this research, the mechanisms of dynamic and adaptive protocol detection in widely used open-source network monitoring tools are examined. Our investigation on HTTP showcases that all evaluated methods are susceptible to evasion tactics, posing significant risks to real-world network surveillance operations. Furthermore, this study reveals that a primary challenge of distinguishing between application protocols remains unresolved in two of the three monitored systems analyzed. To inform enhanced detection methods, this research emphasizes the importance of transparent and unambiguous protocol identification in network surveillance. Moreover, insights from this research can be applied to other application protocols to strengthen their detection mechanisms and foster methodological advancements in the field of network surveillance. Our research sheds light on the pitfalls of relying on automatic and adaptive protocol identification, and we advocate for a more cautious and transparent approach to meet the demands of real-time network surveillance operations. In addition to presenting our original findings, this research introduces a novel approach using HTTP request bodies in protocol identification and introduces 'h3c', a lightweight and versatile tool for evaluating HTTP protocol variants. h3c can aid in manually categorizing HTTP protocol variants, enhance operational efficiency, and reduce errors associated with automatic detection. As a secondary contribution, this research examines the performance of the three monitored systems in handling known and unknown HTTP requests. Our analysis in this study highlights the difficulties of distinguishing between application protocols during the initial stages of connection establishment and when encountering unknown HTTP requests. To facilitate future research, this investigation provides permanent URLs for mirroring the collection of 81,712 known HTTP and 88,114 unknown HTTP samples used in this study. These samples can be accessed via the CCHF II mirror or our research's GitHub repository, accessible at https://github.com/cyderwulf/CCHF_II. To promote methodological transparency, the URL for the snapshot of known HTTP instances is also listed as cyderwulf/cchf-ii-snapshot. To aid researchers in evaluating the performance of their new detection mechanisms, this study maintains an update of the most recent and frequent HTTP attacks and benign scenarios listed at https://github.com/cyderwulf/CCHF_II. To foster collaboration, this research invites researchers to contribute to this collection, accessible at https://github.com/cyderwulf

Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom. The minimal magnetic dissipation in our structure allows for fast operation at frequencies comparable to electron-based technologies. The observed magnon trapping could serve as the basis for manipulating magnons with unprecedented precision, thereby enhancing magnon-based computing and other magnon-based devices. A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. In response, we suggest a unified system addressing the associated issues during federated learning. Our system is evaluated in two distinct settings - 1) when users conceal the new class labels, and 2) when users disclose this information, whereupon we simulate user data representations by comparing class similarities, and use clustering techniques to differentiate among them. Our system is capable of handling disparities among users' labels and models as well. Our framework is experimentally verified on two prominent applications: voice recognition and urban sound detection. It exhibits an average improvement in classification accuracy of around 4% on both platforms across multiple updates and different data patterns. Most notably, the benefits of our system are most pronounced in scenarios where data is particularly dispersed. Our innovations in clustering technique and model training also serve as a reliable benchmark for evaluating the efficacy of class discovery methods. Our code is openly accessible at https://github.com/inf1xr/fed-cs. Our vision is that our system will soon be utilized in various federated learning applications. Our project is part of the DeepFed2b initiative (https://deephfed2b.github.io/), where we aim to bridge the gap between theoretical advancements in federated learning and practical implementations through real-world experiments. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Importantly, our research highlights the benefits of monitoring local news to understand variations in COVID messaging and outreach efforts across different communities and demographics. Furthermore, our method can be applied to analyze other public health crises and social issues by tracking online local news to identify underrepresented perspectives and gauge the effectiveness of public health communications and related initiatives. In addition to theoretical value, our research also possesses significant practical utility, as local news data can be harnessed to develop targeted public health campaigns by understanding the influence of local media dynamics on COVID messaging. Our study ultimately contributes to the growing field of computational health by establishing a novel monitoring system to track local news online and explore their connections to COVID-related epidemiology and societal dynamics. Detailed methods and data availability can be accessed through our research paper's supplementary materials online at a dedicated repository. Our Python code is also available at a dedicated repository for reproducibility purposes. Our research strongly suggests that local news online monitoring holds great promise in understanding variations in COVID messaging and outreach efforts across different communities and demographics, and can be applied to analyze other public health crises and social issues by tracking local news to identify underrepresented perspectives and gauge the effectiveness of public health communications and related initiatives. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items from it - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items across various distributions and lengths, even when only partially informed. To investigate the broader implications of our findings, we compared our results to data from the Stanford Infant Learning Lab and found that, similarly to human children, our AI system performed better after experiencing the inflection point, even in tasks that required counting up to higher numbers. To gain a deeper understanding of this turning point, we analyzed the distribution of our AI's parameter values immediately before and after it. We found that, as our AI became more skilled in choosing the correct number 'N' consistently, its weight matrices became more complex and varied in their patterns, indicating a shift from straightforward reinforcement learning. To further verify that this turning point is unique to this particular task and not just a result of the ESBN architecture, we repeated the study with a different AI system built using a different type of network and found similar results. Based on these findings, we propose the idea that there may be an inherent 'inflection point' in the capabilities of both advanced AI systems and human children, where we can observe a sudden and profound improvement in performance after experiencing such a turning point. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in storage needs similar to or smaller than already compressed sequences while providing similar speeds to those seen in Bloom filters. These filters can be particularly useful in data processing, especially when working with data that resist compression, such as sequences of integers. A group of similar filters was also created, known as the partitioning filter family, by applying various compression algorithms to create approximate, concise, and flexible variants of the Bloom filter. A comprehensive examination was conducted of these existing filters, as well as the xor filter, to evaluate their performance and determine their applications. A key discovery from this study is that, despite considerable efforts, no group of filters can provide efficient approximate membership queries in all scenarios while also providing rapid insertion and deletion capabilities. As a result, a different approach was proposed, in which the dietzfelbinger filter, similar to the xor filter, can provide swift approximate membership queries with minimal storage needs. A key feature of this new solution is its ability to efficiently add and remove sequences, making it particularly suited for use in group sets. A comprehensive comparison was conducted of this new filter, as well as the existing partitioning family, to evaluate their strengths and weaknesses. As part of this study, a key discovery is that, while the family of partitioning filters can provide considerable storage savings, they can be less effective at providing fast approximate membership queries. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Furthermore, our results are linked to the relationship between the augmented Zariski decomposition and the Hartshorne--Lehn Minkowski sum decomposition, and we reveal a significant difference between their applications in projective varieties and K\"ahler manifolds. We introduce specific examples to highlight limitations and complexity of our findings. Lastly, we propose two unresolved conjectures based on our preliminary analysis. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. A comprehensive computational analysis is also conducted to gauge the performance of FLVoogd across various parameter settings. As a key finding, we observe that FLVoogd's ability to block malicious submissions grows with the compute resources allocated to each round, which indicates that cost-efficient client processing can be a crucial factor in the success of this federated learning protocol. This empirical validation not only showcases the viability of FLVoogd but also highlights its potential as a secure and robust foundation for federated learning. We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied intelligence advancements in autonomous driving, by benchmarking the progress in applied autonomy. The Deepracer challenge proved to be complex, especially when translating skills from simulated to real-world settings, so we implemented a two-pronged approach to bridge the domain gap in observation spaces by applying canny edge detection and image cropping techniques. By leveraging a behavioral cloning method using the MLP-MIXER optimization technique, we achieved robust performance despite control noise. Furthermore, our model demonstrated a remarkable runtime efficiency of 2-3 milliseconds on modern CPU architectures, showcasing its real-world applicability. Throughout the development process, we thoroughly tested drift detection and correction strategies to ensure consistency in lap times and successful completion rates of up to 98.75\%, even when introducing sudden changes in environment and vehicle dynamics while in real-time. Moreover, we successfully transferred skills from the simulated to the real-world setting with a remarkable reward stability of 99\%, despite the presence of control noise and sudden changes in vehicle dynamics and environment while in real-time. The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is often impractical due to cost constraints, and sensing conditions can vary greatly. Furthermore, industrial systems may exhibit patterns that repeat over extended periods of time. This work aims to address these challenges by developing an adaptive monitoring framework capable of handling high-dimensional data and adjusting to changing sampling rates. It utilizes a time-adaptive Random Fourier Features representation to extract features from data, incorporating the Fast Whittle Estimator for spectral analysis to identify underlying cyclical patterns. By leveraging these features, the method employs a two-part classifier: the Fast Kernel Thresholding Mean Shift for initial separation and a Distance-Based One-Class Classifier for refined results. Performance was successfully demonstrated across multiple industrial systems, including temperature sensors and a gearbox, in scenarios involving varying sample rates and sensor failures. This approach yields superior performance, according to our comparison with standard methods. As a result, this monitoring technique provides reliable detection of anomalies under practical sampling conditions. Moreover, it offers actionable insights for diagnosing system issues. Finally, its semi-supervised nature enhances reliability when dealing with insufficient labeled data. In conclusion, this adaptive monitoring technique effectively addresses the difficulties of collecting high-dimensional data in industrial settings. It effectively mitigates the drawbacks of practical sampling schemes, identifies systemic issues, provides diagnosing insights, and improves monitoring performance with a sampling-independent approach. This method promotes feature learning by reducing data to its most relevant components for classification, thus preventing overfitting and sample exhaustion. Additionally, it facilitates the transfer of results across different sampling rates and systems, saving time and resources. Ultimately, this adaptive monitoring technique lays the groundwork for scalable condition monitoring applications. It achieves this by adapting to various sampling schemes, transferring results across conditions, and enhancing diagnosing insights with a sampling-independent approach. This approach grounds feature learning in practical sampling conditions, where few samples exist and systems vary in their behavior. As a result, this method trains on the most relevant features for each condition, where possible, to prevent overfitting and sample exhaustion. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our comprehensive evaluation across three diverse document types confirms that selective labeling is a feasible and effective solution for scaling the labeling of complex documents, resulting in only a minimal decline in model performance when compared to full annotation. Furthermore, our active learning method identifies model errors with greater precision, labeling a significantly smaller subset of instances compared to random sampling. The benefits of selective labeling can be implemented without altering the model's architecture, making it a versatile solution for the annotation of visually complex documents. Our methodology is now available through an open-source repository, enabling the replication of our findings. In contrast to full annotation, which necessitates the manual segmentation and highlighting of each document's layout and textual content, our proposed method streamlines the labeling process to a single, straightforward task: confirming or rejecting the model's predictions on partially annotated documents. Convolutional Neural Networks have significant practical value due to their high predictive accuracy, but they require substantial time and resources to train. Researchers have found ways to accelerate this process, but usually at a cost of decreased accuracy. Our click-based method, ClickTrain, offers a balance between speed and accuracy by training a CNN to make initial predictions quickly, using only a few clicks. ClickTrain works by leveraging two key insights. Firstly, many CNN predictions are unnecessary because the model can safely assume the user doesn't click on them, allowing it to be pruned. Secondly, the model can be accurately refined by adjusting the weights based on the user's clicks in a larger network. In testing, ClickTrain reduced the dependency on inaccurate predictions by 94.7% and significantly decreased the training time for pruning and fine-tuning, especially when combined with data augmentation. Ranging from 3 to 38 times faster than traditional methods, ClickTrain strikes a great balance between accuracy and speed. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the simple superconformal quantum mechanics models. The resolution of the hyper-Kahler cone is assumed to have a regular structure with a fixed point of actions for the resolving group, allowing an interpretation of this model within a geometric framework. In particular, an absence of non-trivial BPS states is observed at the action value that corresponds to the fixed point of the resolving group. The presence of BPS states begins at a next level of the resolution, corresponding to actions in a specified range. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characteristics, exploring its spectral variations across different wavelengths and temporal resolutions, utilizing high-resolution time-coded spectra derived from the Hubble Space Telescope's STIS instrument. By combining the observed spectra with an empirical model of atmospheric dispersion, we determine the most likely candidates to contribute to Nereid's spectral complexity. The results suggest that the spectral behavior can be attributed to the interaction of three primary components: volcanic ash particles adhering to a power-law size distribution, aqueous aerosols, and a persistent thin haze. According to our calculations, the parameters of the power-law distribution of ash particles provide the most accurate fit to the observed spectral data at 2830 Angstroms, corresponding to a particle size of 0.73 micrometers and an optical depth of 0.45. Furthermore, we determine the optical characteristics of aqueous aerosols and a thin haze spanning the UV, visible, and near-infrared spectrums. Our analysis also compares the observed optical depths of aerosols to different types of planetary ring systems, concluding that Nereid's aerosols exhibit similarities to those of Saturn's G-rings but could also be comparable to those of Uranus and Neptune. Additionally, we outline a future observational strategy to better comprehend the spectral complexity of Nereid, emphasizing the necessity of high-resolution spectroscopy and precise temporal resolutions. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our general method can be applied to various learning problems beyond the special case of bandits, and a novel optimistically-pessimistic Bayesian deep neural network is developed for solving the dynamic treatment regime problem. Our results show that this new approach not only eliminates the need to set the pessimism degree, but it also provides improved performance over traditional Bayesian methods in both simple and complex scenarios, and often matches the results of state-of-the-art offline learning methods when they succeed. Our optimistically-pessimistic approach is general and can be used with any Bayesian learning method by applying a similar credible set transformation technique. By combining the optimistically-pessimistic approach with a new efficient learning technique, our research allows online learning problems with continuous actions and a special case of bandits to be solved efficiently. Several of our approaches are tested successfully across various contexts, including a medical study and simulated experiments, achieving superior results over current best practices with offline data. Our most effective method consists of a simple and practical approach called O2INFO, which may be used in real-world scenarios. Our research is complemented by eight additional models, which are part of a larger open-source library called BMT, which includes various other approaches for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes using offline data. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances. 

This study has been accepted for publication in an upcoming publication titled "Innovations in multivariate statistical modelling: navigating theoretical and multidisciplinary domains," part of Springer Emerging Topics in Statistics and Biostatistics, edited by Ferreira, J., Bekker, A., Arashi, M., and Chen, D. 

Key approaches studied involve the multivariate normal mixture model, the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances, a hierarchical model based on the spatial autologistic model of species distribution, and a spatial point process model clustering species locations. To evaluate these methods, we utilized two types of data: a small set of simulated data and a larger dataset of 112 species from the South African Cape floral region. Clustering models were fitted using a combination of the Bayesian information criterion and a extended Bayesian approach incorporating the relative Bayesian variance penalty. Results from our simulations show the latently segmented mixture model offers the best fit compared to the other models examined. When applying this model to the Cape species data, we identified six distinct species groups, some of which were linked to geographically confined areas. These results align with existing research and highlight the importance of multivariate statistical methods in species clustering and biotic element identification. Our analysis also sheds light on the distribution patterns of these species groups, some of which were linked to geographically confined areas.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was applied in conjunction with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and our overall ranking was 27th out of 65 participants. We present an analysis of our approach and results, as well as a brief reflection on the performance of our methods against a diverse set of texts. Ultimately, our experience detecting abusive content has provided valuable insights for future applications of machine learning in social media-based tasks. Additionally, our code is available for others to access at their convenience. \cite{umiu_ling_2019} provides more information about our approach.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials based on their unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, an efficient and flexible numerical algorithm is developed using the finite element method to facilitate reconstructions of images affected by these complex factors. Numerical test results are presented to demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method under various challenging conditions. Specifically, two realistic scenarios are simulated: a cargo container filled with hazardous materials and a piece of artificial bone tissue affected by radiation. In both cases, high-quality images of regions of interest are produced, revealing previously unseen details such as different types of hazardous materials and a damaged piece of bone affected by radiation. This research offers a practical and accurate image reconstruction method suitable for real-world CT applications. In particular, it has potential applications in the detection of hazardous materials and the diagnosis of bone diseases affected by radiation. As a result, more accurate predictions of region of interest properties are possible. In addition, 3D color images can be produced that accurately represents the color distribution in internal structures, further enhancing the detection of hazardous materials and the diagnosis of bone diseases. This is achieved by using a material property mapping function that assigns attributes to reconstructed density and spectral properties based on attenuation and energy sorting. As a consequence, more relevant and efficient image reconstruction methods can be designed by focusing on region of interest properties, which can lead to significant time savings. In particular, a proposed variational reconstruction method is developed for detecting two types of hazardous materials and a piece of bone affected by radiation. In each case, an optimized parameter selection approach is employed to determine the minimum required signal strength for accurate image reconstruction. In addition, some practical issues related to X-ray sources and image reconstruction are addressed by proposing constraints on reconstruction parameters to ensure physical feasibility. Specifically, it is shown that accurate image reconstruction can be achieved even at relatively low signal strength by applying a proposed bounded MOSEK

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. Additionally, it investigates the compactness of other related operators such as multiplication and Fejer multipliers, establishing connections between compactness and properties of the domain's boundary. Key factors influencing compactness include the presence of analytic peaks, convexity defects, and non-trivial ends within the domain. Ultimately, it turns to the Bergman space of the projective plane, where compactness of specific operators is linked to properties of its exceptional set. Ultimately, it addresses the question of determining which domains result in non-compact multiplication or Fejer multipliers. The findings provide partial answers to long-standing questions proposed by Shema in 2002 and Fejer in 1933, respectively. The work also reveals an interesting contrast to compactness results identified earlier for the unit disc and the bidisc. Interestingly, the compactness of a Fejer multiplier on the bidisc depends on its symbol's behavior at its analytic compactification, yet this dependence does not translate to the projective plane. The conclusions resonate with earlier discoveries on compactness of operators within other spaces such as the de Bravoa-Lewy spaces and the Kobayashi-de Saxce spaces. Finally, the study compactness of specific operators within the Bergman space of the curve of Klein, effectively closing the operators on compact sets case for this specific domain. The methods employed in this research derive from combinations and extensions of previous approaches, such as the use of first order PDEs, Dirichlet-Neumann operators, transform techniques, proximal analysis and the investigation of properties in compact sets and exceptional sets. The techniques used to establish compactness of multiplication and Fejer multipliers prove to be powerful and versatile tools in the broader operator theory context. The methods of this study also yield insights into the properties and behaviour of other essential entities in this field, such as the Dirichlet-Neumann operators, shift operators, the exceptional sets, compact sets and the invariant metrics. The methods used to establish compactness of specific operators within certain spaces such as the curve of Klein, effectively provide a solution to a long standing question proposed by Shema in 2002. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  Ultimately, DynaSOAr's combined memory allocator and data layout capabilities make it possible to achieve near Peak Memory Bandwidth (PMB) of 1.1 and 1.2 double-precision floating-point operations per byte for our tested solvers, thus nearing the theoretical maximum limit.  In addition to DynaSOAr, we also introduced two new high-performance GPU algorithms for partial-spectral solvers by leveraging a direct transpose approach and transforming $n \times n$ matrix operations over transposed matrices, resulting in high-speed direct transpose of large memory blocks and significant performance improvements of up to 4 times for our test cases.  Both the DynaSOAr framework and our new high-performance GPU algorithms for partial-spectral solvers are now publicly available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/uwhigham/DynaSOAr.  Our work on SMMO parallelism, as embodied by DynaSOAr, indicates a promising new path for high-speed GPU programming that is both accessible and efficient for a broad range of computational biology applications. A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying mathematical model developed in this research accounts for strained and deformed straw tube walls by integrating elasticity and charge collection equations. The computational model simulated a strained straw tube subjected to internal pressure and mechanical stress, yielding Poisson's ratio and Young's modulus of the monolithic straw wall. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in real-world scenarios. We formulate the Maximum Marginal Probability (MARmax) problem, which identifies the maximum probability that a decision function's optimal properties remain intact, even with small changes in its environment. Our method involves analyzing the compact perturbation set of the function space, restricting the space to decision functions with pre-defined characteristics, and calculating the cross-dimension between relevant function sets. With these elements, we develop an efficient algorithm for computing the MARmax at any desired level of precision, using specialized numerical methods for function category analysis and compact perturbation calculations. We apply our approach to decision functions in both real and imaginary domains, depending on their input variables and decision rules, and showcase their computation in typical dimensional structures. For instance, decision functions with a product-based structure or a geometric progression over finite sets can be computed efficiently. Our framework is versatile and applicable to diverse function categories, including those out of standard forms, as long as they can be adequately restricted. With our computational tool, these functions can be analyzed and their general behavior understood. A statistical test based on the MARmax concept is also developed, allowing for the evaluation of decision functions' robustness across different samples and categories. This application is essential for various decision functions, especially those used in medical diagnostics, where limited data is available and situations can be challenging to classify. With our approach and computational tool, the robustness of these functions can be assessed and their performance under different conditions compared. These functions include those with multiple feature inputs, decision rules involving combinations of these features, and functions defined through linear combinations of critical parameters, either integer or fractional. Our method is sufficiently versatile, covering functions with multiple input variables and intricate structures. A corresponding software package is available for computation and data analysis. Our study is the first to calculate the Maximum Marginal Probability (MARmax) for decision functions, enabling their thorough analysis under uncertainty. For specific function categories, our lower and upper bounds for MARmax provide precise estimates of robustness, while general bounds can be computationally demanding. Based on these bounds, function robustness can be assessed, but exact robustness may require more intricate calculations. Our computational tool allows the exploration of function categories, but computing the MARmax for all functions in these categories can be extremely challenging. These issues highlight the need for simplified decision making strategies and more efficient computation methods

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The work utilizes a 180nm CMOS process to build and test a prototype of the temperature sensor, which achieves a superior thermal resolution of less than 0.029degC, and accurately measures temperatures between 0.15V and 1.1V across a vast temperature range of 170K to 300K. The integrated circuit occupies a remarkably small area of 38.3um x 39.3um, and the energy required for a single temperature reading is incredibly low at 0.2nJ. Furthermore, the design's low cost and simplicity make it an ideal solution for temperature monitoring in deeply nested tree architectures and other applications with comparable thermal hierarchies. In particular, this CMOS temperature sensor is suited for use in processors like the Intel Core i7. The design's extremely low power consumption also enables it to monitor system-level temperature, even when the processor's power management is disabled. As a result, the temperature sensor enables precise thermal modeling and accurate forecasting, and enables various advanced features like power capping and thermal comfort monitoring. Ultimately, the CMOS temperature sensor offers precision temperature monitoring with minimal overhead, and facilitates various levels of detail in thermal modeling and prediction. In this way, the temperature sensor promotes several opportunities for improvement in chip design and thermal management. In conclusion, the proposed CMOS temperature sensor offers an excellent trade-off of performance, cost, and complexity, and represents a compelling solution for accurate temperature monitoring in sophisticated systems. The temperature sensor's innovative design and exceptional features have significant potential to improve the field of thermal monitoring and prediction. Various aspects of thermal management and prediction present valuable avenues for further investigation and improvement. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this study proposes adopting multiple loss measures according to device misidentification rates, thus introducing the concept of risk in IoT device classification. Two novel approaches are developed to optimize this risk: one based on the greedy algorithm considering feature costs, and another using deep learning with customized loss functions. Both methodologies show promising outcomes in reducing the cost of accurately classifying IoT devices and minimizing the risk of misidentification. Compared to traditional methods, the proposed approaches achieve a 30% decrease in the cost of accurate classification and lower misidentification rates by at least 40%. Additionally, evaluating the financial benefits of deploying these techniques yields substantial gains, with reduced feature selection costs outweighing increased misidentification expenses when using the deep learning method. Notably, the most critical factors affecting the success of misclassification rate optimizations are the feature extraction costs of the IoT device (40% and 30% improvements, respectively) and marginally, the network traffic (10% improvement). This research lays the groundwork for developing more efficient IoT device classification algorithms through cost-effective feature extraction, highlighting the necessity of balancing feature extraction costs and accuracy. Moreover, this investigation suggests that network architects can implement cost-friendly feature extraction protocols (e.g., limiting unnecessary packet sniffing) to decrease overall costs and align them with current risk assessment practices. Finally, this study posits that assessing feature extraction costs is a crucial requirement for developing responsible and environmentally friendly IoT systems. This study explores algebraic and relational structures for Godel modal logics, specifically considering subvarieties of Godel algebras and corresponding classes of frames with ordered accessibility relations. Our investigation of these relational structures provides a means to examine intutionistic Godel modal logics, encompassing duality theory and the ability to apply techniques from classical Godel logic. We also compare our results with those for intutionistic modal logics based on classical logic. Specifically, we highlight the differences in relational structures, the presence of ordered accessibility in prelinear systems, and the behaviors of normal and weakly normal modalities. Furthermore, we identify classes of Godel algebras that underpin specific classes of frames, and demonstrate how algebraic and relational techniques can be utilized to study independence results for intutionistic Godel modal logics. This research specifically derives independence results for systems incorporating $\Box^2_\bot$ and $\Box^2_{\bot}\vee\Diamond^2$ modalities. We also outline potential avenues for further research, including applying our methods to other systems of Godel logic with modalities and exploring applications in computer science, particularly with regard to systems with nested arrays and safe recursion. Additionally, the study recommends a hybrid approach combining classical and intutionistic methods for specific tasks in Godel modal logic. Specifically, we propose that certain operations can be addressed using a classical approach, whereas other, previously uninvestigated operations can be explored using an intutionistic methodology. Our recommendation to utilize hybrid methods offers greater flexibility and accuracy in determining the complexity of operations in Godel modal logic. Finally, our research confirms that Godel modal logics can serve as strong weakening alternatives to classical modal logics for prelinear frames, thereby providing a means to 'go weaker' in certain logical operations while maintaining strong accessibility principles. This discovery is particularly evident in operations involving second-order modalities, such as $\Box^2_\bot$ and $\Box^2_{\bot}\vee\Diamond^2$, which demonstrate that Godel modal logics can serve as a form of'safe recursion' and 'nested arrays' within transfinite models of Peano arithmetic. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To illustrate the efficacy of this method, two new scale-invariant heat kernels for the Laplace-Beltrami operator on the sphere are formulated. A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a detector that gathers and measures this scattered light; and a medium that facilitates the transmission and reflection of this signal. However, the typical imaging scenario is subject to limitations and restrictions imposed by these components. For instance, sources that produce high-resolution images and cut out unnecessary light prior to reaching the subject are uncommon. Similarly, some materials may offer clear visibility into objects while providing little insight into areas at a distance from the subject, and detectors often rely on a combination of signal intensity and phase information, but the spectrum of available signals is limited to a narrow range. In an effort to overcome these restrictions, we are proposing a novel method for high-resolution image recovery through the use of a single frequency data. The 2D image is recovered via a 3D optimization problem that utilizers the data measured by a lensless computational imaging system. The 3D optimization problem is split into two separate problems into two dimensions. The results of these two problems are combined to form the final high-resolution image of the subject. The method has successfully been tested with images of USA and Europe flags and the results are presented. Moreover, we have extended this new protocol for high-resolution image recovery to work with coherent active imaging systems. The method has successfully been tested with Coherent Active Imaging System with USA flag image and the results are presented. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements was validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This study provides insight into the behavior of complex liquids under stress and may be applied to other complex fluid systems. Additionally, we outline potential avenues for further research into surface processing technologies that modify surface roughness. Due to the inherent viscoelastic properties of the materials used in this study, we also examine the implications of time-dependent effects on the development of stress hysteresis in complex liquid flows. Moreover, we have tailored an extended Maxwell model to fit our measured stress data, which reveals that the time-dependent effects that arise due to surface roughness are comparable to those seen in purely viscoelastic systems. Nonetheless, the contribution of surface roughness to stress hysteresis cannot be solely attributed to viscoelasticity, as evident from our measurements. We have also compared our findings with existing theories on the scaling of surface slippage and mean curvatures in dry foam systems, which has led to the formulation of new scaling laws for stick-slip and stationary regimes. Moreover, we estimate the size of curvature-dependent asperities on the surface, which is consistent with optical observations. This study offers a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of complex liquids under different surface roughness conditions, which holds broad applicability to other complex fluid systems.
